The project is an original, trendy, broadly appealing, user-friendly remote control, intended for all ages and an international market including Australia and America, with functional design, conceptual design, and detailed design as the design stages. The team warmed up by drawing favorite animals and describing their traits: Sarah drew a tiger and called it majestic, independent, and proud; the User Interface participant described a dog as supportive, loyal, and intuitive; the Industrial Designer’s sketch evolved from a T. rex to a pelican and then a crocodile, described as scary and strong; Marketing drew an eagle, noting independence, a free spirit, and being intrepid. The stated selling price was 25 euros, estimated in discussion at about 17 pounds; production cost was 12.50, and the profit aim was 50 million euros, presumed to be for the first year. The team discussed a universal remote’s signal loss and the need to reprogram it, the inconvenience of multiple remotes, and a simple, intuitive design with basic controls and menus for less-used functions; possible features included a mobile-phone-style LCD menu, clear pictures or symbols, larger-print display, and a flip-top screen, while cost, usability for older people, and production in lightweight moulded plastic were considerations. They agreed to work individually before meeting again in half an hour; the Industrial Designer also noted that the company presents itself as putting fashion into electronics, prompting further consideration of an attractive design that need not use metal."}

{"mom":"### Introductions, agenda, and project brief
Sarah introduced herself as the Project Manager and welcomed everyone to their first meeting. She outlined the agenda: get to know one another, complete tool training, review the project plan, and discuss ideas. She understood they had 25 minutes for this work. Sarah said the team was developing a remote control intended to be original and not already available in shops, trendy and appealing to a wide market, but not a heavy metal object, and user-friendly for everyone from children to grannies, possibly even dogs. She described three design stages: functional design, where individuals identify the product’s needs, effects, and how it will achieve them; conceptual design, covering the team’s ideas; and detailed design, determining how to put those ideas into practice.

### Animal-drawing exercise
Sarah asked the team to practise using the pens by drawing favourite animals on the whiteboard and identifying their characteristics. She drew a tiger, describing it as majestic, independent, and proud. The User Interface participant drew a sitting dog and identified three distinctive features: it is supportive and a best friend that does not discriminate, loyal, and intuitive enough to distinguish a thief from another person. The Industrial Designer said their drawing was initially intended as a T. rex, then became a pelican, and could now be a crocodile; they described it as scary and strong. Marketing drew an eagle, noting it was meant to be an eagle and describing eagles as independent, free-spirited, flying around doing their own thing, birds of prey, and intrepid. The group briefly mistook the drawing for a seagull and joked about whether eagles were good at golf; the Industrial Designer clarified the intended animal was an eagle.

### Financial targets and market
Sarah said the proposed selling price was 25 euros and asked for its approximate value in pounds. Participants estimated about £17, with the User Interface participant mentioning an exchange rate of roughly 1.4 euros to the pound; Sarah called £17 expensive. The Industrial Designer said remote controls currently on the market cost about £20 and that the team would need to buy one. Marketing suggested that later pricing should consider whether undercutting competitors would make the product look like a cheap option. Sarah said the production cost was €12.50, about half the selling price, and stated a profit aim of €50 million. When Marketing asked whether this target was for the first year, Sarah said yes, although she qualified that she presumed so. Marketing confirmed the market range was international and that the product should be accessible and usable by all age groups, not specifically aimed at businesses. Sarah agreed that the target was broad and named Australia and America as examples of international markets; she said different languages did not need to be a key design concern.

### Remote-control experience and usability ideas
Sarah asked about the team’s experience with remote controls. She described having three video devices, a TV, and an amplifier, and using a universal remote that had to be programmed for each device. It kept losing its signals, requiring reprogramming, and Sarah thought its low price might have contributed to the problem. She nevertheless valued being able to use one control rather than having six controls in front of her. Marketing said their experience was mainly with the remote supplied with a device, using basic functions such as power, volume, and channels; they wanted the product to be usable by someone who did not know how to programme equipment. Sarah agreed those were the main functions and said she disliked controls with many tiny buttons and labels that made it hard to find functions such as teletext. Marketing also found unfamiliar symbols difficult to understand, and the User Interface participant proposed simplifying the symbols.

Sarah suggested keeping the main functions on the front, with a section or menu for additional options such as sound and recording, so the control would not look complicated at first glance. Marketing proposed borrowing the mobile-phone menu approach, with a small LCD display, and the User Interface participant agreed that a display with menus could make browsing and navigation easier, particularly if it worked like a mobile phone. Sarah raised whether this would suit older users, mentioning her grandfather, who could answer a mobile phone but would not know how to text. Marketing asked whether he could programme his remote; Sarah questioned whether older people used recording functions, while the Industrial Designer said their grandfather was better than they were at using teletext. Marketing observed that older users could remain a challenge regardless of design changes. The Industrial Designer said the controls should be self-intuitive and that pictures on newer phone menus helped make functions clear. Sarah, however, said she found Windows-based phone systems confusing and got lost while trying to use a friend’s new phone.

The Industrial Designer questioned how excellent a screen the team could provide within a €12.50 production cost and suggested keeping it to a black-and-white LCD. Marketing proposed an extra button to enlarge the text, like large-print books, even if less information appeared on screen, so older users could read it. Sarah noted that teletext already had a display-size option. Sarah also suggested a dual-function approach: basic play, volume, and programme buttons, with a menu using clear pictures and symbols for recording and other functions. Marketing proposed a flip-top remote that would reveal a larger screen. Sarah said that could affect cost; the User Interface participant suggested that a flip design might save space and make the remote look smaller rather than bulky, while recognising cost implications. Marketing added that the device did not need to be as fashionable and stylish as a mobile phone and could use lightweight, easily moulded plastic.

### Materials, appearance, and next steps
The Industrial Designer asked whether the remote needed to be fashionable, referring to the company website’s message about putting fashion into electronics. Marketing clarified that the main point was that the product did not have to use metal and said plastic would presumably be cheaper. Sarah agreed that plastic could still look smart, citing moulded Sky remotes and silver-plastic Telewest remotes as examples. Sarah then said the team had half an hour before the next meeting and would go away to work individually, then return to liaise; she expected to give another PowerPoint presentation. The group agreed to break and meet again in half an hour."}

{"summary":"Sarah, the Project Manager, opened the team’s first meeting and outlined a 25-minute agenda covering introductions, tool training, the project plan, and ideas. The team would work individually and reconvene in half an hour. The project is an original, trendy, broadly appealing, user-friendly remote control intended for all ages and an international market, including Australia and America. Sarah described functional, conceptual, and detailed design as the stages. The team warmed up by drawing favorite animals and describing their traits: Sarah drew a tiger and called it majestic, independent, and proud; the User Interface participant described a dog as supportive, loyal, and intuitive; the Industrial Designer’s drawing began as a T. rex, became a pelican, and then a crocodile, described as scary and strong; Marketing drew an eagle, noting its independence, free spirit, and intrepidity. The stated selling price was €25, estimated in discussion at about £17; production cost was €12.50, and the profit aim was €50 million, presumed to be for the first year. The team discussed universal-remote signal loss and reprogramming, the inconvenience of multiple remotes, and a simple, intuitive design with basic controls and menus for less-used functions. Possible features included a mobile-phone-style LCD menu, clear pictures or symbols, larger-print display, and a flip-top screen; cost, usability for older people, and lightweight moulded plastic were considerations. The Industrial Designer raised the company’s message about putting fashion into electronics, prompting further consideration of attractive design without requiring metal.","mom":"### Introductions, agenda, and project brief
Sarah introduced herself as the Project Manager and welcomed everyone to their first meeting. She outlined the agenda: get to know one another, complete tool training, review the project plan, and discuss ideas. Sarah understood they had 25 minutes for this work. She said the team was developing a remote control intended to be original and not already available in shops, trendy and appealing to a wide market, but not a heavy metal object, and user-friendly for everyone from children to grannies, possibly even dogs. Sarah described three design stages: functional design, where individuals identify the product’s needs, effects, and how it will achieve them; conceptual design, covering the team’s ideas; and detailed design, determining how to put those ideas into practice.

### Animal-drawing exercise
Sarah asked the team to practise using the pens by drawing favorite animals on the whiteboard and identifying their characteristics. She said she would go first and leave space for everyone else. She drew a tiger, describing it as majestic, independent, and proud. The User Interface participant drew a sitting dog and identified three distinctive features: it is supportive and a best friend that does not discriminate, loyal, and intuitive enough to distinguish a thief from another person. The Industrial Designer said their drawing was initially intended as a T. rex, then became a pelican, and could now be a crocodile; they described it as scary and strong. Marketing drew an eagle, noting it was meant to be an eagle and describing eagles as independent, free-spirited, flying around doing their own thing, birds of prey, and intrepid. The group briefly mistook the drawing for a seagull and joked about whether eagles were good at golf; the Industrial Designer clarified the intended animal was an eagle.

### Financial targets and market
Sarah said the proposed selling price was €25 and asked for its approximate value in pounds. Participants estimated about £17, with the User Interface participant mentioning an exchange rate of roughly 1.4 euros to the pound; Sarah called £17 expensive. The Industrial Designer said remote controls currently on the market cost about £20 and that they would need to buy one. Marketing suggested that later pricing should consider whether undercutting competitors would make the product look like a cheap option. Sarah said the production cost was €12.50, about half the selling price, and stated a profit aim of €50 million. When Marketing asked whether this target was for the first year, Sarah said yes, although she qualified that she presumed so. Marketing confirmed the market range was international and that the product should be accessible and usable by all age groups, not specifically aimed at businesses. Sarah agreed that the target was broad and named Australia and America as examples of international markets; she said different languages did not need to be a key design concern.

### Remote-control experience and usability ideas
Sarah asked about the team’s experience with remote controls. She described having three video devices, a TV, and an amplifier, and using a universal remote that had to be programmed for each device. It kept losing its signals, requiring reprogramming, and Sarah thought its low price might have contributed to the problem. She nevertheless valued being able to use one control rather than having six controls in front of her. Marketing said their experience was mainly with the remote supplied with a device, using basic functions such as power, volume, and channels; they wanted the product to be usable by someone who did not know how to programme equipment. Sarah agreed those were the main functions and said she disliked controls with many tiny buttons and labels that made it hard to find functions such as teletext. Marketing also found unfamiliar symbols difficult to understand, and the User Interface participant proposed simplifying the symbols.

Sarah suggested keeping the main functions on the front, with a section or menu for additional options such as sound and recording, so the control would not look complicated at first glance. Marketing proposed borrowing the mobile-phone menu approach, with a small LCD display, and the User Interface participant agreed that a display with menus could make browsing and navigation easier, particularly if it worked like a mobile phone. Sarah raised whether this would suit older users, mentioning her grandfather, who could answer a mobile phone but would not know how to text. Marketing asked whether he could programme his remote; Sarah questioned whether older people used recording functions, while the Industrial Designer said their grandfather was better than they were at using teletext. Marketing observed that older users could remain a challenge regardless of design changes. The Industrial Designer said the controls should be self-intuitive and that pictures on newer phone menus helped make functions clear. Sarah, however, said she found Windows-based phone systems confusing and got lost while trying to use a friend’s new phone.

The Industrial Designer questioned how excellent a screen the team could provide within a €12.50 production cost and suggested keeping it to a black-and-white LCD. Marketing proposed an extra button to enlarge the text, like large-print books, even if less information appeared on screen, so older users could read it. Sarah noted that teletext already had a display-size option. Sarah also suggested a dual-function approach: basic play, volume, and programme buttons, with a menu using clear pictures and symbols for recording and other functions. Marketing proposed a flip-top remote that would reveal a larger screen. Sarah said that could affect cost; the User Interface participant suggested that a flip design might save space and make the remote look smaller rather than bulky, while recognizing cost implications. Marketing added that the device did not need to be as fashionable and stylish as a mobile phone and could use lightweight, easily moulded plastic.

### Materials, appearance, and next steps
Sarah said the team had half an hour before the next meeting and that everyone would work individually, then return to liaise; she expected to give another PowerPoint presentation. The Industrial Designer asked whether the remote needed to be fashionable, referring to the company website’s message about putting fashion into electronics. Marketing clarified that the main point was that the product did not have to use metal and said plastic would presumably be cheaper. Sarah agreed that plastic could still look smart, citing moulded Sky remotes and silver-plastic Telewest remotes as examples, and said these were points the team could consider. Sarah then said, “let’s break it up there,” and said goodbye until half an hour later; the group agreed to break and meet again then." ,"actionItems":[{"id":"A1","text":"Work individually before The Industrial Designer proposed a low-cost infrared TV remote with a roughly five-metre range, a compact, easy-to-carry body, and a way to find misplaced units; the User Interface designer also favored a simple flip-top layout, with frequently used controls outside and less-used features inside. Marketing reported usability-lab research with 100 participants, male and female and aged 15 and over: 75% found current remotes ugly, 80% would pay more for a fancier-looking remote, 75% channel-hopped frequently, 50% used only 10% of the buttons, 50% were frustrated by remotes getting lost, 34% found them slow to learn, and slightly more than a quarter reported repetitive-strain concerns; younger users were more interested in an LCD and speech recognition, while interest declined among older groups. The team confirmed the revised requirements: no teletext and a TV-only control, with video functions discussed as an implication; they considered VideoPlus as a simpler alternative to entering recording dates, times, and channels, and agreed that the company image should be incorporated. Ideas included a rechargeable handset with a docking station, a low-cost beep or alarm to locate it, clear labeling and a simple manual, differentiated exterior designs while retaining the same internal engineering, and an ergonomic curved shape; the RSI question remained unresolved and was deferred for further thought. The group discussed targeting the likely purchasing market and adapting styling for different age groups and international markets, but the Project Manager favored concentrating on one core product rather than pursuing many design variants; Marketing also raised retail help for older users, while the team leaned toward telephone customer service and a particularly user-friendly manual. Marketing was asked to look into instruction manuals and related issues before the next meeting, and the meeting ended at lunchtime with an offer to send further questions by email."}

{"mom":"### Previous meeting decisions and agenda
The Project Manager said this was the team’s second meeting and that they might be somewhat disorganized. They recapped the previous meeting’s decisions: develop one universal handset for television and video equipment; make it accessible to a wide age range without excluding consumers; reflect the company’s image of fashion in electronics; keep the product uncluttered and unintimidating while balancing the budget against the desired appearance; and consider a flip-open design, a smaller control, and an electronic panel for additional features such as programming. The team planned three presentations. Marketing asked to present later, explaining that they needed access to more information, and the Industrial Designer presented first.

### Industrial design and technical concept
The Industrial Designer described the proposed control as a device that sends signals to change the state of a television or another appliance, including power, channel, and volume. They had reviewed other products for inspiration but wanted the design to stand out. Most controls use infrared, which they said was likely less costly than computer-style wireless because the control sends little information; most are battery-powered, often using AAA batteries. They questioned whether another power source could reduce bulk and said the team could decide on batteries later, considering power consumption and the amount of data transmitted. The control should be small and easy to carry, with a range of up to about five metres, suitable for ordinary television viewing but not necessarily a cinema. The proposed electronics included a power source, a chip to decode the input and convert it to infrared, and a user interface; the circuit sketch was preliminary and the Industrial Designer was unsure it would work or that the wiring shown was correct. The control would need to follow the communication method television receivers already use. Components should be low-cost to support a wide audience, while the design should be distinct enough to attract consumers. Because small controls are easy to lose, the Industrial Designer suggested exploring a way to prevent it from disappearing down the side of a sofa. Marketing said this was an important issue also identified in market research.

### User-interface concept and accessibility
The User Interface designer said their proposal developed points from the previous brainstorming session, but they needed Marketing’s feedback because they lacked marketing data. The product’s purpose was to simplify interaction with a television. They advocated a user-friendly design with commonly used functions, such as volume and channel controls, rather than a large number of complex buttons. Their concept was a flip-top control: frequently used functions would be on top, with more complex functions, such as programming favourite channels, inside. This could serve a broad audience while allowing additional features, such as a shock-proof body and appealing styling. They said research suggested people preferred user-friendly controls; some users left 30–40 percent of buttons unused after a year, so adding many functions could confuse people. They also mentioned economies of scale at a possible production volume of 50 million, which could allow more features at lower cost. Personally, they favoured a trendy flip-top design and said button softness or firmness should be considered because buttons can become hard with continuous use. Their overall recommendation was a simple, user-friendly design.

### Market research findings
Marketing reported that the company’s usability lab had observed 100 members of the public, selected to represent men and women across all age groups from 15 upwards, using remote controls. The overall finding was that users disliked current controls’ appearance and feel. Seventy-five percent found most controls ugly, and 80 percent said they would spend more for a control that looked stylish. Marketing said current controls did not fit users’ operating behaviour: 75 percent channel-hopped frequently, and 50 percent used only 10 percent of the buttons, suggesting both design and potential cost-reduction implications. The biggest reported frustrations included controls being lost in rooms, particularly slipping behind sofas; 50 percent were especially frustrated by this. Thirty-four percent said controls took too long to learn, which Marketing linked to users not bothering to learn functions beyond the small proportion of buttons they used. Slightly more than a quarter said controls contributed to repetitive strain injury, with small repeated movements potentially causing shoulder and elbow problems. Most respondents aged 35 and under wanted an LCD and speech recognition, partly to help locate a lost control. Marketing proposed, as an idea not tested in the research, that a lost control might beep periodically or flash. Interest in those features diminished among people aged 35–45 and reversed among older age groups, who were less concerned. Marketing offered to email additional research details if needed.

### Project requirements and product scope
The Project Manager stated that the revised requirements excluded teletext because consumers considered it outdated in light of the internet. The control was to be for television only, rather than a universal handset, which would reduce cost and make it easier for consumers to understand. Marketing asked whether it could programme a video recorder; the Project Manager said the requirement specified television only, although they wondered whether Sky-related functions might be included. The Industrial Designer noted that a Sky box could record directly from the television to a hard drive, and the Project Manager assumed the device would still need play, stop, and programming functions. Marketing said the team had not researched demand for combined controls, but recalled that users generally used only about 10 percent of buttons, typically basic channel-hopping and on/off functions, as well as video fast-forwarding. They added that programming video recorders was commonly regarded as difficult. The Industrial Designer cautioned that speech recognition could be expensive to incorporate and was not very reliable.

### Finding lost controls and budget considerations
The Industrial Designer suggested a key-chain-style locator that responds to a whistle with a loud sound. The Project Manager emphasized the budget limitation and preferred a cheaper option if it achieved the same purpose. They proposed placing a small device on the television so that pressing a button there would make the hidden control beep, helping the user locate it. Marketing and the other participants responded positively, and the Project Manager considered this cheaper than more elaborate alternatives.

### Corporate image, target markets, and design variations
The Project Manager said the company’s corporate image should be incorporated into the handset through a logo and fashionable, trendy styling, noting Marketing’s finding that consumers would pay more for attractive products. Marketing said further research was needed because preferences differ by age and across international markets—for example, between a trendy New Yorker and a retired South African—and that interface styling might need to vary by market. The User Interface designer asked whether the team was considering one model or five or six designs. The Industrial Designer said different exterior designs could share the same internal components and features. The Project Manager urged the team to focus on one product rather than becoming bogged down in many possibilities, while allowing the company to adjust size or features later. The Industrial Designer cited Xbox controllers: two sizes had been made because the original controller was too large for many Japanese users, who generally had smaller hands. The User Interface designer suggested that controls might be larger in the United States and smaller in Japan; the Project Manager reiterated that the team should design one product, with internal engineering remaining the same.

### Repetitive strain injury and interaction design
The Project Manager raised large rubber buttons and touch-sensitive panels as ways to make the product distinctive. They described a touch panel as requiring a thumb touch rather than a button press and potentially wearing less. The Project Manager thought this might appeal to young, trendy office workers in Japan, but said it would need clear labels so it remained understandable and unintimidating to older users. The User Interface designer suggested a touchscreen might help address repetitive-use injury. Marketing cautioned that simply moving a finger around a small screen might not adequately address repetitive strain injury, which is caused by repeated small movements, and said the issue remained unresolved and might need to be postponed to a future meeting. The Project Manager and Industrial Designer discussed speech recognition as a possible way to reduce repeated movement, but the Project Manager said it was extremely expensive. Marketing asked whether the product should initially target a younger group and expand later. The User Interface designer suggested focusing on the biggest market, including people aged 20–35. The Project Manager said the company wanted fashionable, trendy products but noted that older baby-boomer generations were more numerous; they nevertheless described the intended market as mid-range, business-class consumers. Marketing added that broad-scale marketing should avoid wasting money and should initially focus where purchasing power for this kind of product was most likely to be found.

### Television and video programming functions
The Project Manager proposed using VideoPlus, described as a five- or six-digit code printed after programme details in television guides, as an alternative to entering recording dates, times, and channels. They said the code would schedule a programme—for example, a Tuesday at ten o’clock on the seventeenth—without the user having to enter those details. The Industrial Designer said the feature had existed for a long time but was not well advertised. The Project Manager suggested raising awareness of it; the Industrial Designer noted that Sky users could select a programme and press a button to record it, or press it twice to record a whole series. The Project Manager described VideoPlus as potentially replacing separate date- and channel-entry buttons and said it could be promoted through advertising and explained simply in the instruction manual. Marketing asked whether VideoPlus was a project requirement or an additional feature; the Project Manager clarified that it was a way to reduce the number of functions and simplify programming, not a stated requirement.

### Customer support and instruction manuals
Marketing proposed that retail outlets offer help to older users who might otherwise be deterred from buying the control, similar to the support available for mobile phones. The Industrial Designer noted that mobile-phone providers have obligations because customers sign contracts, and questioned the cost of a comparable service. The Project Manager suggested that users could bring in their television and control to demonstrate a problem, but the User Interface designer thought it would be too much effort to go to a shop for help with a remote control. The Project Manager proposed a customer-service telephone number, avoiding a call-out charge or the need to walk to a high-street shop. The team agreed that the instruction manual should be as user-friendly as possible: manuals often have tiny print and many pages, discouraging people from reading them, and may end up unused in a drawer until something goes wrong. The Project Manager asked Marketing to consider instruction manuals for the next meeting, noting that people often have piles of manuals but rarely use them.

### Battery and charging concept
The Project Manager asked what type of battery mobile phones use. The Industrial Designer said mobile phones use specially made batteries supplied with a charger and suggested bundling a charger with the control. The Project Manager proposed a rechargeable battery and docking station, similar to mobile or cordless phones that sit in their chargers when not in use. The Industrial Designer agreed that this could reduce the control’s size and spare users from repeatedly buying batteries; the Project Manager said it would also be cheaper over the long run. The team accepted the rechargeable, dockable concept for consideration.

### Form, appearance, and next steps
The Project Manager said the control should not be a large box crowded with functions or an extremely tiny device, since small controls could still contribute to repetitive strain injury even if they had fewer functions. Marketing urged the team to avoid the familiar long brown rectangles with same-coloured buttons crowded across the surface. The Project Manager summarized the emerging concept as a flip-screen. The User Interface designer described a Nokia design from almost six or seven years earlier: a flat, box-like form was strenuous because the thumb had to bend upward, while a curled, slightly banana-shaped form let the thumb rest more naturally. They suggested a smooth, hand-moulded shape, with a semi-circular lower section. The Project Manager proposed exploring the company logo and incorporating a recognizable company-associated shape, such as a shell-like form that opens into the flip-top, to make the product distinctive. The User Interface designer preferred placing the logo in a corner rather than shaping the device like a shell. Marketing liked the shell concept, saying a lightweight plastic flip-top could fit comfortably in the palm and that opening it might help limit repetitive strain. Marketing also suggested a conch- or scallop-shell exterior. The Project Manager proposed interchangeable fascias or casings, with psychedelic designs for younger users and sleek alternatives. Marketing said an attractive control might be less likely to disappear down a sofa and could be kept on display as an ornament. The User Interface designer suggested developing five or six designs and choosing the most popular as the common design. As the meeting ended around lunchtime, Marketing reviewed the revised requirements: no teletext, television and by implication video, incorporation of the corporate image, and consideration of VideoPlus. The Project Manager confirmed that beeping to locate a lost control, ease of learning, and a simple instruction manual were issues to consider; they said the design should differ from existing products. The Project Manager invited further questions by email, though they joked that they might not be able to answer them."}

The Project Manager said they would go over the previous meeting’s decisions (line 10); the Industrial Designer volunteered to go first (line 30). The Industrial Designer presented a low-cost infrared remote with an approximately five-metre range and a compact, portable body, and suggested investigating a way to find misplaced units. The User Interface designer favored a simple flip-top layout, with frequently used controls outside and less-used features inside, and said they would take feedback from Marketing because they lacked marketing data. Marketing reported usability-lab research with 100 male and female participants aged 15 and over: 75% found current remotes ugly, 80% would pay more for a fancier-looking remote, 75% channel-hopped frequently, 50% used only 10% of the buttons, 50% were frustrated by remotes getting lost, 34% found them slow to learn, and slightly more than a quarter reported repetitive-strain concerns. Younger users were more interested in an LCD and speech recognition, while interest declined among older groups. The revised requirements excluded teletext and specified a TV-only control, though video functions were discussed as an implication. The team considered VideoPlus as a simpler alternative to entering recording dates, times, and channels, and agreed that the company image should be incorporated. Ideas included a rechargeable handset with a docking station, a low-cost beep or alarm to locate a lost remote, clear labeling and a simple manual, differentiated exterior designs sharing the same internal engineering, and an ergonomic curved shape. The RSI question remained unresolved and was suggested for a future meeting. The group discussed likely purchasing markets and age- and country-specific styling; the Project Manager favored focusing on one core product rather than many variants. The meeting was wrapping up at lunchtime, and the Project Manager offered to receive further questions by email.","mom":"### Previous meeting decisions and agenda
The Project Manager said this was the team’s second meeting and that they might be somewhat disorganized. They recapped the previous meeting’s decisions: develop one universal handset for television and video equipment; make it accessible to a wide age range without excluding consumers; reflect the company’s image of fashion in electronics; keep the product uncluttered and unintimidating while balancing the budget against the desired appearance; and consider a flip-open design, a smaller control, and an electronic panel for additional features such as programming. The Project Manager said they would go over what the team had decided at the previous meeting. The team planned three presentations. Marketing asked to present later, explaining that they needed access to more information, and the Industrial Designer agreed to present first.

### Industrial design and technical concept
The Industrial Designer described the proposed control as a device that sends signals to change the state of a television or another appliance, including power, channel, and volume. They had reviewed other products for inspiration but wanted the design to stand out, while acknowledging that the Industrial Designer’s focus was mainly on the inside. Most controls use infrared, which they said was likely less costly than computer-style wireless because the control sends little information; most are battery-powered, often using AAA batteries. They questioned whether another power source could reduce bulk and said the team could decide on batteries later, considering power consumption and the amount of data transmitted. The control should be small and easy to carry, with a range of up to about five metres, suitable for ordinary television viewing but not necessarily a cinema. The proposed electronics included a power source, a chip to decode the input and convert it to infrared, and a user interface; the circuit sketch was preliminary and the Industrial Designer was unsure it would work or that the wiring shown was correct. The control would need to follow the communication method television receivers already use. Components should be low-cost to support a wide audience, while the design should be distinct enough to attract consumers. Because small controls are easy to lose, the Industrial Designer suggested exploring a way to prevent it from disappearing down the side of a sofa. Marketing said this was an important issue also identified in market research.

### User-interface concept and accessibility
The User Interface designer said their proposal developed points from the previous brainstorming session, but they needed Marketing’s feedback because they lacked marketing data. The product’s purpose was to simplify interaction with a television. They advocated a user-friendly design with commonly used functions, such as volume and channel controls, rather than a large number of complex buttons. Their concept was a flip-top control: frequently used functions would be on top, with more complex functions, such as programming favourite channels, inside. This could serve a broad audience while allowing additional features, such as a shock-proof body and appealing styling. They said research suggested people preferred user-friendly controls; some users left 30–40 percent of buttons unused after a year, so adding many functions could confuse people. They also mentioned economies of scale at a possible production volume of 50 million, which could allow more features at lower cost. Personally, they favoured a trendy flip-top design and said button softness or firmness should be considered because buttons can become hard with continuous use. Their overall recommendation was a simple, user-friendly design.

### Market research findings
Marketing reported that the company’s usability lab had observed 100 members of the public, selected to represent men and women across all age groups from 15 upwards, using remote controls. The overall finding was that users disliked current controls’ appearance and feel. Seventy-five percent found most controls ugly, and 80 percent said they would spend more for a control that looked stylish. Marketing said current controls did not fit users’ operating behaviour: 75 percent channel-hopped frequently, and 50 percent used only 10 percent of the buttons, suggesting both design and potential cost-reduction implications. The biggest reported frustrations included controls being lost in rooms, particularly slipping behind sofas; 50 percent were especially frustrated by this. Thirty-four percent said controls took too long to learn, which Marketing linked to users not bothering to learn functions beyond the small proportion of buttons they used. Slightly more than a quarter said controls contributed to repetitive strain injury, with small repeated movements potentially causing shoulder and elbow problems. Most respondents aged 35 and under wanted an LCD and speech recognition, partly to help locate a lost control. Marketing proposed, as an idea not tested in the research, that a lost control might beep periodically or flash. Interest in those features diminished among people aged 35–45 and reversed among older age groups, who were less concerned. Marketing offered to email additional research details if needed.

### Project requirements and product scope
The Project Manager stated that the revised requirements excluded teletext because consumers considered it outdated in light of the internet. The control was to be for television only, rather than a universal handset, which would reduce cost and make it easier for consumers to understand. Marketing asked whether it could programme a video recorder; the Project Manager said the requirement specified television only, although they wondered whether Sky-related functions might be included. The Industrial Designer noted that a Sky box could record directly from the television to a hard drive, and the Project Manager assumed the device would still need play, stop, and programming functions. Marketing said the team had not researched demand for combined controls, but recalled that users generally used only about 10 percent of buttons, typically basic channel-hopping and on/off functions, as well as video fast-forwarding. They added that programming video recorders was commonly regarded as difficult. The Industrial Designer cautioned that speech recognition could be expensive to incorporate and was not very reliable.

### Finding lost controls and budget considerations
The Industrial Designer suggested a key-chain-style locator that responds to a whistle with a loud sound. The Project Manager emphasized the budget limitation and preferred a cheaper option if it achieved the same purpose. They proposed placing a small device on the television so that pressing a button there would make the hidden control beep, helping the user locate it. Marketing and the other participants responded positively, and the Project Manager considered this cheaper than more elaborate alternatives.

### Corporate image, target markets, and design variations
The Project Manager said the company’s corporate image should be incorporated into the handset through a logo and fashionable, trendy styling, noting Marketing’s finding that consumers would pay more for attractive products. Marketing said further research would be needed because preferences differ by age and across international markets—for example, between a trendy New Yorker and a retired South African—and that interface styling might need to vary by market. The User Interface designer asked whether the team was considering one model or five or six designs. The Industrial Designer said different exterior designs could share the same internal components and features. The Project Manager urged the team to focus on one product rather than becoming bogged down in many possibilities, while allowing the company to adjust size or features later. The Industrial Designer cited Xbox controllers: two sizes had been made because the original controller was too large for many Japanese users, who generally had smaller hands. The User Interface designer suggested that controls might be larger in the United States and smaller in Japan; the Project Manager reiterated that the team should design one product, with internal engineering remaining the same.

### Repetitive strain injury and interaction design
The Project Manager raised large rubber buttons and touch-sensitive panels as ways to make the product distinctive. They described a touch panel as requiring a thumb touch rather than a button press and potentially wearing less. The Project Manager thought this might appeal to young, trendy office workers in Japan, but said it would need clear labels so it remained understandable and unintimidating to older users. The User Interface designer suggested a touchscreen might help address repetitive-use injury. Marketing cautioned that simply moving a finger around a small screen might not adequately address repetitive strain injury, which is caused by repeated small movements, and said the issue remained unresolved and might need to be postponed to a future meeting. The Project Manager and Industrial Designer discussed speech recognition as a possible way to reduce repeated movement, but the Project Manager said it was extremely expensive. Marketing asked whether the product should initially target a younger group and expand later. The User Interface designer suggested focusing on the biggest market, including people aged 20–35. The Project Manager said the company wanted fashionable, trendy products but noted that older baby-boomer generations were more numerous; they nevertheless described the intended market as mid-range, business-class consumers. Marketing added that broad-scale marketing should avoid wasting money and should initially focus where purchasing power for this kind of product was most likely to be found.

### Television and video programming functions
The Project Manager proposed using VideoPlus, described as a five- or six-digit code printed after programme details in television guides, as an alternative to entering recording dates, times, and channels. They said the code would schedule a programme—for example, a Tuesday at ten o’clock on the seventeenth—without the user having to enter those details. The Industrial Designer said the feature had existed for a long time but was not well advertised. The Project Manager suggested raising awareness of it; the Industrial Designer noted that Sky users could select a programme and press a button to record it, or press it twice to record a whole series. The Project Manager described VideoPlus as potentially replacing separate date- and channel-entry buttons and said it could be promoted through advertising and explained simply in the instruction manual. Marketing asked whether VideoPlus was a project requirement or an additional feature; the Project Manager clarified that it was a way to reduce the number of functions and simplify programming, not a stated requirement.

### Customer support and instruction manuals
Marketing proposed that retail outlets offer help to older users who might otherwise be deterred from buying the control, similar to the support available for mobile phones, including support at high-street outlets such as Carphone Warehouse. The Industrial Designer noted that mobile-phone providers have obligations because customers sign contracts, and questioned the cost of a comparable service. The Project Manager suggested that users could bring in their television and control to demonstrate a problem, but the User Interface designer thought it would be too much effort to go to a shop for help with a remote control. The Project Manager proposed a customer-service telephone number, avoiding a call-out charge or the need to walk to a high-street shop. The team agreed that the instruction manual should be as user-friendly as possible: manuals often have tiny print and many pages, discouraging people from reading them, and may end up unused in a drawer until something goes wrong. The Project Manager asked Marketing to consider instruction manuals for the next meeting, noting that people often have piles of manuals but rarely use them.

### Battery and charging concept
The Project Manager asked what type of battery mobile phones use. The Industrial Designer said mobile phones use specially made batteries supplied with a charger and suggested bundling a charger with the control. The Project Manager proposed a rechargeable battery and docking station, similar to mobile or cordless phones that sit in their chargers when not in use. The Industrial Designer agreed that this could reduce the control’s size and spare users from repeatedly buying batteries; the Project Manager said it would also be cheaper over the long run. The team accepted the rechargeable, dockable concept for consideration.

### Form, appearance, and next steps
The Project Manager said the control should not be a large box crowded with functions or an extremely tiny device, since small controls could still contribute to repetitive strain injury even if they had fewer functions. Marketing urged the team to avoid the familiar long brown rectangles with same-coloured buttons crowded across the surface. The Project Manager summarized the emerging concept as a flip-screen. The User Interface designer described a Nokia design from almost six or seven years earlier: a flat, box-like form was strenuous because the thumb had to bend upward, while a curled, slightly banana-shaped form let the thumb rest more naturally. They suggested a smooth, hand-moulded shape, with a semi-circular lower section. The Project Manager proposed exploring the company logo and incorporating a recognizable company-associated shape, such as a shell-like form that opens into the flip-top, to make the product distinctive. The User Interface designer preferred placing the logo in a corner rather than shaping the device like a shell. Marketing liked the shell concept, saying a lightweight plastic flip-top could fit comfortably in the palm and that opening it might help limit repetitive strain. Marketing also suggested a conch- or scallop-shell exterior. The Project Manager proposed interchangeable fascias or casings, with psychedelic designs for younger users and sleek alternatives. Marketing said an attractive control might be less likely to disappear down a sofa and could be kept on display as an ornament. The User Interface designer suggested developing five or six designs and choosing the most popular as the common design. As the meeting ended around lunchtime, Marketing reviewed the revised requirements: no teletext, television and by implication video, incorporation of the corporate image, and consideration of VideoPlus. The Project Manager confirmed that beeping to locate a lost control, ease of learning, and a simple instruction manual were issues to consider; they said the design should differ from existing products. The meeting was wrapping up at lunchtime, and the Project Manager offered to receive further questions by email.","mom":"### Previous meeting decisions and agenda
The Project Manager said this was the team’s second meeting and that they might be somewhat disorganized. They recapped the previous meeting’s decisions: develop one universal handset for television and video equipment; make it accessible to a wide age range without excluding consumers; reflect the company’s image of fashion in electronics; keep the product uncluttered and unintimidating while balancing the budget against the desired appearance; and consider a flip-open design, a smaller control, and an electronic panel for additional features such as programming. The Project Manager said they would go over what the team had decided at the previous meeting. The team planned three presentations. Marketing asked to present later, explaining that they needed access to more information, and the Industrial Designer agreed to present first.

### Industrial design and technical concept
The Industrial Designer described the proposed control as a device that sends signals to change the state of a television or another appliance, including power, channel, and volume. They had reviewed other products for inspiration but wanted the design to stand out, while acknowledging that the Industrial Designer’s focus was mainly on the inside. Most controls use infrared, which they said was likely less costly than computer-style wireless because the control sends little information; most are battery-powered, often using AAA batteries. They questioned whether another power source could reduce bulk and said the team could decide on batteries later, considering power consumption and the amount of data transmitted. The control should be small and easy to carry, with a range of up to about five metres, suitable for ordinary television viewing but not necessarily a cinema. The proposed electronics included a power source, a chip to decode the input and convert it to infrared, and a user interface; the circuit sketch was preliminary and the Industrial Designer was unsure it would work or that the wiring shown was correct. The control would need to follow the communication method television receivers already use. Components should be low-cost to support a wide audience, while the design should be distinct enough to attract consumers. Because small controls are easy to lose, the Industrial Designer suggested exploring a way to prevent it from disappearing down the side of a sofa. Marketing said this was an important issue also identified in market research.

### User-interface concept and accessibility
The User Interface designer said their proposal developed points from the previous brainstorming session, but they needed Marketing’s feedback because they lacked marketing data. The product’s purpose was to simplify interaction with a television. They advocated a user-friendly design with commonly used functions, such as volume and channel controls, rather than a large number of complex buttons. Their concept was a flip-top control: frequently used functions would be on top, with more complex functions, such as programming favourite channels, inside. This could serve a broad audience while allowing additional features, such as a shock-proof body and appealing styling. They said research suggested people preferred user-friendly controls; some users left 30–40 percent of buttons unused after a year, so adding many functions could confuse people. They also mentioned economies of scale at a possible production volume of 50 million, which could allow more features at lower cost. Personally, they favoured a trendy flip-top design and said button softness or firmness should be considered because buttons can become hard with continuous use. Their overall recommendation was a simple, user-friendly design.

### Market research findings
Marketing reported that the company’s usability lab had observed 100 members of the public, selected to represent men and women across all age groups from 15 upwards, using remote controls. The overall finding was that users disliked current controls’ appearance and feel. Seventy-five percent found most controls ugly, and 80 percent said they would spend more for a control that looked stylish. Marketing said current controls did not fit users’ operating behaviour: 75 percent channel-hopped frequently, and 50 percent used only 10 percent of the buttons, suggesting both design and potential cost-reduction implications. The biggest reported frustrations included controls being lost in rooms, particularly slipping behind sofas; 50 percent were especially frustrated by this. Thirty-four percent said controls took too long to learn, which Marketing linked to users not bothering to learn functions beyond the small proportion of buttons they used. Slightly more than a quarter said controls contributed to repetitive strain injury, with small repeated movements potentially causing shoulder and elbow problems. Most respondents aged 35 and under wanted an LCD and speech recognition, partly to help locate a lost control. Marketing proposed, as an idea not tested in the research, that a lost control might beep periodically or flash. Interest in those features diminished among people aged 35–45 and reversed among older age groups, who were less concerned. Marketing offered to email additional research details if needed.

### Project requirements and product scope
The Project Manager stated that the revised requirements excluded teletext because consumers considered it outdated in light of the internet. The control was to be for television only, rather than a universal handset, which would reduce cost and make it easier for consumers to understand. Marketing asked whether it could programme a video recorder; the Project Manager said the requirement specified television only, although they wondered whether Sky-related functions might be included. The Industrial Designer noted that a Sky box could record directly from the television to a hard drive, and the Project Manager assumed the device would still need play, stop, and programming functions. Marketing said the team had not researched demand for combined controls, but recalled that users generally used only about 10 percent of buttons, typically basic channel-hopping and on/off functions, as well as video fast-forwarding. They added that programming video recorders was commonly regarded as difficult. The Industrial Designer cautioned that speech recognition could be expensive to incorporate and was not very reliable.

### Finding lost controls and budget considerations
The Industrial Designer suggested a key-chain-style locator that responds to a whistle with a loud sound. The Project Manager emphasized the budget limitation and preferred a cheaper option if it achieved the same purpose. They proposed placing a small device on the television so that pressing a button there would make the hidden control beep, helping the user locate it. Marketing and the other participants responded positively, and the Project Manager considered this cheaper than more elaborate alternatives.

### Corporate image, target markets, and design variations
The Project Manager said the company’s corporate image should be incorporated into the handset through a logo and fashionable, trendy styling, noting Marketing’s finding that consumers would pay more for attractive products. Marketing said further research would be needed because preferences differ by age and across international markets—for example, between a trendy New Yorker and a retired South African—and that interface styling might need to vary by market. The User Interface designer asked whether the team was considering one model or five or six designs. The Industrial Designer said different exterior designs could share the same internal components and features. The Project Manager urged the team to focus on one product rather than becoming bogged down in many possibilities, while allowing the company to adjust size or features later. The Industrial Designer cited Xbox controllers: two sizes had been made because the original controller was too large for many Japanese users, who generally had smaller hands. The User Interface designer suggested that controls might be larger in the United States and smaller in Japan; the Project Manager reiterated that the team should design one product, with internal engineering remaining the same.

### Repetitive strain injury and interaction design
The Project Manager raised large rubber buttons and touch-sensitive panels as ways to make the product distinctive. They described a touch panel as requiring a thumb touch rather than a button press and potentially wearing less. The Project Manager thought this might appeal to young, trendy office workers in Japan, but said it would need clear labels so it remained understandable and unintimidating to older users. The User Interface designer suggested a touchscreen might help address repetitive-use injury. Marketing cautioned that simply moving a finger around a small screen might not adequately address repetitive strain injury, which is caused by repeated small movements, and said the issue remained unresolved and might need to be postponed to a future meeting. The Project Manager and Industrial Designer discussed speech recognition as a possible way to reduce repeated movement, but the Project Manager said it was extremely expensive. Marketing asked whether the product should initially target a younger group and expand later. The User Interface designer suggested focusing on the biggest market, including people aged 20–35. The Project Manager said the company wanted fashionable, trendy products but noted that older baby-boomer generations were more numerous; they nevertheless described the intended market as mid-range, business-class consumers. Marketing added that broad-scale marketing should avoid wasting money and should initially focus where purchasing power for this kind of product was most likely to be found.

### Television and video programming functions
The Project Manager proposed using VideoPlus, described as a five- or six-digit code printed after programme details in television guides, as an alternative to entering recording dates, times, and channels. They said the code would schedule a programme—for example, a Tuesday at ten o’clock on the seventeenth—without the user having to enter those details. The Industrial Designer said the feature had existed for a long time but was not well advertised. The Project Manager suggested raising awareness of it; the Industrial Designer noted that Sky users could select a programme and press a button to record it, or press it twice to record a whole series. The Project Manager described VideoPlus as potentially replacing separate date- and channel-entry buttons and said it could be promoted through advertising and explained simply in the instruction manual. Marketing asked whether VideoPlus was a project requirement or an additional feature; the Project Manager clarified that it was a way to reduce the number of functions and simplify programming, not a stated requirement.

### Customer support and instruction manuals
Marketing proposed that retail outlets offer help to older users who might otherwise be deterred from buying the control, similar to the support available for mobile phones, including support at high-street outlets such as Carphone Warehouse. The Industrial Designer noted that mobile-phone providers have obligations because customers sign contracts, and questioned the cost of a comparable service. The Project Manager suggested that users could bring in their television and control to demonstrate a problem, but the User Interface designer thought it would be too much effort to go to a shop for help with a remote control. The Project Manager proposed a customer-service telephone number, avoiding a call-out charge or the need to walk to a high-street shop. The team agreed that the instruction manual should be as user-friendly as possible: manuals often have tiny print and many pages, discouraging people from reading them, and may end up unused in a drawer until something goes wrong. The Project Manager asked Marketing to consider instruction manuals for the next meeting, noting that people often have piles of manuals but rarely use them.

### Battery and charging concept
The Project Manager asked what type of battery mobile phones use. The Industrial Designer said mobile phones use specially made batteries supplied with a charger and suggested bundling a charger with the control. The Project Manager proposed a rechargeable battery and docking station, similar to mobile or cordless phones that sit in their chargers when not in use. The Industrial Designer agreed that this could reduce the control’s size and spare users from repeatedly buying batteries; the Project Manager said it would also be cheaper over the long run. The team accepted the rechargeable, dockable concept for consideration.

### Form, appearance, and next steps
The Project Manager said the control should not be a large box crowded with functions or an extremely tiny device, since small controls could still contribute to repetitive strain injury even if they had fewer functions. Marketing urged the team to avoid the familiar long brown rectangles with same-coloured buttons crowded across the surface. The Project Manager summarized the emerging concept as a flip-screen. The User Interface designer described a Nokia design from almost six or seven years earlier: a flat, box-like form was strenuous because the thumb had to bend upward, while a curled, slightly banana-shaped form let the thumb rest more naturally. They suggested a smooth, hand-moulded shape, with a semi-circular lower section. The Project Manager proposed exploring the company logo and incorporating a recognizable company-associated shape, such as a shell-like form that opens into the flip-top, to make the product distinctive. The User Interface designer preferred placing the logo in a corner rather than shaping the device like a shell. Marketing liked the shell concept, saying a lightweight plastic flip-top could fit comfortably in the palm and that opening it might help limit repetitive strain. Marketing also suggested a conch- or scallop-shell exterior. The Project Manager proposed interchangeable fascias or casings, with psychedelic designs for younger users and sleek alternatives. Marketing said an attractive control might be less likely to disappear down a sofa and could be kept on display as an ornament. The User Interface designer suggested developing five or six designs and choosing the most popular as the common design. As the meeting ended around lunchtime, Marketing reviewed the revised requirements: no teletext, television and by implication video, incorporation of the corporate image, and consideration of VideoPlus. The Project Manager confirmed that beeping to locate a lost control, ease of learning, and a simple instruction manual were issues to consider; they said the design should differ from existing products. The Project Manager asked Marketing to focus on instruction manuals and offered to receive any further questions by email, adding jokingly that they might not be able to answer them.","actionItems":[],"notCommitments":[{"i":222,"reason":"Fragmentary remark during the meeting’s equipment setup; no clear task or commitment is expressed."},{"i":226,"reason":"Marketing’s statement about moving the cable/equipment is an immediate setup remark, not a project commitment."}]}

{"mom":"### Meeting purpose and previous decisions
The Project Manager welcomed everyone back after lunch and said this was the conceptual design meeting, covering properties, materials, user interface, and trend-watching. The team was slightly ahead of where they had expected to be after the previous meeting, so they would review the relevant material. The Project Manager recapped the prior changes: teletext could not be used as the control for everything, the company’s image needed to be incorporated, voice recognition had previously been left out, and the team had chosen a flip design with an unconventional shape, possibly shell-like. The Industrial Designer had been asked to investigate rechargeable batteries; the team had also planned to consider a port and an alarm to help locate a lost remote. The target market was described as young business users.

### Marketing research and trends
Marketing reported that the team had conducted its usual market-research study with 100 subjects to identify important requirements for a remote control. The company, which aimed to be a forerunner in putting fashion into technology, had also consulted fashion and design advisers in Paris and Milan. Findings indicated that customers valued a fancy look and feel most, ahead of technological innovation and ease of use. Fancy appearance was twice as important as technological innovation, which was itself twice as important as ease of use; ease of use remained important but ranked third among the subjects studied. The fashion advisers had found fruit and vegetables emerging as themes for clothes, shoes, and furniture, and a trend toward spongy-feeling materials compared with the previous year. Marketing invited the design team to consider whether those trends could inform the remote’s design.

### Components and power options
The Industrial Designer said the presentation covered the design of the components and their current availability. The basic purpose was to let users press buttons to activate functions on a television, with the remote being easy to find. Some materials considered at the previous meeting were unavailable. The designer described the TA1835 chip as widely used in remote controls because it sends standard signals based on user input, and outlined battery alternatives. No rechargeable option was available among the standard components examined; AA and AAA batteries seemed too bulky. Dynamo charging would require a winding handle and take more space, and the designer considered it impractical. Solar charging was discussed, including whether artificial room light could charge it; the Project Manager stressed not wanting to limit the market, including international customers and people in basement flats. The Industrial Designer noted that solar cells would need to be placed on the case, would affect the exterior design, and could be vulnerable to drops, a concern because remotes are often thrown around more than calculators. Standard batteries were expected to be cheapest, with solar charging more expensive. The User Interface representative asked which option would be lightest and longest-lasting, noting that customers should not need to charge a remote daily like a mobile phone.

The Industrial Designer proposed kinetic charging, like that used in wristwatches: ordinary movement could generate charge stored in a small cell about the size of a watch battery. The designer said they were not sure how long the cell would last, but had never seen one run out; the Project Manager questioned whether a remote, which is mostly set down after use, would move enough compared with a watch worn all day. The designer argued that a remote is used only briefly to send a signal and that watch batteries do not run out overnight when left aside. Marketing asked whether solar charging could work alongside standard batteries, and the Industrial Designer said a dual-power arrangement might be possible, though solar cells would affect the case. The Project Manager suggested keeping an attachment or clip-on feature in mind alongside kinetic charging, as portability might reduce the chance of losing the remote. Marketing said this had not emerged from focus groups or market research and was not something customers had asked for, but agreed it could remain a secondary idea.

### Circuit boards, buttons, and standby mode
The Industrial Designer explained that most current remotes use a silicone printed circuit board. Pressing a rubber button joins contacts, connecting two chip legs; the chip translates the input into a code that is transmitted by an LED through bursts of light. The board can be made to fit the required layout, including nine buttons, and thin tracks could allow smaller switches placed close together. Another possible arrangement was an array of switches. To conserve battery life, the remote should enter standby when unused. If illuminated buttons were chosen, their lights could switch off after five or ten seconds without use.

The designer also described possible interfaces: a bare printed circuit board touched directly, rubber buttons, or a thin LCD touch display with an array of on-screen controls. An LCD could be black and white and would be flat, limiting curved design features; the printed circuit board, unlike the LCD, would have wires coming off it. The Project Manager asked how users would identify touch points on a bare board and suggested that opening a rubber exterior could reveal a more striking interior. Marketing proposed an optional stylus or small pointer, but the Industrial Designer and User Interface representative warned that it could be easily lost, irritating for frequent channel-switching, and potentially damaging to a touch surface if repeatedly jabbed. Marketing noted that users could use an ordinary pen or pencil instead. The User Interface representative asked whether the flip-top could hold separate circuits for standard buttons on top and more complex controls underneath. The Industrial Designer said this was feasible with two separate circuit boards joined by wires or cabling through the hinge.

### Case materials and replaceable covers
The Industrial Designer said plastic was the likely main case material and that wood would be impractical. Titanium would be expensive to process and, according to the designer, would constrain the case to a standard box shape; plastic allowed more curved shapes. Rubber was considered for its spongy feel, particularly for buttons, which the factory said could use material used in stress-ball manufacture and described as anti-RSI. The designer expressed uncertainty about how the claimed RSI benefit would work. The User Interface representative asked whether customers could change the cover or skin, for example from parrot green to chilli red. The designer said a replaceable titanium case would be possible but very expensive; Marketing added that a titanium phone they owned marked easily when dropped.

Marketing proposed a plastic mould with a removable rubber cover or sleeve, giving a spongy feel while allowing different colours and styles. The Project Manager and others agreed this could be comfortable to hold and would be a relatively cheap way for customers to change the appearance. The Project Manager noted that interchangeable mobile-phone covers had been popular. The Industrial Designer confirmed the rubber outer piece could be peeled off and replaced. The team later clarified that the main shell would be plastic and the removable outer cover rubber; the plastic case itself would not need to be replaced.

### Interface concept and competitor review
The User Interface representative said the design work used input from the previous meeting, especially from Marketing and Industrial Design, to check customer needs and feasibility, and also reviewed competitors. Competitor remotes were generally rectangular, monotonous, and lacked variety; customers were bored with black-and-white designs. There was no consistent standard for most buttons: channel and volume controls were the common features, while other buttons were arranged inconsistently and could cause confusion. The User Interface representative proposed a graphic user interface in the middle of the flip-top, using an LCD with icons or touch controls, so users could select an icon rather than rely on a separate pointer. Frequently repeated controls, such as volume and channel changes, could remain physical buttons for people who change channels often.

The Project Manager suggested swapping the layout so the controls used most often would be on the lower part, reachable by the thumbs while holding the device like a mobile phone. The group discussed how the open flip-top would be held, with the display and buttons visible while the remote rested in the palm. The User Interface representative agreed that the central volume-and-channel pattern should remain standardized because it was the most consistent feature across remote models. They also reported that a company division had developed a speech-recognition feature, which could help users locate a lost remote: a user could ask where it was and the device could respond with a sound or beep. The team would assess whether it was financially feasible at low cost. The User Interface representative suggested taking inspiration from fruit colours, such as chilli or tomato red, rather than shaping the remote like a fruit.

### Design direction and decisions
The Project Manager called for decisions on the options discussed. The team agreed on kinetic charging, which uses a small watch-type battery. The Industrial Designer said the internal components were fairly standardized. The team’s working interface choice was an LCD on the top side of the flip-top and rubberized, anti-RSI buttons on the bottom. The LCD would initially be black and white rather than full colour, with the possibility of upgrading later; the Industrial Designer noted that black-and-white LCDs were less expensive and used in calculators.

The team favoured a plastic body with a rubberized outer cover, with fruit and vegetable colours for the cover. They would use the trend for colour and spongy feel rather than make the remote itself look like a vegetable or fruit. Marketing asked whether a palm-sized, plastic, rubber-covered design would meet the research finding that customers most wanted a fancy look and feel. The Project Manager argued that an unconventional shape would distinguish it from existing products, while Marketing agreed it would be different from the anonymous, similar-looking remotes on the market. The removable rubber covers could be produced relatively cheaply and changed as trends changed; possible finishes and textures could offer variety without changing the core product. The User Interface representative also supported making the outer case changeable, and the Industrial Designer clarified that this referred to the rubber covering around the plastic shell.

### Locating the remote and company identity
The team discussed how to locate a misplaced remote. Voice recognition was considered a good idea but remained subject to a cost check. If it was not financially feasible, the User Interface representative suggested a whistle-based locator, like a key-chain device. The team also revisited the earlier beeper idea; the Project Manager and Industrial Designer said its suitability depended on expense and on the company’s memo indicating that the feature was being investigated and that parts might already be in stock. If it proved very expensive, they might need to reduce costs elsewhere, so they would learn more about the cost before deciding.

Marketing asked about incorporating the company logo and noted that earlier feedback called for the product to be recognizably the company’s, not merely to have a small, hidden mark. The User Interface representative confirmed that the company identity would be incorporated into the design. The Project Manager said the product would have a logo like other products, but its distinctive design should make it stand out; advertising could associate the name with the individual product. The team considered the design distinctive enough without adding further branding features.

### Close
The Project Manager said there were about five minutes left and then wrapped up. Marketing recapped the decisions: kinetic charging with a watch-type battery, an LCD display on the top of the flip-top, rubberized buttons on the bottom, fruit and vegetable colours for the rubber cover, and a plastic case. Voice recognition and an alternative whistle or beeper locator still required cost assessment. The User Interface representative said the group was now moving in a clear direction, and the Project Manager checked whether everyone was satisfied."}
