The Project Manager welcomed everyone back after lunch and said this was the conceptual design meeting, covering properties, materials, user interface, and trend-watching. The team was slightly ahead of where they had expected to be after the previous meeting, so they would review the relevant material. The Project Manager recapped the prior changes: teletext could not be used as the control for everything, the company’s image needed to be incorporated, voice recognition had previously been left out, and the team had chosen a flip design with an unconventional shape, possibly shell-like. The Industrial Designer had been asked to investigate rechargeable batteries; the team had also planned to consider a port and an alarm to help locate a lost remote. The target market was described as young business users. The Project Manager said they would go over the items already touched on (line 35); the Project Manager proposed starting inside and working outward (line 85).

### Marketing research and trends
Marketing reported that the team had conducted its usual market-research study with 100 subjects to identify important requirements for a remote control. The company, which aimed to be a forerunner in putting fashion into technology, had also consulted fashion and design advisers in Paris and Milan. Findings indicated that customers valued a fancy look and feel most, ahead of technological innovation and ease of use. Fancy appearance was twice as important as technological innovation, which was itself twice as important as ease of use; ease of use remained important but ranked third among the subjects studied. The fashion advisers had found fruit and vegetables emerging as themes for clothes, shoes, and furniture, and a trend toward spongy-feeling materials compared with the previous year. Marketing invited the design team to consider whether those trends could inform the remote’s design. Marketing said they would return to the most important required aspect later (line 64).

### Components and power options
The Industrial Designer said the presentation covered the design of the components and their current availability. The basic purpose was to let users press buttons to activate functions on a television, with the remote being easy to find. Some materials considered at the previous meeting were unavailable. The designer described the TA1835 chip as widely used in remote controls because it sends standard signals based on user input, and outlined battery alternatives. No rechargeable option was available among the standard components examined; AA and AAA batteries seemed too bulky. Dynamo charging would require a winding handle and take more space, and the designer considered it impractical. Solar charging was discussed, including whether artificial room light could charge it; the Project Manager stressed not wanting to limit the market, including international customers and people in basement flats. The Industrial Designer noted that solar cells would need to be placed on the case, would affect the exterior design, and could be vulnerable to drops, a concern because remotes are often thrown around more than calculators. Standard batteries were expected to be cheapest, with solar charging more expensive. The User Interface representative asked which option would be lightest and longest-lasting, noting that customers should not need to charge a remote daily like a mobile phone, and said the battery life needed consideration (line 361).

The Industrial Designer proposed kinetic charging, like that used in wristwatches: ordinary movement could generate charge stored in a small cell about the size of a watch battery. The designer said they were not sure how long the cell would last, but had never seen one run out; the Project Manager questioned whether a remote, which is mostly set down after use, would move enough compared with a watch worn all day. The designer argued that a remote is used only briefly to send a signal and that watch batteries do not run out overnight when left aside. Marketing asked whether solar charging could work alongside standard batteries, and the Industrial Designer said a dual-power arrangement might be possible, though solar cells would affect the case. The Project Manager suggested keeping an attachment or clip-on feature in mind alongside kinetic charging, as portability might reduce the chance of losing the remote. Marketing said this had not emerged from focus groups or market research and was not something customers had asked for, but agreed it could remain a secondary idea.

### Circuit boards, buttons, and standby mode
The Industrial Designer explained that most current remotes use a silicone printed circuit board (PCB). Pressing a rubber button joins contacts, connecting two chip legs; the chip translates the input into a code that is transmitted by an LED through bursts of light. The board can be made to fit the required layout, including nine buttons, and thin tracks could allow smaller switches placed close together. Another possible arrangement was an array of switches. To conserve battery life, the remote should enter standby when unused. If illuminated buttons were chosen, their lights could switch off after five or ten seconds without use. The Industrial Designer said they would explain the switch-array option in the next part (line 434).

The designer also described possible interfaces: a bare printed circuit board touched directly, rubber buttons, or a thin LCD touch display with an array of on-screen controls. An LCD could be black and white and would be flat, limiting curved design features; the printed circuit board, unlike the LCD, would have wires coming off it. The Project Manager asked how users would identify touch points on a bare board and suggested that opening a rubber exterior could reveal a more striking interior. Marketing proposed an optional stylus or small pointer, but the Industrial Designer and User Interface representative warned that it could be easily lost, irritating for frequent channel-switching, and potentially damaging to a touch surface if repeatedly jabbed. Marketing noted that users could use an ordinary pen or pencil instead. The User Interface representative asked whether the flip-top could hold separate circuits for standard buttons on top and more complex controls underneath. The Industrial Designer said this was feasible with two separate circuit boards joined by wires or cabling through the hinge.

### Case materials and replaceable covers
The Industrial Designer said plastic was the likely main case material and that wood would be impractical. Titanium would be expensive to process and, according to the designer, would constrain the case to a standard box shape; plastic allowed more curved shapes. Rubber was considered for its spongy feel, particularly for buttons, which the factory said could use material used in stress-ball manufacture and described as anti-RSI. The designer expressed uncertainty about how the claimed RSI benefit would work. The User Interface representative asked whether customers could change the cover or skin, for example from parrot green to chilli red. The designer said a replaceable titanium case would be possible but very expensive; Marketing added that a titanium phone they owned marked easily when dropped.

Marketing proposed a plastic mould with a removable rubber cover or sleeve, giving a spongy feel while allowing different colours and styles. The Project Manager and others agreed this could be comfortable to hold and would be a relatively cheap way for customers to change the appearance. The Project Manager noted that interchangeable mobile-phone covers had been popular. The Industrial Designer confirmed the rubber outer piece could be peeled off and replaced. The team later clarified that the main shell would be plastic and the removable outer cover rubber; the plastic case itself would not need to be replaced.

### Interface concept and competitor review
The User Interface representative said the design work used input from the previous meeting, especially from Marketing and Industrial Design, to check customer needs and feasibility, and also reviewed competitors. Competitor remotes were generally rectangular, monotonous, and lacked variety; customers were bored with black-and-white designs. There was no consistent standard for most buttons: channel and volume controls were the common features, while other buttons were arranged inconsistently and could cause confusion. The User Interface representative proposed a graphic user interface (GUI) in the middle of the flip-top, using an LCD with icons or touch controls, so users could select an icon rather than rely on a separate pointer. Frequently repeated controls, such as volume and channel changes, could remain physical buttons for people who change channels often.

The Project Manager suggested swapping the layout so the controls used most often would be on the lower part, reachable by the thumbs while holding the device like a mobile phone. The group discussed how the open flip-top would be held, with the display and buttons visible while the remote rested in the palm. The User Interface representative agreed that the central volume-and-channel pattern should remain standardized because it was the most consistent feature across remote models. They also reported that a company division had developed a speech-recognition feature, which could help users locate a lost remote: a user could ask where it was and the device could respond with a sound or beep. The team would assess whether it was financially feasible at low cost. The User Interface representative suggested taking inspiration from fruit colours, such as chilli or tomato red, rather than shaping the remote like a fruit. The User Interface representative said they had discussed the GUI with William (line 806).

### Design direction and decisions
The Project Manager called for decisions on the options discussed. The team agreed on kinetic charging, which uses a small watch-type battery. The Industrial Designer said the internal components were fairly standardized. The team’s working interface choice was an LCD on the top side of the flip-top and rubberized, anti-RSI buttons on the bottom. The LCD would initially be black and white rather than full colour, with the possibility of upgrading later; the Industrial Designer noted that black-and-white LCDs were less expensive and used in calculators.

The team favoured a plastic body with a rubberized outer cover, with fruit and vegetable colours for the cover. They would use the trend for colour and spongy feel rather than make the remote itself look like a vegetable or fruit. Marketing asked whether a palm-sized, plastic, rubber-covered design would meet the research finding that customers most wanted a fancy look and feel. The Project Manager argued that an unconventional shape would distinguish it from existing products, while Marketing agreed it would be different from the anonymous, similar-looking remotes on the market. The removable rubber covers could be produced relatively cheaply and changed as trends changed; possible finishes and textures could offer variety without changing the core product. The User Interface representative also supported making the outer case changeable, and the Industrial Designer clarified that this referred to the rubber covering around the plastic shell.

### Locating the remote and company identity
The team discussed how to locate a misplaced remote. Voice recognition was considered a good idea but remained subject to a cost check. If it was not financially feasible, the User Interface representative suggested a whistle-based locator, like a key-chain device. The team also revisited the earlier beeper idea; the Project Manager and Industrial Designer said its suitability depended on expense and on the company’s memo indicating that the feature was being investigated and that parts might already be in stock. If it proved very expensive, they might need to reduce costs elsewhere, so they would learn more about the cost before deciding.

Marketing asked about incorporating the company logo and noted that earlier feedback called for the product to be recognizably the company’s, not merely to have a small, hidden mark. The User Interface representative confirmed that the company identity would be incorporated into the design. The Project Manager said the product would have a logo like other products, but its distinctive design should make it stand out; advertising could associate the name with the individual product. The team considered the design distinctive enough without adding further branding features.

### Close
The Project Manager said there were about five minutes left and then wrapped up. Marketing recapped the decisions: kinetic charging with a watch-type battery, an LCD display on the top of the flip-top, rubberized buttons on the bottom, fruit and vegetable colours for the rubber cover, and a plastic case. Voice recognition and an alternative whistle or beeper locator still required cost assessment. Marketing asked Sarah to confirm the decisions (line 1166). The User Interface representative said the group was now moving in a clear direction, and the Project Manager checked whether everyone was satisfied. {"title":"ES2004d Remote-Control Prototype Evaluation and Cost Review","summary":"The team reviewed its remote-control specification and prototype: a kinetic charger with a standard chip, standby function, soft, rubbery, interchangeable outer casing, LCD and rubber buttons designed to reduce repetitive strain injury, bright fruit-inspired designs, and voice recognition, pending cost information. William and the User Interface representative presented a clamshell design with a neutral white or light-blue plastic body, customizable colored and patterned rubber covers, an inset black-and-white touch screen on top, standard volume, channel, and power buttons below, and infrared transmission; the team discussed placing the infrared sender at the front and using separate PCBs connected through the hinge. Marketing led a team evaluation of market-research criteria using a seven-point scale, where 1 meant true and 7 false, with individual ratings averaged: fancy look and feel averaged 2.75, technological innovation was around 2.5 after a rating correction, ease of use was close to 2, fashion trends and easy location received the strongest ratings, and reducing repetitive strain injury averaged 4.25; the team considered the prototype ready to proceed, noting limited scope to improve strain reduction. In the finance review, the team confirmed one standard chip, one sample sensor, one sample speaker, and the component and casing entries; changing the kinetic battery to a standard battery made only a small cost difference, while removing voice recognition brought the estimated cost to about €12.25 per unit, or €12.50 in the final discussion, against a €25 price and a stated budget limit. The team agreed it had met its assigned specification and could recommend voice recognition as an optional business-class upgrade, while noting its distinctive shape and colors could already make the remote easy to find; it did not expand the project remit to investigate overheads or funding. They reviewed teamwork and process, describing constructive feedback, shared participation, and effective coordination by Sarah, while noting that earlier access to marketing findings might have affected the initial specification and that more time or separation could have encouraged greater use of email. The project was considered evaluated, and the team noted a meeting survey and final questionnaire, about 50 minutes for the Project Manager to catch up and delegate as Project Supervisor, and a possible £25 celebration."}

{"mom":"### Meeting decisions and prototype specification
The Project Manager recapped the agreed design: a kinetic charger with a standard chip, selected because it comes in different sizes and would not be a problem factor; a standby function; a soft, rubbery, changeable case; buttons combining LCD and rubber; bright, funky fruit-inspired designs; and exploration of voice-recognition software until its cost was clearer. The rubber buttons were intended to minimise repetitive strain injury (RSI).

### Prototype presentation
The User Interface representative said they and William had worked on a prototype, and the Industrial Designer presented the look-and-feel design. The exterior was described as a plastic body in a neutral standard colour such as white or light blue, covered by a detachable rubberised casing available in a wide range of colours and patterns for customisation. The design was a clamshell with an inset black-and-white touchscreen in the top, flush buttons at the bottom, and a flat closing profile. The team discussed using the kinetic batteries and possibly connecting them to the opening and closing movement.

The Industrial Designer said the voice-recognition components appeared readily available and were presumed inexpensive. The suggested locating function would respond when someone asked where the remote was, though the Project Manager noted that a more elaborate system that identified its exact location could be too complicated and might be considered later. The remote would use standard infrared transmission and chips; because the two layers were separate, it would need two PCBs joined through cabling at the hinge. The infrared sender would be at the front of the lower layer so it could point toward the TV when the remote was open. The upper touchscreen would provide the available remote functions; the lower screen would have standard controls such as volume up and down, channel up and down, and power on and off. A company logo could be inset, bevelled, or engraved inside, provided it did not detract from the product’s overall appearance. The presentation concluded with the aim of bringing fashion into electronics.

### Evaluation criteria and ratings
Marketing explained that this evaluation was intended for the team to check whether the product specification and prototype met criteria drawn from user requirements and trends in the company’s marketing reports and strategy, discussed at the previous meeting. The criteria were a fancy look and feel, technological innovation, ease of use, current fashion trends, RSI minimisation, and ease of locating the remote. Fashion considerations included a spongy texture and strong fruit-and-vegetable colours. The team had favoured voice recognition for locating the remote but remained somewhat uncertain and had also considered a beeper. They agreed to use a seven-point scale, with 1 meaning true and 7 meaning false, and to give individual ratings and average them.

For criterion A, fancy look and feel, Marketing rated the prototype 2; the Industrial Designer settled on 3 after considering 2 or 3; the Project Manager rated it 2; and the User Interface representative rated it 4. Marketing calculated an average of 2.75. For criterion B, technological innovation, Marketing rated it 3, the Industrial Designer 1, and the Project Manager 2. The User Interface representative corrected their first rating to 2. The Project Manager stated an average of 2.5, and Marketing recorded 2.5. For ease of use, Marketing initially proposed 1, while the Industrial Designer, Project Manager, and User Interface representative each gave 2; Marketing noted that the result was almost 2 and did not want to use excessive decimal places.

For current fashion trends, Marketing clarified that the prototype materials were limited, but the intended product could have a white or light-blue plastic base and interchangeable rubber covers in customised strong fruit-and-vegetable colours. The rubber casing would provide the spongy feel, unlike the hard plastic beneath it. Marketing and the Industrial Designer rated this criterion 1, as did the Project Manager and User Interface representative. For RSI minimisation, Marketing said the team had not developed a clearly feasible solution and questioned how RSI could be reduced on a small remote used for channel surfing. The Project Manager said the lower buttons’ material was intended to minimise RSI and that the design used relatively few functions and large, obvious buttons with more space between them, reducing the need to move around to hit small buttons accurately. Marketing rated the criterion 4, the Industrial Designer 5, and the Project Manager and User Interface representative 4 each; Marketing recorded an average of 4.25.

For ease of locating the remote, the team confirmed voice recognition as the proposed feature and considered its cost feasible. The volume could be adjusted, as with a TV. The Industrial Designer said the response would be quite loud; the Project Manager suggested that if it could not be heard in the room where someone was standing, they could check another room. Marketing, the Industrial Designer, and the Project Manager rated the criterion 1. Marketing summarised that two of the six criteria had the strongest possible rating of 1—current fashion trends and ease of locating—and that RSI minimisation had the weakest result, around neutral. The team agreed the results were sufficient to proceed with the prototype and marketing; the Project Manager said they were set, and Marketing said current technology and the team’s capabilities were unlikely to improve RSI much further.

### Finance and specification adjustments
The Project Manager brought up the finance calculation and asked whether the team still wanted kinetic power; the Industrial Designer and Marketing confirmed that they did. The Project Manager noted that the finance information would have been useful earlier and might have influenced the choice. While entering the electronics, the Industrial Designer corrected the kinetic-cell quantity from three to one. The team clarified that the electronics comprised one standard chip, one sample sensor, and one sample speaker, and discussed the curved components and the casing. They distinguished a double-curved component from a second component curved at the sides but flattened underneath so it could sit without rolling over. The Project Manager and User Interface representative also checked how the plastic and rubber were represented in the costing; they agreed to account for the rubber casing in the total cost, ultimately entering it as one because plastic was zero in that calculation. Marketing noted that special colours could be needed for more unusual choices such as aubergine.

The Project Manager questioned the cost estimate and whether it was in euros or dollars. The Industrial Designer said that if the figure were in dollars, the exchange rate would make it about 12; the User Interface representative thought the estimate was in euros. The Project Manager said electronics were the highest cost. The team explored removing voice recognition, which the Industrial Designer said would bring the estimate to 12.35; changing from kinetic power to a standard battery would subtract 3, while removing voice recognition added 2. The Project Manager suggested voice recognition could instead be offered as an upgraded or business-class version. The Industrial Designer said customers had indicated willingness to pay more for a better product, rather than limiting the selling price to 25 euros. Marketing said the team still had to work to head-office specifications, but could include recommendations based on its research and meeting consensus. The team agreed voice recognition could be recommended as an option for business-class customers, while the distinctive design itself could help make the remote easy to locate. After discussion of the cost and budget, the Project Manager gave the total as 12.5, and the User Interface representative confirmed that it was under budget. The Industrial Designer said the additional voice-recognition parts were a bought-on extra that could be removed without affecting the rest of the electronics.

### Product evaluation and teamwork
The Project Manager said the team had covered room for creativity and leadership and teamwork. The Industrial Designer and User Interface representative agreed that the group had worked as a team. Marketing said members had separate tasks but had interacted extensively, bounced ideas off one another, and been able to give and take and adjust their remit where necessary. The User Interface representative described feedback as constructive and the work as cohesive teamwork, and credited Sarah with coordinating it well. The Industrial Designer said everyone had been listened to and raised points had been resolved, while noting that voice recognition had not made it into the final product. They thought it might have been included if the marketing findings had been available before the initial specification was issued. The Project Manager said suggestions could be challenged without anyone feeling dismissed.

The team discussed its communication tools. The Industrial Designer said they might have used the external email system more if there had been more time and if members had been more separated. The Project Manager said direct discussion would have been easier than emailing, though having the shared information available was useful; the User Interface representative also valued moving around the room and working individually at times. The team described the flip-top remote as a fresh application of ideas from other areas, including mobile phones, rather than claiming that nothing about it had precedents. They discussed how remote controls often receive less design attention than the devices they accompany, such as DVD players and TVs, and how a distinctive, customised product could stand out. The Project Manager suggested customers might provide an idea for a design that could be created in Photoshop and printed on plastic for an additional charge.

### Close and follow-up
The Project Manager concluded that the project had been evaluated and that the team had a meeting survey and questionnaire to complete. The Project Manager said there were about 50 minutes to catch up on outstanding work and would delegate in the Project Supervisor role. The team discussed a celebration, with the Project Manager referring to 25 pounds or, alternatively, dancing on desks. They completed the questionnaire and confirmed that the meeting was finished."}

{"summary":"The team reviewed its remote-control specification and prototype: a kinetic charger with a standard chip, standby function, soft, rubbery, interchangeable outer casing, LCD and rubber buttons designed to reduce repetitive strain injury (RSI), bright fruit-inspired designs, and voice recognition, pending cost information. William and the User Interface representative presented a clamshell design with a neutral white or light-blue plastic body, customizable colored and patterned rubber covers, an inset black-and-white touch screen on top, standard volume, channel, and power buttons below, and infrared transmission; the team discussed placing the infrared sender at the front and using separate PCBs connected through the hinge. Marketing led a team evaluation of market-research criteria using a seven-point scale, where 1 meant true and 7 false, with individual ratings averaged: fancy look and feel averaged 2.75, technological innovation was around 2.5 after a rating correction, ease of use was close to 2, fashion trends and easy location received the strongest ratings, and reducing RSI averaged 4.25; the team considered the prototype ready to proceed, noting limited scope to improve RSI reduction. In the finance review, the team confirmed one standard chip, one sample sensor, one sample speaker, and the component and casing entries; changing the kinetic battery to a standard battery made only a small cost difference, while removing voice recognition brought the estimated cost to about €12.25 per unit, or €12.50 in the final discussion, against a €25 price and a stated budget limit. The team agreed it had met its assigned specification and could recommend voice recognition as an optional business-class upgrade, while noting its distinctive shape and colors could already make the remote easy to find; it did not expand the project remit to investigate overheads or funding. They reviewed teamwork and process, describing constructive feedback, shared participation, and effective coordination by Sarah, while noting that earlier access to marketing findings might have affected the initial specification and that more time or separation could have encouraged greater use of email. The project was considered evaluated, and the team noted a meeting survey and final questionnaire, about 50 minutes for the Project Manager to catch up and delegate as Project Supervisor, and a possible £25 celebration.","mom":"### Meeting decisions and prototype specification
The Project Manager recapped the agreed design: a kinetic charger with a standard chip, selected because it comes in different sizes and would not be a problem factor; a standby function; a soft, rubbery, changeable case; buttons combining LCD and rubber; bright, funky fruit-inspired designs; and exploration of voice-recognition software until its cost was clearer. The rubber buttons were intended to minimise repetitive strain injury (RSI).

### Prototype presentation
The User Interface representative said they and William had worked on a prototype, and the Industrial Designer presented the look-and-feel design. The exterior was described as a plastic body in a neutral standard colour such as white or light blue, covered by a detachable rubberised casing available in a wide range of colours and patterns for customisation. The design was a clamshell with an inset black-and-white touchscreen in the top, flush buttons at the bottom, and a flat closing profile. The team discussed using the kinetic batteries and possibly connecting them to the opening and closing movement.

The Industrial Designer said the voice-recognition components appeared readily available and were presumed inexpensive. The suggested locating function would respond when someone asked where the remote was, though the Project Manager noted that a more elaborate system that identified its exact location could be too complicated and might be considered later. The remote would use standard infrared transmission and chips; because the two layers were separate, it would need two PCBs joined through cabling at the hinge. The infrared sender would be at the front of the lower layer so it could point toward the TV when the remote was open. The upper touchscreen would provide the available remote functions; the lower screen would have standard controls such as volume up and down, channel up and down, and power on and off. A company logo could be inset, bevelled, or engraved inside, provided it did not detract from the product’s overall appearance. The presentation concluded with the aim of bringing fashion into electronics.

### Evaluation criteria and ratings
Marketing explained that this evaluation was intended for the team to check whether the product specification and prototype met criteria drawn from user requirements and trends in the company’s marketing reports and strategy, discussed at the previous meeting. The criteria were a fancy look and feel, technological innovation, ease of use, current fashion trends, RSI minimisation, and ease of locating the remote. Fashion considerations included a spongy texture and strong fruit-and-vegetable colours. The team had favoured voice recognition for locating the remote but remained somewhat uncertain and had also considered a beeper. They agreed to use a seven-point scale, with 1 meaning true and 7 meaning false, and to give individual ratings and average them.

For criterion A, fancy look and feel, Marketing rated the prototype 2; the Industrial Designer settled on 3 after considering 2 or 3; the Project Manager rated it 2; and the User Interface representative rated it 4. Marketing calculated an average of 2.75. For criterion B, technological innovation, Marketing rated it 3, the Industrial Designer 1, and the Project Manager 2. The User Interface representative corrected their first rating to 2. The Project Manager stated an average of 2.5, and Marketing recorded 2.5. For ease of use, Marketing initially proposed 1, while the Industrial Designer, Project Manager, and User Interface representative each gave 2; Marketing noted that the result was almost 2 and did not want to use excessive decimal places.

For current fashion trends, Marketing clarified that the prototype materials were limited, but the intended product could have a white or light-blue plastic base and interchangeable rubber covers in customised strong fruit-and-vegetable colours. The rubber casing would provide the spongy feel, unlike the hard plastic beneath it. Marketing and the Industrial Designer rated this criterion 1, as did the Project Manager and User Interface representative. For RSI minimisation, Marketing said the team had not developed a clearly feasible solution and questioned how RSI could be reduced on a small remote used for channel surfing. The Project Manager said the lower buttons’ material was intended to minimise RSI and that the design used relatively few functions and large, obvious buttons with more space between them, reducing the need to move around to hit small buttons accurately. Marketing rated the criterion 4, the Industrial Designer 5, and the Project Manager and User Interface representative 4 each; Marketing recorded an average of 4.25.

For ease of locating the remote, the team confirmed voice recognition as the proposed feature and considered its cost feasible. The volume could be adjusted, as with a TV. The Industrial Designer said the response would be quite loud; the Project Manager suggested that if it could not be heard in the room where someone was standing, they could check another room. Marketing, the Industrial Designer, and the Project Manager rated the criterion 1. Marketing summarised that two of the six criteria had the strongest possible rating of 1—current fashion trends and ease of locating—and that RSI minimisation had the weakest result, around neutral. The team agreed the results were sufficient to proceed with the prototype and marketing; the Project Manager said they were set, and Marketing said current technology and the team’s capabilities were unlikely to improve RSI much further.

### Finance and specification adjustments
The Project Manager brought up the finance calculation and asked whether the team still wanted kinetic power; the Industrial Designer and Marketing confirmed that they did. The Project Manager noted that the finance information would have been useful earlier and might have influenced the choice. While entering the electronics, the Industrial Designer corrected the kinetic-cell quantity from three to one. The team clarified that the electronics comprised one standard chip, one sample sensor, and one sample speaker, and discussed the curved components and the casing. They distinguished a double-curved component from a second component curved at the sides but flattened underneath so it could sit without rolling over. The Project Manager questioned the cost estimate and whether it was in euros or dollars. The Industrial Designer said that if the figure were in dollars, the exchange rate would make it about 12; the User Interface representative thought the estimate was in euros. The Project Manager said electronics were the highest cost. {"mom":"### Meeting purpose and introductions
The Project Manager opened the first meeting, noting that it would last 25 minutes. The team was to get acquainted, receive tool training, and discuss the project plan. Robin introduced herself as Marketing Manager, Louisa as User Interface Designer, Nick as Industrial Designer, and Alastair as project leader. Louisa and the Project Manager were unsure what “tool training” meant.

### Project brief and whiteboard exercise
Alastair explained that the team would develop a new remote control based on an existing model, aiming to make it more user-friendly and trendier, and thereby gain a larger market share and audience. The work would proceed through functional, conceptual, and detailed design phases, with the designers developing the device through meetings during the day. To test the whiteboard, everyone was asked to draw a favourite animal. Louisa drew a cat, which she liked for its independence, intelligence, affection, and ability to look after itself. Nick drew a bear, noting that bears feature in cartoon characters such as those from The Jungle Book. Robin drew a dog, appreciating dogs’ loyalty, cheerfulness, companionship, and suitability for exercise. Alastair drew fish kept by his daughters, explaining that fish require little care: a feeder can provide food during holidays of a couple of weeks, and the water needs changing every couple of months. He noted that fish sometimes die, but are otherwise low-maintenance pets. There were some microphone and camera difficulties during the exercise.

### Commercial targets
Alastair said prior project work set an expected selling price of €25, based on information from Robin. The product was intended for international sales, not just Europe, and production costs were to be limited to €12.50 per unit. He clarified that overheads and other costs would have to be deducted before calculating profit per unit; the overhead costs would determine the projected number of units to sell.

### Initial remote-control requirements and concepts
Nick noted that buttons on some remote controls were too small and difficult to press, and suggested making them easier to press because that was the device’s main function. Alastair summarized the desired qualities as robustness, ease of use, and visibility; Nick added that buttons should be accessible.

Louisa asked whether the brief was for a television remote or a combined remote for systems such as television and DVD, since having several remotes in a home was annoying. Alastair said he would confirm the scope, but agreed that having three or four devices around a room was inconvenient and described a single device for all remotes as sensible. Robin added that market research found people were often confused by the large number of buttons. She also said remotes could be out of reach, forcing people to get up merely to pick one up, and suggested considering a remote that could move around the room. Louisa jokingly suggested one that came when called; Robin said that might be for the future, when people could talk to their televisions.

Alastair observed that simplicity and a single remote for multiple devices might be competing requirements: a multi-device remote could need more buttons, while the aim was for anyone to be able to use it. He suggested that people’s increasing familiarity with remotes might make more complicated controls acceptable over time. Nick asked whether the team was designing the remote alone or its instructions as well; Alastair supported the idea of better instructions. Robin described research into cutting-edge handheld devices, including mini-laptop-like systems, and suggested a miniature computer that could control a television, stereo, and future devices added to the system.

### Next steps and scope
With five minutes left in the meeting, Alastair began winding up and said the next meeting would be in 30 minutes. He outlined the next 30 minutes’ work: Nick would develop the working design, Louisa the technical functions design, and Robin the user requirements specification. Specific instructions would be sent by each person’s personal coach. The team confirmed that the objectives were clear.

Louisa said she was still unsure what the remote was for and asked whether it should be multifunctional or whether the team should decide as it worked. Nick recalled that the initial brief had described a television remote and suggested sticking to that unless told otherwise. Alastair agreed that later information or meetings might change the direction, but for now the team would design a television-only remote. The team would break off to work, and Alastair would write up the minutes; they would meet again in half an hour."}

{"summary":"### Meeting purpose and introductions
Alastair, the project leader, opened the first meeting, which was scheduled for 25 minutes. The team was to get acquainted, receive tool training, and discuss the project plan. Robin introduced herself as Marketing Manager, Louisa as User Interface Designer, Nick as Industrial Designer, and Alastair as project leader. Louisa and Alastair were unsure what “tool training” meant.

### Project brief and whiteboard exercise
Alastair explained that the team would develop a new remote control based on an existing model, aiming to make it more user-friendly and trendier, and thereby gain a larger market share and audience. The work would proceed through functional, conceptual, and detailed design phases. Designers would develop the device through meetings during the day and produce various designs. To test the whiteboard, everyone was asked to draw a favourite animal. Louisa chose a cat for its independence, intelligence, affection, and ability to look after itself. Nick chose a bear, partly because of familiar cartoon characters such as those in The Jungle Book. Robin chose a dog for its loyalty, upbeat nature, companionship, and encouragement to exercise. Alastair drew fish kept by his daughters, explaining that a feeder could provide food during holidays of a couple of weeks and that the water needed changing every couple of months; although fish often die, they are otherwise low-maintenance pets. There were microphone and camera difficulties during the exercise.

### Commercial targets
Alastair said prior project work set an expected international selling price of €25, based on information from Robin. Production costs were to be limited to €12.50 per unit. Overheads and other costs would be deducted to calculate profit per unit, and the overhead costs would determine the projected number of units to sell.

### Initial remote-control requirements and concepts
Nick noted that some remote-control buttons were too small and difficult to press, and suggested making them easier to press because that is the device’s main function. Alastair summarized the desired qualities as robustness, ease of use, and visibility; Nick added that buttons should be accessible.

Louisa asked whether the brief was for a television remote or a combined remote for systems such as television/video or television/DVD, since having several remotes at home was annoying. Alastair said he would get back to her on the scope, while agreeing that having three or four devices around a room was inconvenient and that one device for all remotes seemed sensible. Robin said market research found people were often confused by the number of buttons. She also noted that remotes could be out of reach, forcing people to get up just to pick one up, and suggested considering a remote that could move around the room. Louisa jokingly suggested one that came when called; Robin said that might be for the future, when people could talk to their televisions.

Alastair observed a tension between simplicity and a single remote for multiple devices: a multi-device remote might need more buttons, while the aim was for anyone to be able to use it. He suggested that people’s increasing familiarity with remotes might make more complicated controls acceptable over time. Nick asked whether the team was designing the remote alone or its instructions as well; Alastair supported better instructions. Robin described research into cutting-edge handheld devices, including mini-laptop-like systems, and suggested a miniature computer-like controller that could operate a television and stereo and link to future devices.

### Next steps and scope
Alastair said the meeting had five minutes remaining and that the next meeting would be in 30 minutes. For the next 30 minutes, Nick would develop the working design, Louisa the technical-functions design, and Robin the user-requirements specification. Each person’s personal coach would send specific instructions. The team confirmed the objectives were clear. Alastair said he would write up minutes for the next meeting.

{"mom":"### Meeting purpose and project requirements
The Project Manager opened by noting that the team had new project requirements and three presentations to discuss within the meeting’s 40-minute allocation. The Industrial Designer, User Interface Designer, and Marketing representative each had a presentation. The Project Manager reviewed three requirements received by email: the remote must be for television only, to avoid complexity and protect time to market; teletext was considered outdated because of the popularity of the internet; and the finished product must incorporate the company logo, corporate colour, and slogan. The Project Manager had received the corporate-image information by email, but had not yet presented it. The group had not obtained further information about teletext. The Project Manager also said only about four hours remained to complete the project and that speed of delivery was important.

### Industrial design presentation: remote components and operation
The Industrial Designer presented research into existing remote controls, based on information found on the internet, and described the components and how they interact. The remote would need a power source, likely batteries; a user interface made up of buttons for functions such as changing channels and adjusting volume; a chip to interpret button presses; and an infrared sender that transmits a signal to a receiver in the television. The designer said battery power was preferable because of the remote’s size and because a cable would undermine its portability. Infrared had been used successfully, provided the battery had reasonable power, and the user did not need to point directly at the television. The designer also noted that battery configurations in existing models varied, including two or four batteries.

### User interface presentation and initial design discussion
Louisa, the User Interface Designer, described the basic function as sending a signal from the remote to the television to perform a desired action. Examples included volume up and down, channel selection by number or channel up/down, and switching the television on or off, potentially with a standby button. She compared two example remotes: one appeared crowded and complicated, while the other looked simpler and more user-friendly. She preferred the simpler remote because it had large, clearly labelled buttons, a limited number of controls, recognizable symbols such as triangles, squares, and arrows alongside words, and a small amount of colour; she suggested that it could use more colour. The Project Manager reminded the group that the product must use the company’s own logo and colour scheme and incorporate the corporate colour and slogan. The Project Manager thought the red visible on an example remote might relate to the corporate colour scheme, but was unsure.

The Industrial Designer suggested removing the circular section and other video-related buttons from the example remote, leaving a simpler television-only control. The User Interface Designer proposed limiting the number of number keys to one through six plus channel up and down, questioning the need for seven, eight, and nine. The Project Manager argued that the design should allow for expanding television-channel availability: there were five standard channels, the BBC had added a further six, and services such as Sky offered additional channels. The group discussed channel up/down, favourite-channel shortcuts, and ways of navigating larger channel ranges, including selecting channel ranges and then a specific channel. They agreed that number keys could be used in combinations to reach higher channel numbers, with a short delay—about one or two seconds—allowing a second digit to be entered. The Industrial Designer estimated that 14 buttons would be needed and considered this manageable for a user guide. The Project Manager reiterated that the television-only scope was intended to keep the project simple and avoid endangering time to market.

### Marketing research and product preferences
The Marketing representative said the team had researched users’ functional requirements using a questionnaire. The questions covered useful buttons, the remote’s appearance and feel, and desired improvements. Three quarters of respondents considered remote controls ugly, and an even higher proportion said they would pay more for a fancier remote. Respondents rarely used picture, brightness, and audio-setting buttons; they mainly used channel, volume, and power controls. Younger people were more receptive to speech recognition, while interest declined in the 35–40 and 40–45 age groups and among older respondents; more older people were unsure whether they wanted the feature. The most common frustration was losing the remote somewhere in the room and being unable to find it. The second most common was difficulty learning a new remote’s buttons and functions.

The Marketing representative recommended a sleek, attractive, high-tech design with fewer buttons, prioritizing channels, power, and volume. A menu or LCD menu for other functions was raised as a possibility, as was speech recognition, particularly if the product were aimed at younger customers. The representative suggested using speech recognition to help locate a lost remote rather than to change channels, because television sound could cause the remote to respond to the television and change channels unintentionally. The Industrial Designer cautioned that speech recognition might require advanced technology and could exceed the 12.50 budget. The group also discussed a buzzer or sensor to locate a misplaced remote, possibly activated by a button kept in a fixed place; Marketing noted that a separate device would mean producing two products and could add expense. The User Interface Designer mentioned inexpensive key-ring devices that respond to a whistle or clap. The group favored keeping the locating function within the remote rather than adding a second product.

### Prioritizing features and agreeing the remote’s functions
The Project Manager emphasized that any added feature, including speech recognition, had to be simple and quick to develop because time to market was critical. The three primary requirements—company branding, television-only operation, and omission of outdated teletext—were described as constraints on the design. The Project Manager said the team needed to complete the project within the short time window, then add extras only if possible. The group decided to focus on a simple whistle-back or sound-activated locating function, addressing the leading consumer frustration. The Project Manager preferred a clap over a whistle because it might be easier for a wider age range; Marketing and the Industrial Designer agreed that clapping was more broadly accessible. The group also agreed to remove teletext, since management considered it dated as internet use grew.

The group settled on ten number keys and a mechanism to allow multiple digits to be entered, with a short delay between presses. The front of the remote was to include the number keys, volume up and down, channel up and down, a mute button, and a power/standby control. The participants counted 16 front buttons in total. They discussed discouraging standby use because of electricity waste, including the suggestion of a small warning on the front; the User Interface Designer recommended a smaller sign as a compromise. Market research also supported including channel up/down because many users zap between channels.

### Secondary controls and design layout
The team discussed keeping less frequently used controls on the back or under a sliding, hidden panel, so the front could remain simple while the additional functions were available when needed. The User Interface Designer said this could suit older users who might dislike navigating menus but could read clearly displayed buttons. The Project Manager and Industrial Designer agreed that the team needed to decide which functions belonged on the front and which on the back. Brightness, contrast, audio functions, and television tuning were discussed as secondary controls. The Industrial Designer noted that a television may need tuning when first set up and again when replaced; the Project Manager said the remote needed to work with televisions that did not tune automatically, including for an international market and a product positioned toward the lower end of the cost scale. Marketing observed that replacement remotes might be used with older televisions, supporting retention of a tuning function.

The group considered an LCD menu for secondary settings, but raised expense and usability concerns, especially because learning a new remote had been the second-largest user frustration. A hidden panel with clearly labelled controls was considered preferable to requiring users to learn a menu or rely on a complicated instruction booklet. The Marketing representative identified brightness and contrast as secondary controls, and the User Interface Designer added audio functions. The group also discussed a channel tuner with up/down selection and an enter/select button to confirm a chosen channel. The Industrial Designer and Project Manager favored keeping audio controls limited to volume up and down, rather than adding more audio functions. Dolby or surround-sound controls were mentioned, but the participants were unsure what they did; the Project Manager suggested researching them before deciding whether they were needed.

### Follow-up and next meeting
The Project Manager said the team needed to clarify each person’s task and know the next meeting date so progress could be reviewed then. Any relevant information discovered before the next meeting should be shared promptly by email rather than held back, because it could affect others’ decisions; information found just before the meeting could be brought for discussion then. The Industrial Designer suggested that someone prepare a list of the secondary functions and report back at the start of the next meeting. The Project Manager agreed to write the minutes. The team expected to meet again in about 40 minutes, though the exact time was not confirmed."}

The Industrial Designer outlined a remote using battery power, buttons and a chip to control an infrared sender communicating with the television’s receiver, while Louisa, the User Interface Designer, favoured a simpler design with large, clearly labelled buttons and discussed channel, volume, power and standby functions. Marketing research found that three quarters of respondents considered remotes ugly, many would pay more for a better-looking model, users mainly relied on channel, volume and power buttons, and losing the remote and learning a replacement were the leading frustrations; interest in speech recognition declined among older age groups. The group prioritized a simple, affordable TV remote and agreed to remove teletext and video controls, retain number entry with a delay for multiple digits, and explore a clap-activated finder rather than speech recognition or a separate whistle-back device. They discussed keeping frequently used controls on the front and hiding less-used functions—such as brightness, contrast, audio and channel tuning—on a rear or concealed panel; the proposed front set included number, channel-up/down, volume-up/down, mute and power/standby controls, with 16 buttons counted, while the detailed functions still needed a list and further consideration. The Project Manager agreed to write the minutes, and the group expected to meet again in about 40 minutes.","mom":"### Meeting purpose and project requirements
The Project Manager opened by noting that the team had new project requirements and three presentations to discuss within the meeting’s 40-minute allocation. The Industrial Designer, User Interface Designer, and Marketing representative each had a presentation. The Project Manager reviewed three requirements received by email: the remote must be for television only, to avoid complexity and protect time to market; teletext was considered outdated because of the popularity of the internet; and the finished product must incorporate the company logo, corporate colour, and slogan. The Project Manager had received the corporate-image information by email, but had not yet presented it. The group had not obtained further information about teletext. The Project Manager also said only about four hours remained to complete the project and that speed of delivery was important.

### Industrial design presentation: remote components and operation
The Industrial Designer presented research into existing remote controls, based on information found on the internet, and described the components and how they interact. The remote would need a power source, likely batteries; a user interface made up of buttons for functions such as changing channels and adjusting volume; a chip to interpret button presses; and an infrared sender that transmits a signal to a receiver in the television. The designer said battery power was preferable because of the remote’s size and because a cable would undermine its portability. Infrared had been used successfully, provided the battery had reasonable power, and the user did not need to point directly at the television. The designer also noted that battery configurations in existing models varied, including two or four batteries.

### User interface presentation and initial design discussion
Louisa, the User Interface Designer, described the basic function as sending a signal from the remote to the television to perform a desired action. Examples included volume up and down, channel selection by number or channel up/down, and switching the television on or off, potentially with a standby button. She compared two example remotes: one appeared crowded and complicated, while the other looked simpler and more user-friendly. She preferred the simpler remote because it had large, clearly labelled buttons, a limited number of controls, recognizable symbols such as triangles, squares, and arrows alongside words, and a small amount of colour; she suggested that it could use more colour. The Project Manager reminded the group that the product must use the company’s own logo and colour scheme and incorporate the corporate colour and slogan. The Project Manager thought the red visible on an example remote might relate to the corporate colour scheme, but was unsure.

The Industrial Designer suggested removing the circular section and other video-related buttons from the example remote, leaving a simpler television-only control. The User Interface Designer proposed limiting the number of number keys to one through six plus channel up and down, questioning the need for seven, eight, and nine. The Project Manager argued that the design should allow for expanding television-channel availability: there were five standard channels, the BBC had added a further six, and services such as Sky offered additional channels. The group discussed channel up/down, favourite-channel shortcuts, and ways of navigating larger channel ranges, including selecting channel ranges and then a specific channel. They agreed that number keys could be used in combinations to reach higher channel numbers, with a short delay—about one or two seconds—allowing a second digit to be entered. The Industrial Designer estimated that 14 buttons would be needed and considered this manageable for a user guide. The Project Manager reiterated that the television-only scope was intended to keep the project simple and avoid endangering time to market.

### Marketing research and product preferences
The Marketing representative said the team had researched users’ functional requirements using a questionnaire. The questions covered useful buttons, the remote’s appearance and feel, and desired improvements. Three quarters of respondents considered remote controls ugly, and an even higher proportion said they would pay more for a fancier remote. Respondents rarely used picture, brightness, and audio-setting buttons; they mainly used channel, volume, and power controls. Younger people were more receptive to speech recognition, while interest declined in the 35–40 and 40–45 age groups and among older respondents; more older people were unsure whether they wanted the feature. The most common frustration was losing the remote somewhere in the room and being unable to find it. The second most common was difficulty learning a new remote’s buttons and functions.

The Marketing representative recommended a sleek, attractive, high-tech design with fewer buttons, prioritizing channels, power, and volume. A menu or LCD menu for other functions was raised as a possibility, as was speech recognition, particularly if the product were aimed at younger customers. The representative suggested using speech recognition to help locate a lost remote rather than to change channels, because television sound could cause the remote to respond to the television and change channels unintentionally. The Industrial Designer cautioned that speech recognition might require advanced technology and could exceed the 12.50 budget. The group also discussed a buzzer or sensor to locate a misplaced remote, possibly activated by a button kept in a fixed place; Marketing noted that a separate device would mean producing two products and could add expense. The User Interface Designer mentioned inexpensive key-ring devices that respond to a whistle or clap. The group favored keeping the locating function within the remote rather than adding a second product.

### Prioritizing features and agreeing the remote’s functions
The Project Manager emphasized that any added feature, including speech recognition, had to be simple and quick to develop because time to market was critical. The three primary requirements—company branding, television-only operation, and omission of outdated teletext—were described as constraints on the design. The Project Manager said the team needed to complete the project within the short time window, then add extras only if possible. The group decided to focus on a simple whistle-back or sound-activated locating function, addressing the leading consumer frustration. The Project Manager preferred a clap over a whistle because it might be easier for a wider age range; Marketing and the Industrial Designer agreed that clapping was more broadly accessible. The group also agreed to remove teletext, since management considered it dated as internet use grew.

The group settled on ten number keys and a mechanism to allow multiple digits to be entered, with a short delay between presses. The front of the remote was to include the number keys, volume up and down, channel up and down, a mute button, and a power/standby control. The participants counted 16 front buttons in total. They discussed discouraging standby use because of electricity waste, including the suggestion of a small warning on the front; the User Interface Designer recommended a smaller sign as a compromise. Market research also supported including channel up/down because many users zap between channels.

### Secondary controls and design layout
The team discussed keeping less frequently used controls on the back or under a sliding, hidden panel, so the front could remain simple while the additional functions were available when needed. The User Interface Designer said this could suit older users who might dislike navigating menus but could read clearly displayed buttons. The Project Manager and Industrial Designer agreed that the team needed to decide which functions belonged on the front and which on the back. Brightness, contrast, audio functions, and television tuning were discussed as secondary controls. The Industrial Designer noted that a television may need tuning when first set up and again when replaced; the Project Manager said the remote needed to work with televisions that did not tune automatically, including for an international market and a product positioned toward the lower end of the cost scale. Marketing observed that replacement remotes might be used with older televisions, supporting retention of a tuning function.

The group considered an LCD menu for secondary settings, but raised expense and usability concerns, especially because learning a new remote had been the second-largest user frustration. A hidden panel with clearly labelled controls was considered preferable to requiring users to learn a menu or rely on a complicated instruction booklet. The Marketing representative identified brightness and contrast as secondary controls, and the User Interface Designer added audio functions. The group also discussed a channel tuner with up/down selection and an enter/select button to confirm a chosen channel. The Industrial Designer and Project Manager favored keeping audio controls limited to volume up and down, rather than adding more audio functions. Dolby or surround-sound controls were mentioned, but the participants were unsure what they did; the Project Manager suggested researching them before deciding whether they were needed.

### Follow-up and next meeting
The Project Manager said the team needed to clarify each person’s task and know the next meeting date so progress could be reviewed then. Any relevant information discovered before the next meeting should be shared promptly by email rather than held back, because it could affect others’ decisions; information found just before the meeting could be brought for discussion then. The Industrial Designer suggested that someone prepare a list of the secondary functions and report back at the start of the next meeting. The Project Manager agreed to write the minutes. {"title":"Remote-Control Design Decisions and Concept Development","summary":"The team reviewed the previous meeting’s decisions: incorporate the company logo and colour scheme on the remote, keep the design straightforward to meet the project schedule, and use a two-page layout that foregrounds customer-priority features while keeping technical backup features on a second page. After reviewing components, they agreed on a kinetic power supply, simple push buttons, and a simple circuit board to control cost; speech recognition would be an optional finder feature, with its cost and technical requirements still to be confirmed. They rejected a scroll wheel because it would add cost and bulk, reduce the sleek appearance, and offer little benefit, and they set a single-curved case rather than a double-curved one. The team favored a standard rubber case with rubber buttons, while cautioning that novelty fruit-shaped controls and changing fashions could confuse users, complicate production, and leave unsold stock; they chose an apple-shaped standby button as a restrained way to add a distinctive element, with colour details still to be established. Marketing research emphasized a fancy appearance first, technological innovation second, and ease of use third; the group also discussed positioning the product internationally and distinguishing it as a remote finder rather than competing with advanced voice-controlled remotes. They noted that the company logo could be applied as a badge to cases of different colours, but questioned whether interchangeable cases would attract a sufficiently large market and add production or packaging costs. The team planned to keep other button shapes and labels simple and self-explanatory, and assigned the designers to develop the model in Plasticine and refine the button design."}

{"mom":"### Review of previous decisions
The Project Manager summarized the last meeting: the company logo and its color scheme would be incorporated into the remote; the design should remain simple so the project could be completed on time; and the interface would have two pages. The front page would show the features customers most wanted, while backup features needed to meet technical requirements would be on a second page for occasional use. The Project Manager said the previous meeting’s minutes had not been sent successfully.

### Components and power supply
The Industrial Designer reviewed the remote’s components: the user interface and buttons, a chip, a sender, and a power supply. Power options from Real Reaction included a standard battery, a hand-wound dynamo, kinetic power that generates energy through movement, and solar cells. Kinetic power would avoid replacing batteries, but was thought to cost more. The Industrial Designer favored kinetic power for convenience; it works through movement, with internal ball bearings described as a possible mechanism, and the remote would be moved around to power it.

### Buttons, circuit board, and speech-recognition feature
The Industrial Designer described integrated push buttons and a scroll wheel, which could be used for volume. Rubber buttons require a rubber case. Real Reaction supplied simple, regular, and advanced circuit boards at different prices. The scroll wheel requires at least a regular chip, which is in a higher price range; a simple push button requires a simple chip and keeps costs down. The Project Manager clarified that the circuit board must accommodate whichever feature requires the more capable option.

The group agreed to use simple push buttons rather than a scroll wheel: participants felt the wheel would add cost without a corresponding benefit, could make the remote look bulky and less sleek, and would affect materials and price. The group also favored a simple circuit board to keep costs down. The speech-recognition concept was described as recording a set message and responding to it. Participants were unsure whether it would require a more advanced board, and the User Interface participant suggested it might operate separately from the remote’s circuit board. The group treated it as an extra possibility, not a core remote function, and proposed positioning it as a finder feature for locating the remote rather than as general voice control. The Industrial Designer said its cost still needed to be found out so the team would not have to change everything at the last minute. The User Interface participant noted that voice recognition was already available in coffee machines, but the cost was not stated in the information reviewed.

### Market research and product positioning
The User Interface participant reported that existing remotes were not particularly sleek, often had many rubber buttons, and varied in size and curvature. One voice-enabled competitor could control four devices: TV, cable, satellite, video, DVD, and audio. The User Interface participant recommended not competing on broad functions, but instead marketing the product around finding a lost remote. The Project Manager confirmed that the product was intended for the international rather than only the local market, and said a basic model could later be supplemented with paid features for specialist market segments. A children’s remote with bright colors, few buttons, and restricted channel access was discussed as an example of a specialist product, but the group did not want to focus on that market.

Marketing summarized the remote-control market investigation and fashion research, including observations in Paris and Milan. The research suggested that customers valued a fancy look and feel most, technological innovation second, and ease of use third. Fashion observations indicated interest in fruit-and-vegetable themes and spongy-feeling materials, unlike the previous year’s trend. Marketing suggested emphasizing attractive design, adding an innovation such as finding the remote with a hand clap, and keeping the controls simple, potentially using fewer buttons and functions.

Participants cautioned that fruit-shaped functional buttons could confuse users and that fashion trends may change quickly. The Project Manager warned that frequent design changes could force changes to production schedules and molds, and leave old stock needing to be discounted. The team discussed keeping any trend element subtle, such as making only the standby button fruit-shaped, while preserving clear, functional controls. A rubber case and rubber buttons were seen as a possible way to achieve a softer feel without an overly unusual design. The group favored the standard rubber case and standard rubber buttons, rather than changing the whole product to follow short-lived trends. Interchangeable or differently colored cases were considered, but participants raised added production complexity and cost, the need to put the company logo on each case, and uncertainty about whether there would be a sufficiently large secondary market. The Project Manager also noted that a standard case would stack for storage and could avoid more costly packaging.

### Design decisions and follow-up
The group chose a single-curved case as a compromise between a flat and a double-curved design. The Industrial Designer confirmed the decision. The group also agreed to kinetic power, rubber buttons with a rubber case, a simple circuit board, and simple push buttons. Participants agreed that speech recognition could be included as a finder function without affecting the circuit board, while retaining the option to drop it if new information warranted.

The group discussed button labeling and shape to avoid ambiguity, using volume-up and volume-down controls as an example: shapes and labels that contradict one another could mislead users. The Industrial Designer suggested labeling the function clearly and placing directional indications on the buttons. The team reaffirmed that the button shapes and labels should be simple and self-explanatory, with a limited number of buttons; the Project Manager recalled that the target had been reduced to 16 buttons. The standby button would be distinct and fruit-shaped, with an apple selected as a recognizable option; a red apple was suggested if color could be incorporated, subject to confirming the company color scheme and logo requirements. The Project Manager said a company badge could be attached to cases in different colors, though a white case might make a white-background logo less distinct.

The Project Manager closed by asking the team to work through the decisions and said the Industrial Designer and another team member should proceed with Plasticine modeling."}
