{"summary":"The team reviewed the previous meeting’s decisions: incorporate the company logo and colour scheme on the remote, keep the design straightforward to meet the project schedule, and use a two-page layout that foregrounds customer-priority features while keeping technical backup features on a second page. The Project Manager said customers would only need to look at the backup features when required. The Project Manager also noted that the previous meeting’s minutes had not been sent successfully. After reviewing components, they agreed on a kinetic power supply, simple push buttons, and a simple circuit board to control cost; speech recognition would be an optional finder feature, with its cost and technical requirements still to be confirmed. They rejected a scroll wheel because it would add cost and bulk, reduce the sleek appearance, and offer little benefit, and they set a single-curved case rather than a double-curved one. The team favored a standard rubber case with rubber buttons, while cautioning that novelty fruit-shaped controls and changing fashions could confuse users, complicate production, and leave unsold stock; they chose an apple-shaped standby button as a restrained way to add a distinctive element, with colour details still to be established. Marketing research emphasized a fancy appearance first, technological innovation second, and ease of use third; the group also discussed positioning the product internationally and distinguishing it as a remote finder rather than competing with advanced voice-controlled remotes. They noted that the company logo could be applied as a badge to cases of different colours, but questioned whether interchangeable cases would attract a sufficiently large market and add production or packaging costs. The team planned to keep other button shapes and labels simple and self-explanatory, and assigned two team members to develop the model in Plasticine and refine the button design.","mom":"### Review of previous decisions
The Project Manager summarized the last meeting: the company logo and its color scheme would be incorporated into the remote; the design should remain simple so the project could be completed on time; and the interface would have two pages. The front page would show the features customers most wanted, while backup features needed to meet technical requirements would be on a second page for occasional use. The Project Manager said customers would only need to look at the backup features as and when required. The Project Manager said the previous meeting’s minutes had not been sent successfully.

### Components and power supply
The Industrial Designer reviewed the remote’s components: the user interface and buttons, a chip, a sender, and a power supply. Power options from Real Reaction included a standard battery, a hand-wound dynamo, kinetic power that generates energy through movement, and solar cells. Kinetic power would avoid replacing batteries, but was thought to cost more. The Industrial Designer favored kinetic power for convenience; it works through movement, with internal ball bearings described as a possible mechanism, and the remote would be moved around to power it.

### Buttons, circuit board, and speech-recognition feature
The Industrial Designer described integrated push buttons and a scroll wheel, which could be used for volume. Rubber buttons require a rubber case. Real Reaction supplied simple, regular, and advanced circuit boards at different prices. The scroll wheel requires at least a regular chip, which is in a higher price range; a simple push button requires a simple chip and keeps costs down. The Project Manager clarified that the circuit board must accommodate whichever feature requires the more capable option.

The group agreed to use simple push buttons rather than a scroll wheel: participants felt the wheel would add cost without a corresponding benefit, could make the remote look bulky and less sleek, and would affect materials and price. The group also favored a simple circuit board to keep costs down. The speech-recognition concept was described as recording a set message and responding to it. Participants were unsure whether it would require a more advanced board, and the User Interface participant suggested it might operate separately from the remote’s circuit board. The group treated it as an extra possibility, not a core remote function, and proposed positioning it as a finder feature for locating the remote rather than as general voice control. The Industrial Designer said its cost still needed to be found out so the team would not have to change everything at the last minute. The User Interface participant noted that voice recognition was already available in coffee machines, but the cost was not stated in the information reviewed.

### Market research and product positioning
The User Interface participant reported that existing remotes were not particularly sleek, often had many rubber buttons, and varied in size and curvature. One voice-enabled competitor could control four devices: TV, cable, satellite, video, DVD, and audio. The User Interface participant recommended not competing on broad functions, but instead marketing the product around finding a lost remote. The Project Manager confirmed that the product was intended for the international rather than only the local market, and said a basic model could later be supplemented with paid features for specialist market segments. A children’s remote with bright colors, few buttons, and restricted channel access was discussed as an example of a specialist product, but the group did not want to focus on that market.

Marketing summarized the remote-control market investigation and fashion research, including observations in Paris and Milan. The research suggested that customers valued a fancy look and feel most, technological innovation second, and ease of use third. Fashion observations indicated interest in fruit-and-vegetable themes and spongy-feeling materials, unlike the previous year’s trend. Marketing suggested emphasizing attractive design, adding an innovation such as finding the remote with a hand clap, and keeping the controls simple, potentially using fewer buttons and functions.

Participants cautioned that fruit-shaped functional buttons could confuse users and that fashion trends may change quickly. The Project Manager warned that frequent design changes could force changes to production schedules and molds, and leave old stock needing to be discounted. The team discussed keeping any trend element subtle, such as making only the standby button fruit-shaped, while preserving clear, functional controls. A rubber case and rubber buttons were seen as a possible way to achieve a softer feel without an overly unusual design. The group favored the standard rubber case and standard rubber buttons, rather than changing the whole product to follow short-lived trends. Interchangeable or differently colored cases were considered, but participants raised added production complexity and cost, the need to put the company logo on each case, and uncertainty about whether there would be a sufficiently large secondary market. The Project Manager also noted that a standard case would stack for storage and could avoid more costly packaging.

### Design decisions and follow-up
The group chose a single-curved case as a compromise between a flat and a double-curved design. The Industrial Designer confirmed the decision. The group also agreed to kinetic power, rubber buttons with a rubber case, a simple circuit board, and simple push buttons. Participants agreed that speech recognition could be included as a finder function without affecting the circuit board, while retaining the option to drop it if new information warranted.

The group discussed button labeling and shape to avoid ambiguity, using volume-up and volume-down controls as an example: shapes and labels that contradict one another could mislead users. The Industrial Designer suggested labeling the function clearly and placing directional indications on the buttons. The team reaffirmed that the button shapes and labels should be simple and self-explanatory, with a limited number of buttons; the Project Manager recalled that the target had been reduced to 16 buttons. The standby button would be distinct and fruit-shaped, with an apple selected as a recognizable option; a red apple was suggested if color could be incorporated, subject to confirming the company color scheme and logo requirements. The Project Manager said a company badge could be attached to cases in different colors, though a white case might make a white-background logo less distinct.

The Project Manager closed by asking the team to work through the decisions and said the Industrial Designer and another team member should proceed with Plasticine ES2014d: {"title":"Remote-control prototype evaluation and budget redesign","summary":"The team presented a remote-control prototype with a curved case, a pull-down panel for extra function buttons, a company-logo badge, volume and channel controls, and a cherry-shaped feature button; they favored a cherry over an apple because of the Apple/Mac association. They reviewed the design against market-research and finance criteria using a 1-to-7 scale, where 1 meant true, 7 false, and 4 neutral, and discussed fanciness, technical innovation, ease of use, fashion appeal, and fit with Real Reaction’s product identity. The initial design was estimated at 13.7, above the 12.5 production-cost limit, so the group compared options including kinetic power, voice recognition using a sample sensor and speaker, rubber versus plastic casing, and special button materials, shapes, and colours; the cost discussion also cited figures of 9.7, 12.7, 11.7, and 12.3. They settled on a plastic case, retaining kinetic power and voice recognition, with a push-button interface, one special-form button, and two special-colour supplements; this brought the estimate to 12.3, within budget, and was said to save two euros, though the team noted trade-offs in fashion and fanciness and planned to reassess the criteria after changes. They also considered fruit-shaped volume buttons and changing the featured fruit in a future model, while leaving the hidden-panel buttons standard; the company colour had not been established, and 0.2 was discussed as a possible reserve for profitability or legal costs. The closing project-process review found creativity adequate but noted that meeting divisions and information flow could feel arbitrary or disjointed, that the remote-control brief was restrictive and did not fully fit the company’s high-tech product range, and that the whiteboard and digital pens helped despite computer difficulties; teamwork was considered to have gone reasonably well, while leadership was harder for the other participants to assess because the Project Manager led. The team identified kinetic power and voice recognition as new ideas, confirmed that the costs were within budget and the project had been evaluated, and noted that a final questionnaire and meeting summary remained; the Project Manager said an earlier save at 12.3 had not appeared to be stored."}

{"mom":"### File saving and prototype presentation
The Project Manager and Marketing discussed difficulty saving or transferring a file to My Documents. Marketing said the save window needed to be closed before locating the file; the Project Manager decided to redo the spreadsheet because that seemed easiest. The User Interface representative said the prototype was ready to review, and Marketing suggested passing it around.

### Prototype design and cost considerations
The User Interface representative described a case curved around the sides and toward the main display, with a line indicating the pull-down panel and extra function buttons beneath it. The company logo was on a button, and the Industrial Designer presented a fruit motif, described as an apple or cherry, at the top. Marketing favored a cherry, partly because an apple could evoke Apple Mac and raise copyright concerns. The team identified a mute button and noted that individual button labels were difficult to make small enough to read, so simple shapes were chosen. Volume buttons were made larger; the Industrial Designer proposed distinguishing volume buttons in orange from channel buttons in blue. The Project Manager warned that extra colors could affect cost, having initially budgeted for only the red apple button as a special color. The team also discussed a slide-away lower panel.

### Evaluation plan and initial budget review
The Project Manager said the prototype presentation had been completed and outlined evaluation criteria and finance as the next work. The prototype was to be assessed against requirements from the previous meeting, including its missing second layer, red apple button, and button colors. The Project Manager said the next finance review needed to consider production cost and how easy the design would be to manufacture. The original cost requirement was below €12.50. The Industrial Designer asked to display the figures; the team connected a device to review production costs alongside the prototype. The Project Manager listed a simple chip, kinetic energy source, single curved case, rubber case material, rubber buttons, and a push-button interface. The Project Manager and Marketing clarified whether a different-material button supplement applied to one button or all 16 buttons. They considered making only the apple button special and leaving the rest standard; the Project Manager said the total had to stay under €12.50. The figures were stated as 9.1 and then corrected by the Project Manager to 9.7.

### Options to meet the cost limit
The Industrial Designer said a sample sensor and sample speaker for voice recognition could raise the cost by up to 4, while reducing other specifications or choosing a special-form button might help. The Project Manager calculated a total of 12.7 and said the team needed to reduce it to the 12.5 limit. They considered removing special colors, but the User Interface representative pointed out that the simple chip and sample speaker were separate components and might both be needed. The team discussed replacing kinetic power with a battery, which would save one cost point, but the Project Manager noted that avoiding battery replacement was attractive to users. The Industrial Designer referred to market research indicating that people liked interesting gadgets and asked whether voice recognition would be worthwhile alongside batteries. The User Interface representative preferred voice recognition as more impressive than a battery-free design, while the Project Manager recalled that its main purpose was helping users find a lost remote. Marketing proposed evaluating the existing prototype first and making changes afterward.

### Prototype evaluation criteria and ratings
Marketing explained that the design team made the prototype and evaluated it against criteria based on market research and finance. The rating scale ran from 1 for true to 7 for false, with 4 neutral; Marketing said a financial criterion also needed to be added. The criteria were whether the product looked and felt fancy, demonstrated technical innovation, was easy to use, incorporated fashion to attract buyers, and was recognizable as a Real Reaction product. For the fancy criterion, the team considered the single curve and rubbery, spongy feel. They noted that the prototype did not have the intended double curve, and settled on a rating around 2 or 3. For technical innovation, the team discussed kinetic power and voice recognition; the prototype had speech recognition but not kinetic power, because they could not afford both. The group initially considered a rating of 2 for innovation, while acknowledging that the prototype did not yet meet the full target and that the total needed to fall from 13.7 to 12.5. Marketing said the current design should be evaluated before deciding changes.

### Cost adjustments and design decisions
The Project Manager said the team needed to reduce the 13.7 total by at least 1.2 to meet the requirement. They discussed cheaper alternatives, including a plastic case instead of rubber. The Project Manager explained that special materials such as rubber, wood, and titanium added 0.6, while special colors added 0.2. They considered keeping the kinetic feature and sample sensor while using plastic and reducing a special-form or special-color supplement. The team decided on a plastic case, noting that it would save two points and keep the total within budget; the Industrial Designer later gave the revised total as 11.7. The team also reviewed button supplements: they treated the apple button as one special form, discussed how to count special colors, and settled on two special-color supplements in addition to the original color. The volume buttons could be larger, which might count as another special form. The Industrial Designer calculated a total of 12.3, still within budget. The Project Manager and Industrial Designer agreed that the changes sacrificed some fashion and fanciness but retained the other product attributes. They considered a rating of 3 for fashion, then discussed using an additional fruit-shaped button, possibly lemon-shaped volume buttons, to preserve some fashion appeal. They noted that having a rubber case required rubber buttons, but the revised design did not have a rubber case. The Project Manager said the design had saved two euros.

### Corporate identity and button design
The team discussed whether the revised product remained recognizable as a Real Reaction product. Marketing described the corporate image as sleek, new technology and asked whether the design fit with the company's coffee makers and spacecraft. The User Interface representative noted that the product shared a speech feature with the coffee machine and that the logo would be recognizable. The Industrial Designer said the rubbery feel might be more comfortable than sleek and new, depending on how it was viewed. The group considered ratings around 2 or 3 for recognizability and settled on 2. They also discussed whether buttons on the hidden second panel should be standard blue, with the User Interface representative saying small, round blue buttons would be adequate, including an enter button. The Industrial Designer suggested prioritizing the visible buttons and treating hidden functional buttons more simply. Marketing agreed that obvious controls for channel and volume should be easy to find, while color differences mattered less when users opened the panel to tune settings. The Project Manager suggested applying the remaining 0.2 to profitability. The team also discussed the company logo as a stick-on badge and said a black outline or double edge could separate the logo from the product regardless of its color. They had not established the company's color. The team planned to reassess the ratings after making the financial adjustments.

### Closing project review and feedback on the process
The Project Manager said the finance work, Excel project, and redesign were complete, and moved to evaluating the project process and course. Marketing said the divisions between individual meetings seemed arbitrary: information gathered between meetings did not always carry forward, and topics such as remote-control curves and buttons had been split across meetings. The Project Manager explained that a manufacturing process typically involves agreeing tasks, gathering information, returning to discuss it, changing the design, and reviewing it again. The Project Manager described creativity as generally acceptable but said information flow on a given subject was sometimes disjointed. The User Interface representative felt the remote-control assignment could have been a more creative project, while the Industrial Designer said choosing a familiar product made it possible to assess and improve it within a set time. Marketing considered the brief restrictive and said the inexpensive remote control did not seem to fit the company's high-tech products, including high-definition DVD equipment and portable 7-inch lightweight computer screens. The Project Manager suggested the software was intended to demonstrate a project process. The team praised the whiteboard and digital pens for making work easier, and Marketing identified the kinetic remote control and voice recognition as new ideas. The Project Manager said teamwork went reasonably well; Marketing and the Industrial Designer said team members had separate ideas and discussed them. The User Interface representative said the team could not fairly assess leadership because the Project Manager had led it. The Project Manager said the computer had not worked as well as desired. The User Interface representative questioned the value of digital pens because it was unclear how to retrieve the recordings; Marketing thought a small chip connected to another device might be involved, and the team was unsure how the output worked.

### Remaining tasks
The Project Manager reviewed the closing items: confirm that costs were within budget, confirm that the project had been evaluated, complete the final questionnaire and meeting summary, and then celebrate. Marketing said there were two questionnaires and a report on the previous meeting. The Project Manager said a previous attempt to save the file at 12.3 had not appeared to save anywhere, and noted that the earlier figure had been different."}

{"summary":"The team presented a remote-control prototype with a curved case, a pull-down panel for extra function buttons, a company-logo badge, volume and channel controls, and a cherry-shaped feature button; they favored a cherry over an apple because of the Apple/Mac association and possible copyright concerns. Marketing said the save window needed to be closed before locating the file, and the Project Manager said they would redo the spreadsheet because it seemed easiest. They reviewed the design against market-research and finance criteria using a 1-to-7 scale, where 1 meant true, 7 false, and 4 neutral, and discussed fanciness, technical innovation, ease of use, fashion appeal, and fit with Real Reaction’s product identity. The initial design was estimated at 13.7, above the 12.5 production-cost limit, so the group compared options including kinetic power, voice recognition using a sample sensor and speaker, rubber versus plastic casing, and special button materials, shapes, and colours; the cost discussion also cited figures of 9.7, 12.7, 11.7, and 12.3. They settled on a plastic case, retaining kinetic power and voice recognition, with a push-button interface, one special-form button, and two special-colour supplements; this brought the estimate to 12.3, within budget, and was said to save two euros, though the team noted trade-offs in fashion and fanciness and planned to reassess the criteria after changes. They also considered fruit-shaped volume buttons and changing the featured fruit in a future model, while leaving the hidden-panel buttons standard; the company colour had not been established, and 0.2 was discussed as a possible reserve for profitability or legal costs. The closing project-process review found creativity adequate but noted that meeting divisions and information flow could feel arbitrary or disjointed, that the remote-control brief was restrictive and did not fully fit the company’s high-tech product range, and that the whiteboard and digital pens helped despite computer difficulties; teamwork was considered to have gone reasonably well, while leadership was harder for the other participants to assess because the Project Manager led. The team identified kinetic power and voice recognition as new ideas, confirmed that the costs were within budget and the project had been evaluated, and noted that a final questionnaire and meeting summary remained; the Project Manager said an earlier save at 12.3 had not appeared to be stored.","mom":"### File saving and prototype presentation
The Project Manager and Marketing discussed difficulty saving or transferring a file to My Documents. Marketing said the save window needed to be closed before locating the file; the Project Manager decided to redo the spreadsheet because that seemed easiest. The User Interface representative said the prototype was ready to review, and Marketing suggested passing it around.

### Prototype design and cost considerations
The User Interface representative described a case curved around the sides and toward the main display, with a line indicating the pull-down panel and extra function buttons beneath it. The company logo was on a button, and the Industrial Designer presented a fruit motif, described as an apple or cherry, at the top. Marketing favored a cherry, partly because an apple could evoke Apple Mac and raise copyright concerns. The team identified a mute button and noted that individual button labels were difficult to make small enough to read, so simple shapes were chosen. Volume buttons were made larger; the Industrial Designer proposed distinguishing volume buttons in orange from channel buttons in blue. The Project Manager warned that extra colors could affect cost, having initially budgeted for only the red apple button as a special color. The team also discussed a slide-away lower panel.

### Evaluation plan and initial budget review
The Project Manager said the prototype presentation had been completed and outlined evaluation criteria and finance as the next work. The prototype was to be assessed against requirements from the previous meeting, including its missing second layer, red apple button, and button colors. The Project Manager said the next finance review needed to consider production cost and how easy the design would be to manufacture. The original cost requirement was below €12.50. The Industrial Designer asked to display the figures; the team connected a device to review production costs alongside the prototype. The Project Manager listed a simple chip, kinetic energy source, single curved case, rubber case material, rubber buttons, and a push-button interface. The Project Manager and Marketing clarified whether a different-material button supplement applied to one button or all 16 buttons. They considered making only the apple button special and leaving the rest standard; the Project Manager said the total had to stay under €12.50. The figures were stated as 9.1 and then corrected by the Project Manager to 9.7.

### Options to meet the cost limit
The Industrial Designer said a sample sensor and sample speaker for voice recognition could raise the cost by up to 4, while reducing other specifications or choosing a special-form button might help. The Project Manager calculated a total of 12.7 and said the team needed to reduce it to the 12.5 limit. They considered removing special colors, but the User Interface representative pointed out that the simple chip and sample speaker were separate components and might both be needed. The team discussed replacing kinetic power with a battery, which would save one cost point, but the Project Manager noted that avoiding battery replacement was attractive to users. The Industrial Designer referred to market research indicating that people liked interesting gadgets and asked whether voice recognition would be worthwhile alongside batteries. The User Interface representative preferred voice recognition as more impressive than a battery-free design, while the Project Manager recalled that its main purpose was helping users find a lost remote. Marketing proposed evaluating the existing prototype first and making changes afterward.

### Prototype evaluation criteria and ratings
Marketing explained that the design team made the prototype and evaluated it against criteria based on market research and finance. The rating scale ran from 1 for true to 7 for false, with 4 neutral; Marketing said a financial criterion also needed to be added. The criteria were whether the product looked and felt fancy, demonstrated technical innovation, was easy to use, incorporated fashion to attract buyers, and was recognizable as a Real Reaction product. For the fancy criterion, the team considered the single curve and rubbery, spongy feel. They noted that the prototype did not have the intended double curve, and settled on a rating around 2 or 3. For technical innovation, the team discussed kinetic power and voice recognition; the prototype had speech recognition but not kinetic power, because they could not afford both. The group initially considered a rating of 2 for innovation, while acknowledging that the prototype did not yet meet the full target and that the total needed to fall from 13.7 to 12.5. Marketing said the current design should be evaluated before deciding changes.

### Cost adjustments and design decisions
The Project Manager said the team needed to reduce the 13.7 total by at least 1.2 to meet the requirement. They discussed cheaper alternatives, including a plastic case instead of rubber. The Project Manager explained that special materials such as rubber, wood, and titanium added 0.6, while special colors added 0.2. They considered keeping the kinetic feature and sample sensor while using plastic and reducing a special-form or special-color supplement. The team decided on a plastic case, noting that it would save two points and keep the total within budget; the Industrial Designer later gave the revised total as 11.7. The team also reviewed button supplements: they treated the apple button as one special form, discussed how to count special colors, and settled on two special-color supplements in addition to the original color. The volume buttons could be larger, which might count as another special form. The Industrial Designer calculated a total of 12.3, still within budget. The Project Manager and Industrial Designer agreed that the changes sacrificed some fashion and fanciness but retained the other product attributes. They considered a rating of 3 for fashion, then discussed using an additional fruit-shaped button, possibly lemon-shaped volume buttons, to preserve some fashion appeal. They noted that having a rubber case required rubber buttons, but the revised design did not have a rubber case. The Project Manager said the design had saved two euros.

### Corporate identity and button design
The team discussed whether the revised product remained recognizable as a Real Reaction product. Marketing described the corporate image as sleek, new technology and asked whether the design fit with the company's coffee makers and spacecraft. The User Interface representative noted that the product shared a speech feature with the coffee machine and that the logo would be recognizable. The Industrial Designer said the rubbery feel might be more comfortable than sleek and new, depending on how it was viewed. The group considered ratings around 2 or 3 for recognizability and settled on 2. They also discussed whether buttons on the hidden second panel should be standard blue, with the User Interface representative saying small, round blue buttons would be adequate, including an enter button. The Industrial Designer suggested prioritizing the visible buttons and treating hidden functional buttons more simply. Marketing agreed that obvious controls for channel and volume should be easy to find, while color differences mattered less when users opened the panel to tune settings. The Project Manager suggested applying the remaining 0.2 to profitability. The team also discussed the company logo as a stick-on badge and said a black outline or double edge could separate the logo from the product regardless of its color. They had not established the company's color. The team planned to reassess the ratings after making the financial adjustments.

### Closing project review and feedback on the process
The Project Manager said the finance work, Excel project, and redesign were complete, and moved to evaluating the project process and course. Marketing said the divisions between individual meetings seemed arbitrary: information gathered between meetings did not always carry forward, and topics such as remote-control curves and buttons had been split across meetings. The Project Manager explained that a manufacturing process typically involves agreeing tasks, gathering information, returning to discuss it, changing the design, and reviewing it again. The Project Manager described creativity as generally acceptable but said information flow on a given subject was sometimes disjointed. The User Interface representative felt the remote-control assignment could have been a more creative project, while the Industrial Designer said choosing a familiar product made it possible to assess and improve it within a set time. Marketing considered the brief restrictive and said the inexpensive remote control did not seem to fit the company's high-tech products, including high-definition DVD equipment and portable 7-inch lightweight computer screens. The Project Manager suggested the software was intended to demonstrate a project process. The team praised the whiteboard and digital pens for making work easier, and Marketing identified the kinetic remote control and voice recognition as new ideas. The Project Manager said teamwork went reasonably well; Marketing and the Industrial Designer said team members had separate ideas and discussed them. The User Interface representative said the team could not fairly assess leadership because the Project Manager had led it. The Project Manager said the computer had not worked as well as desired. The User Interface representative questioned the value of digital pens because it was unclear how to retrieve the recordings; Marketing thought a small chip connected to another device might be involved, and the team was unsure how the output worked.

### Remaining tasks
The Project Manager reviewed the closing items: confirm that costs were within budget, confirm that the project had been evaluated, complete the final questionnaire and meeting summary, and then celebrate. Marketing said there were two questionnaires and a report on the previous meeting. The Industrial Designer asked to display the figures; the team connected a device to review production costs alongside the prototype. The Project Manager listed a simple chip, kinetic energy source, single curved case, rubber case material, rubber buttons, and a push-button interface. The Project Manager and Marketing clarified whether a different-material button supplement applied to one button or all 16 buttons. They considered making only the apple button special and leaving the rest standard; the Project Manager said the total had to stay under €12.50. The figures were stated as 9.1 and then corrected by the Project Manager to 9.7.

### Options to meet the cost limit
The Industrial Designer said a sample sensor and sample speaker for voice recognition could raise the cost by up to 4, while reducing other specifications or choosing a special-form button might help. The Project Manager calculated a total of 12.7 and said the team needed to reduce it to the 12.5 limit. They considered removing special colors, but the User Interface representative pointed out that the simple chip and sample speaker were separate components and might both be needed. The team discussed replacing kinetic power with a battery, which would save one cost point, but the Project Manager noted that avoiding battery replacement was attractive to users. The Industrial Designer referred to market research indicating that people liked interesting gadgets and asked whether voice recognition would be worthwhile alongside batteries. The User Interface representative preferred voice recognition as more impressive than a battery-free design, while the Project Manager recalled that its main purpose was helping users find a lost remote. Marketing proposed evaluating the existing prototype first and making changes afterward.

### Prototype evaluation criteria and ratings
Marketing explained that the design team made the prototype and evaluated it against criteria based on market research and finance. The rating scale ran from 1 for true to 7 for false, with 4 neutral; Marketing said a financial criterion also needed to be added. The criteria were whether the product looked and felt fancy, demonstrated technical innovation, was easy to use, incorporated fashion to attract buyers, and was recognizable as a Real Reaction product. For the fancy criterion, the team considered the single curve and rubbery, spongy feel. They noted that the prototype did not have the intended double curve, and settled on a rating around 2 or 3. For technical innovation, the team discussed kinetic power and voice recognition; the prototype had speech recognition but not kinetic power, because they could not afford both. The group initially considered a rating of 2 for innovation, while acknowledging that the prototype did not yet meet the full target and that the total needed to fall from 13.7 to 12.5. Marketing said the current design should be evaluated before deciding changes.

### Cost adjustments and design decisions
The Project Manager said the team needed to reduce the 13.7 total by at least 1.2 to meet the requirement. They discussed cheaper alternatives, including a plastic case instead of rubber. The Project Manager explained that special materials such as rubber, wood, and titanium added 0.6, while special colors added 0.2. They considered keeping the kinetic feature and sample sensor while using plastic and reducing a special-form or special-color supplement. The team decided on a plastic case, noting that it would save two points and keep the total within budget; the Industrial Designer later gave the revised total as 11.7. The team also reviewed button supplements: they treated the apple button as one special form, discussed how to count special colors, and settled on two special-color supplements in addition to the original color. The volume buttons could be larger, which might count as another special form. The Industrial Designer calculated a total of 12.3, still within budget. The Project Manager and Industrial Designer agreed that the changes sacrificed some fashion and fanciness but retained the other product attributes. They considered a rating of 3 for fashion, then discussed using an additional fruit-shaped button, possibly lemon-shaped volume buttons, to preserve some fashion appeal. They noted that having a rubber case required rubber buttons, but the revised design did not have a rubber case. The Project Manager said the design had saved two euros.

### Corporate identity and button design
The team discussed whether the revised product remained recognizable as a Real Reaction product. Marketing described the corporate image as sleek, new technology and asked whether the design fit with the company's coffee makers and spacecraft. The User Interface representative noted that the product shared a speech feature with the coffee machine and that the logo would be recognizable. The Industrial Designer said the rubbery feel might be more comfortable than sleek and new, depending on how it was viewed. The group considered ratings around 2 or 3 for recognizability and settled on 2. They also discussed whether buttons on the hidden second panel should be standard blue, with the User Interface representative saying small, round blue buttons would be adequate, including an enter button. The Industrial Designer suggested prioritizing the visible buttons and treating hidden functional buttons more simply. Marketing agreed that obvious controls for channel and volume should be easy to find, while color differences mattered less when users opened the panel to tune settings. The Project Manager suggested applying the remaining 0.2 to profitability. The team also discussed the company logo as a stick-on badge and said a black outline or double edge could separate the logo from the product regardless of its color. They had not established the company's color. The team planned to reassess the ratings after making the financial adjustments.

### Closing project review and feedback on the process
The Project Manager said the finance work, Excel project, and redesign were complete, and moved to evaluating the project process and course. Marketing said the divisions between individual meetings seemed arbitrary: information gathered between meetings did not always carry forward, and topics such as remote-control curves and buttons had been split across meetings. The Project Manager explained that a manufacturing process typically involves agreeing tasks, gathering information, returning to discuss it, changing the design, and reviewing it again. The Project Manager described creativity as generally acceptable but said information flow on a given subject was sometimes disjointed. The User Interface representative felt the remote-control assignment could have been a more creative project, while the Industrial Designer said choosing a familiar product made it possible to assess and improve it within a set time. Marketing considered the brief restrictive and said the inexpensive remote control did not seem to fit the company's high-tech products, including high-definition DVD equipment and portable 7-inch lightweight computer screens. The Project Manager suggested the software was intended to demonstrate a project process. The team praised the whiteboard and digital pens for making work easier, and Marketing identified the kinetic remote control and voice recognition as new ideas. The Project Manager said teamwork went reasonably well; Marketing and the Industrial Designer said team members had separate ideas and discussed them. The User Interface representative said the team could not fairly assess leadership because the Project Manager had led it. The Project Manager said the computer had not worked as well as desired. The User Interface representative questioned the value of digital pens because it was unclear how to retrieve the recordings; Marketing thought a small chip connected to another device might be involved, and the team was unsure how the output worked.

### Remaining tasks
The Project Manager reviewed the closing items: confirm that costs were within budget, confirm that the project had been evaluated, complete the final questionnaire and meeting summary, and then celebrate. Marketing said there were two questionnaires and a report on the previous meeting. {"mom":"### Introductions and roles
Betty, the project manager, opened by asking everyone to introduce themselves and describe their function. Francina said she was responsible for user interface design and would design the television remote control. Eileen said she worked in marketing and would work out how to sell the product. Jeanne-Oui said she was the industrial designer, responsible for the technical-functional designs and specifications of the user interface and for working with its design. Betty identified herself as project manager for the meeting and suggested that the team review the presentation.

### Project plan and design brief
Betty outlined the meeting plan: an opening and introductions, tool training, and a project plan. She said the team would receive instructions and proceed from there, and that there was no major discussion planned at that point. The project was to design a new remote control that should be original, trendy, and user-friendly. Betty said functional design, conceptual design, and detailed design would each involve individual work followed by a team discussion. Eileen summarized these as the three design types. When Betty said she could not write with the tool, Eileen joked that they could redesign it after finishing the remote control.

### Whiteboard tool training
Betty proposed trying the whiteboard so participants could draw their favourite animal, helping the team learn how it worked in case they needed to present something on it at the next meeting. She asked Eileen to try it; Eileen agreed and said she would see whether she remembered how to draw a cat or rabbit. Betty reminded her to press the control so the drawing would be recorded. Francina also tried the whiteboard, drawing a snake after Jeanne-Oui suggested one. Betty invited Francina to try it herself so she could get a feel for the tool. The team briefly clarified that the marks did not need to be wiped off immediately.

### Project finances
Betty said the team needed to keep project finances in mind while designing. The intended selling price was 25 euros, the company’s profit target was 50 million euros, the market was international with an unlimited range, and production cost should ideally be below 12.50 euros and must not exceed that amount. Betty emphasized that the budget should inform choices such as materials and cost. Eileen noted that the targets would keep the team challenged.

### Initial ideas for the remote control
Betty asked whether anyone had experience with remote controls and what they disliked or wanted to improve, including whether the device should be smaller or larger and whether it needed more or better-marked buttons. Francina said remotes should be compact because current ones were very long, and suggested a multipurpose device that could control a television as well as other household equipment, such as an audio player, temperature, air-conditioning, and heating systems. Betty agreed that the idea was a multifunctional gadget for household devices.

Eileen agreed that successful marketing would require the product to do more than existing remotes. Betty and Francina said it should be new and different, and the design should be trendy. Betty, Jeanne-Oui, and Francina discussed distinguishing it through different colours, materials, and shapes. Betty suggested a kidney-shaped form that would feel better in the hand, and Eileen agreed that a friendly shape would help.

### Finding a misplaced remote
Eileen proposed that the remote beep when someone clapped, because people often lose it. Betty agreed that remotes can end up under a newspaper or behind a plant, particularly when someone wants to turn off the television after the phone rings. The group considered a sound or light signal to help locate it. Jeanne-Oui suggested a light so users could recognize where the remote was; Betty said the signal could be a beep or a light.

Eileen asked what should trigger the signal, suggesting a clap or voice response. Betty proposed a sensor that would activate when the remote was hidden in a dark place, such as under a newspaper or sweater or behind a plant. Eileen restated that a light sensor would activate the signal, and Betty agreed. Betty thought voice or clapping might not be specific or reliable enough, noting that clap-operated lamps only work to a certain degree. Eileen observed that a remote could be in an obvious place and still be difficult to find. The discussion was cut short so the team could move on, with Betty saying they had good initial points.

### Individual work and next meeting
Betty said the next meeting would be in 30 minutes and checked that participants had received notices on their computers. She assigned Jeanne-Oui the working design, clarifying that it concerned the technical-functional design, and assigned Francina the functional design. Eileen, as marketing manager, was to develop user requirement specifications, including friendliness and the general ideas discussed, as well as consider the price. Eileen said the team would need to justify the given price by providing enough features to make the product sell at that price. Betty said specific instructions would be provided. She noted that about two or three minutes remained, invited questions or suggestions, and said the team would meet again in about 30 minutes to review what they had developed."}

{"summary":"Betty, the project manager for today, opened the meeting with introductions: Francina handles user-interface design for a television remote control; Eileen works in marketing and sales; and Jeanne-Oui is the industrial designer, responsible for technical-functional design and user-interface specifications. The team reviewed the project plan and agreed the remote should be original, trendy, and user-friendly. Functional, conceptual, and detailed design work would be done individually and discussed at meetings, with instructions to follow. Eileen volunteered to try the whiteboard so the team could learn it before a future presentation, and participants practiced drawing. The stated financial targets were a selling price of 25 euros, a company profit aim of 50 million euros, an unlimited international market, and production cost below 12.50 euros. The team favored a compact, multi-purpose remote that could control household devices such as audio equipment, air-conditioning, and heating, with distinctive styling, colors, materials, and shapes. They also discussed a beep or light to help locate a misplaced remote, potentially activated by a sensor when it is in a dark or covered spot; voice or clapping might not be reliable enough. For the next work period, Jeanne-Oui would develop the working, technical-functional design; Francina was assigned the functional design; and Eileen would prepare user-requirement specifications covering friendliness and features that justify the given price. Betty said specific instructions would be provided and the team would reconvene in about 30 minutes.","mom":"### Introductions and roles
Betty said she was the project manager for today. She asked everyone to introduce themselves and describe their function. Francina said she was responsible for user-interface design and would design the television remote control. Eileen said she worked in marketing and wanted to figure out how to sell the product. Jeanne-Oui said she was the industrial designer, responsible for technical-functional designs and user-interface specifications and design. Betty suggested that the team review the presentation.

### Project plan and design brief
Betty outlined the opening, introductions, tool training, and project plan. She said each person would receive instructions and they would take it from there; she did not expect a major discussion at that point. The project was to design a new remote control that should be original, trendy, and user-friendly. Betty said functional, conceptual, and detailed design would involve individual work followed by discussion at a meeting. Eileen summarized these as three types of design. When Betty said she could not write with the tool, Eileen joked that they could redesign it after finishing the remote control.

### Whiteboard tool training
Betty proposed trying the whiteboard by drawing favourite animals, so the team could learn how it worked in case they needed to present something on it at the next meeting. She asked Eileen to try it; Eileen agreed and said she would see whether she remembered how to draw a cat or rabbit. Betty reminded her to press the control so the drawing would be recorded. Francina also tried the whiteboard, drawing a snake after Jeanne-Oui suggested one; Betty invited Francina to try it to get a feel for the tool. The team clarified that the marks did not need to be wiped off immediately, and Betty said they would deal with that later.

### Project finances
Betty said everyone had to consider project finances when designing. The selling-price target was 25 euros, the company’s profit aim was 50 million euros, the market range was unlimited (international), and production cost should ideally be less than 12.50 euros and must not exceed that amount. Betty said the budget should inform choices such as materials and cost. Eileen noted that the targets would keep everyone challenged.

### Initial ideas for the remote control
Betty asked about experience with remote controls and what participants disliked or wanted to improve, including size and whether more or better-marked buttons were needed. Francina said remotes should be very compact because current ones were very long, and suggested a multi-purpose remote that could control a television as well as other household equipment, such as an audio player, temperature, air-conditioning, and heating systems. Betty agreed that it could be a multifunctional gadget for household devices.

Eileen said successful marketing would require the product to do more than existing remotes. Betty, Francina, and Jeanne-Oui supported making it new, different, and trendy, with different colors, materials, and shapes. Betty suggested a kidney-shaped form that would feel better in the hand; Eileen agreed that a friendly shape would help.

### Finding a misplaced remote
Eileen proposed that the remote beep when someone clapped because people often lose it. Betty agreed that remotes can end up under a newspaper or behind a plant, and described wanting to turn off the television when the phone rings but not being able to find the remote. The group considered a sound or light signal. Jeanne-Oui suggested a light to help users recognize where the remote was; Betty said the signal could be a beep or a light.

Eileen asked what should trigger the signal, suggesting a clap or voice response. Betty proposed a sensor that would activate when the remote was hidden in a dark place, such as under a newspaper or sweater or behind a plant. Eileen restated that a light sensor would activate the signal, and Betty agreed. Betty said a sensor was needed and thought voice or clapping might not be specific enough, noting that clap-operated lamps only work to a certain degree. Eileen observed that a remote could be in an obvious place and still be difficult to find. The discussion was cut short so the team could move on; Betty said they had good initial points.

### Individual work and next meeting
Betty said the next meeting would be in 30 minutes and checked whether participants had received computer notices. She assigned Jeanne-Oui the working design, clarifying that it was the technical-functional design, and assigned Francina the functional design. Eileen, as marketing manager, was to develop user-requirement specifications covering friendliness and the general ideas discussed, as well as price. Eileen said the given price would have to be justified with enough features to make the product sell at that price. Betty said specific instructions would be provided. {"title":"TV Remote-Control Design, Features, and Target Market","summary":"The team discussed the remote-control project’s marketing and design direction: collect broad, specific feature suggestions, then screen them for design and budget feasibility and prioritize customer appeal. Marketing proposed an attractive, intuitive product with few easy-to-learn buttons, features to help locate it such as light and a beep, and a €25 impulse-purchase price aimed at Christmas; it would need to be on the market by September. Management constraints ruled out whole-house or multi-device control and teletext, limiting the product to TV control, and required the company’s corporate colors and design to be recognizable. The industrial designer described the remote’s battery-powered circuitry and infrared signaling, and suggested illuminated or fluorescent markings, a beep, child lock, varied shapes and colors, clear labels, and a clock; the interface presentation also raised timers, alarms, channel locks, compactness, safe materials, and child-safe rounded design. The team considered one basic remote with optional cosmetic variations or replaceable cases, rather than three separate devices, and discussed accommodating children, older adults, and users who find small buttons or mode changes difficult; larger or differently shaped buttons were possible, but cost and budget would determine feasibility. The project manager summarized the target market as essentially everyone with a TV, with subgroup features considered only if money permits; the meeting ended for lunch, with some points left for further research and discussion."}

{"mom":"### Marketing approach and commercial requirements
The Project Manager confirmed that participants had received instructions and asked Marketing to begin by addressing needs and desires. Marketing said the initial process should gather broad suggestions, including unconventional ideas, then eliminate options that were infeasible in design or budget and prioritize those most attractive to customers. Marketing would consult the Industrial Designer about development difficulty, cost, and schedule, and consult the User Interface representative about usability, features, appearance, and color. Timing was as important as money: Marketing wanted the product on the market by September to sell for Christmas, with a target price of 25 euros and the appeal of an impulse purchase. Marketing emphasized a compelling selling point, intuitive use, as few buttons as practical, and a product attractive enough to prompt an immediate purchase; a possible marketing motto was “fashion in electronics.”

### Scope restrictions and customer research
Marketing reported that initial research suggested whole-house control was not feasible within the intended budget, and asked for specific suggestions that could be evaluated and crossed off. Marketing thought control of a TV, VCR, stereo, and perhaps a coffee pot or lamp might fit the price point. The Project Manager relayed instructions from higher management: teletext should be excluded as outdated; the product should control only the TV because adding other devices was considered too complex and would threaten time to market; and the company’s corporate image, color, and design should be maintained so the product would be clearly identifiable as the company’s. The Project Manager said these constraints were mandatory and reiterated that the scope was TV control only.

Marketing cited research indicating that 34 percent of complaints about current remote controls concerned the time needed to learn them, while another major complaint was that remotes were often lost in a room. Marketing therefore supported simplicity, intuitive operation, and ways to locate the remote, such as an emitting light or beep. Marketing also stressed that engineering effectiveness alone would not ensure Christmas sales to purchasers buying for a child, spouse, or another family member.

### Industrial design: operating principle and proposed features
The Industrial Designer explained that a remote’s integrated circuit acts as its brain, drawing power from a battery so the remote can be carried around rather than connected to mains electricity. A button press supplies an input; the circuitry converts it into infrared signals sent to the controlled device, such as a TV or air conditioner. A remote designed for multiple devices would require compatible frequencies and devices able to recognize the signals and respond. The designer said multi-device control would be difficult, and the group noted that management had already eliminated it. The designer described the user interface as buttons or a switch pad that directs the circuit to send commands such as changing channels or volume, muting, or applying a child lock.

The Industrial Designer proposed relatively simple, low-investment additions: fluorescent or light-emitting button markings to make the remote easier to find in the dark; a beep when many buttons are pressed at once, such as when a child plays with it; and a child lock to prevent unwanted button presses. The designer also suggested a range of hand-comfortable shapes, including animal shapes, and different colors. The Project Manager said that making one mold would mean the shape—square or otherwise—would not greatly change the budget. Marketing asked whether the same electronics and buttons could be offered in several shapes for marketing appeal; the designer said this was possible, while the Project Manager said the budget would need review and considered the idea fun. Marketing suggested an adult-oriented shape and playful shapes for children, such as an animal or elephant that might help a child remember where the remote was. The designer agreed that different shapes and colors were possible.

The designer noted a trade-off between adding features and increasing button count: more buttons could make the remote more complicated, while too few features might make it unattractive. The designer considered assigning multiple operations to buttons in different modes, but acknowledged that this could add complexity. Marketing said this needed discussion with the User Interface representative and argued for one button per feature because mode changes can be difficult to learn, particularly for users who do not work with computers constantly. The Project Manager noted that older users or people with arthritic hands could struggle with small buttons and accidentally press the wrong one, becoming frustrated. Marketing suggested differently shaped buttons to support tactile recognition, such as a triangle for volume and a square for channel changes. The Industrial Designer also stressed that button text should be clear and unambiguous.

The Industrial Designer proposed displaying a clock, saying it could be added to the integrated circuit without extra cost. Marketing supported the idea as user-friendly, noting that viewers may want to check the time while watching a program or the news. The designer also listed components: buttons and switches, bulbs or lights, a battery, an integrated circuit, connecting wires, and a case or holder. One lighting idea was for the remote to light when the TV was on, helping users locate it even if the TV had been switched on by another means; infrared bulbs were also mentioned for use in darkness. The designer said they had consulted the company website for points about how the working design operates and offered to let the team review it.

### User Interface research and preferences
The User Interface representative said they had researched features users might want. A remote should switch the TV on and off and control its functions from a distance, transmitting signals by radio wave, infrared light, or LED. The representative proposed a timer to switch the TV on for a chosen program—for example, at 9 o’clock—and a child lock to block a channel from children of a particular age. They also described compactness as desirable, personally suggesting a T-shaped form, and said the material should be safe for children and adults and not cause skin disease or allergy. An alarm clock was proposed as another feature; the representative gave 8 p.m. as an example time for setting an alarm and thought it would not cost much. The Industrial Designer agreed that a clock could support an alarm clock. The representative also proposed fluorescent buttons that glow differently so users can identify them in the dark, and a design without sharp projections that could harm a child playing with the remote. Their research found remotes using infrared and others using radio waves, with different signal sources available for controlling television functions. The representative’s stated preferences included multipurpose use as a TV control and alarm clock, a child lock, and limiting circuitry to help save electricity. They also proposed automatically switching the TV off at 10 o’clock if parents set that time.

### Target group and product variants
The Project Manager said the meeting needed to decide the target group and the product’s function and working design. The initial view was that the target group was essentially everyone who owned a TV, since few people were thought to be without one. The Project Manager identified subgroups, including older people with limited finger and hand function, people who might be nervous about pressing small buttons unless controls were very clear, and children; the Project Manager asked how much the product should cater to children. Marketing noted the saying that children under six never shop alone and argued that a product appealing to children could influence parents’ purchases. The Project Manager suggested that children’s appeal could be addressed through shape and color, while asking whether the team should make one design for everyone or consider different shapes and buttons for subgroups.

The User Interface representative suggested a general design for people aged 10 to 40, with additional functional buttons for children, older people, and people with nervous problems. The Industrial Designer suggested different remotes with larger buttons for older users. The User Interface representative countered that a family would include older people, children, and middle-aged adults and would not want to buy three separate remotes; the family would prefer one that served all of them. The designer agreed one shared design was possible but said it could not simply be made very large for older users, so a separate larger remote might be considered. Marketing asked whether different electronics would affect cost, and the designer said the cost would not change much.

The Project Manager clarified that the main question was the target group and how the remote would function, especially its buttons, and whether the budget could support more than one design. As an example, the Project Manager asked whether 40 percent of production could have large buttons and the rest regular buttons. The Project Manager summarized the target group as everyone with a TV and said subgroup-specific features would depend on available money. Marketing asked whether one remote could serve everyone or whether the same electronics could be put in three different shapes. Marketing suggested that only the plastic case might differ; the Industrial Designer did not think molded plastic would add much cost. The Project Manager proposed removable plastic cases, like those on portable phones, with a striped or fluorescent-blue case and another color included in the package, while additional colors could be purchased separately. Marketing agreed that this was a promising idea, and the Industrial Designer compared it to interchangeable mobile-phone covers. The User Interface representative raised the cost-effectiveness question of including features for different groups in one remote versus designing three remotes for three categories. The Project Manager favored one remote with cosmetic or functional variations such as larger, illuminated, or differently shaped buttons, but said the budget would determine whether this was possible.

### Conclusion and next steps
The Project Manager summarized the tentative position: the target group was everyone, and features for subgroups could be addressed if money permitted. The Industrial Designer proposed a possible allocation of 70 percent for a standard remote and 30 percent for a distinctive version; the Project Manager said the budget would determine whether that could be done. The group agreed to continue research and revisit some points at the next meeting. The Project Manager said the meeting would break for lunch and that participants would meet again afterward."}
