{"mom":"### Opening and agenda
The Project Manager opened the second meeting and said the team was moving into the functional-design phase. The goal was to agree on the user requirements, technical functional design, and working design so the project could proceed to the second phase. The Project Manager announced that air-conditioning work in wings C and E could cause temporary discomfort for a couple of days; it was expected to be cold, so the system would not be needed. The Project Manager would take the minutes. Each participant would present, with 40 minutes available for all presentations, discussion of the new project requirements that had been sent to the Project Manager, and decisions about which control functions to include. The Project Manager suggested about 7 minutes per presentation; Marketing volunteered to present first.

### Marketing research and recommendations
Freek Van Ponnen, the Market Expert, reported on usability-lab research in which users operated remote controls and completed a questionnaire; there were 100 test subjects. The team had also researched the market and age distribution. He said 75% of respondents considered their remote controls ugly, while a further 80% said they would pay more for a more attractive remote. Half said they used only about 10% of the buttons, and half said their remote tended to get lost in the room. Channel selection and volume selection each scored 10 out of 10 for relevance, the power button scored 9, and teletext scored 6.5. Audio, video, and channel-setting buttons were less frequently used but still considered somewhat important. Channel selection was reportedly used 168 times per hour.

Freek said 60% of the market consisted of users aged 16–45, while users aged 46–65 made up 40%. He described the younger group as interested in new features but critical and reluctant to spend money; the older group was less interested in features but spent more readily. He recommended a future-oriented, attractive remote aimed at ages 16–45, which he identified as the largest market segment and the main source of potential profit. He also said about one quarter of respondents thought remote controls caused RSI, and 34% found it difficult to learn to operate a new remote; he recommended accounting for both concerns in the design.

He suggested using few buttons and emphasizing the most frequently used controls, especially channel and audio selection, so they would be robust and less likely to break. Because many respondents lost their remotes, he proposed considering a docking station that could send a signal to make the remote beep and recharge its batteries. He cautioned that this could substantially increase production costs. He also said many respondents, particularly those aged 16–25, preferred an LCD screen; it remained feasible up to age 45, but would also increase production costs. The Project Manager invited questions about the functional requirements; the User Interface Designer and Industrial Designer had none.

### User-interface concept
The User Interface Designer presented an idea for a remote that could control multiple devices, such as a DVD player, television, and stereo, while remaining user-friendly. They proposed retaining familiar general controls, including a red on/off button, and using a touchscreen display for device-specific functions. Physical buttons would select the device, with a separate display area and buttons for each device rather than showing every function at once. The Designer recommended keeping the physical buttons simple and large enough for both older and younger users.

The Industrial Designer questioned whether a touchscreen would exceed the 12.5-euro price point. The User Interface Designer replied that a basic, single-colour touchscreen could be inexpensive, citing an internet example priced at 20 euros or less. The Marketing representative noted that a touchscreen could make the design attractive; the Industrial Designer cautioned that it would be fragile and could be scratched. The Project Manager suggested continuing with the remaining presentation before discussing requirements and design.

### Working-design presentation
The Industrial Designer explained that pressing a remote button causes the remote to identify the button and send an infrared signal to the television, which then changes channel or performs the indicated function. The circuit plate has conductive disks for each button; pressing one sends a signal to a chip, which controls the infrared LED. The Designer described the device as technically simple and recommended standard materials, such as simple plastics, and straightforward internal components to ensure robustness. They argued that the team should invest in aesthetics, design, and user interface rather than high-tech materials, which would sharply increase the price and add cost to every product, whereas the remote would only need to be designed once.

### Revised product requirements and target market
The Project Manager introduced new requirements: the remote would be suitable only for televisions, because supporting more functions would make it too complex and lengthen time to market. It should therefore be simple. The Project Manager proposed omitting teletext, reasoning that it would become obsolete as internet access became available on televisions, and mentioned internet as a possible function. The stated target was customers aged 40 and above, because the company was developing a new product specifically for younger customers; the Project Manager acknowledged that this differed from Marketing’s proposed younger target. The product should clearly express the corporate image through its design and operation.

Marketing objected to omitting teletext, arguing that television internet access was unlikely to be common among people aged 40 and above for perhaps the next 20 years, and that respondents had identified teletext as an important remote-control feature. Marketing also questioned whether the 40-plus market was large enough. The Project Manager responded that people aged 40 and above, including those over 50, represented the largest share of the population in Holland, and suggested a design using only two or three buttons could serve that segment. Marketing countered that this was not necessarily the largest market, and described older users as less critical and likely to accept any remote that worked and looked acceptable. Marketing said a distinctive, attractive remote would be more compelling to people aged 16–45, who were more critical and wanted a fancy product, while people over 40 mainly wanted it to work. The Industrial Designer suggested that suitable marketing could make a product for older customers successful, comparing the opportunity to an elderly-oriented mobile phone reported as a big success; the Designer said a change in project focus could still lead to sales, while emphasizing functionality as well as design.

The Project Manager proposed examining requirements for an older target group and restated that channel selection, volume selection, and power were important functions. Although Marketing noted that the board seemed to disagree about teletext, the Project Manager clarified that no vote had yet occurred and said teletext could be retained if it did not raise costs substantially. The User Interface Designer noted that deaf users needed teletext for subtitles, and Marketing agreed. No participant objected to retaining teletext. The Project Manager suggested a dedicated button for large subtitles, which could be useful to older users, and the Industrial Designer supported the idea.

### Control functions, docking station, and display
The Project Manager agreed that the remote should have few buttons and remain simple. Marketing said that, since the remote would operate only a television, it would not require many controls: number buttons from 0 to 9, next- and previous-channel controls, volume up and down, and some teletext buttons. Marketing argued that many television remotes already had a minimal set of buttons, so reducing the count alone would provide little competitive advantage. The Project Manager maintained that button placement and design mattered and could be improved with fewer buttons. Marketing replied that differentiating a television-only remote would be difficult and might require a substantial marketing campaign, one reason for limiting the product to television given the short time to market. The Project Manager suggested prioritizing a docking station or other additional functions rather than spending much time reducing button count; Marketing agreed that button placement mattered but did not warrant much time.

The Project Manager asked whether a docking station could fit the budget. The Industrial Designer said it should be possible if it was not too elaborate and the remote remained small. The Project Manager considered a distinctive docking station a potential advantage, and the group agreed to focus on extras. Marketing proposed researching what older users would want in a new remote. The Project Manager returned to the finding that 50% of respondents said their remotes tended to get lost. The group discussed an audio signal activated from the docking station, like a phone that rings when a button is pressed, as a way to locate the remote; the Project Manager thought this should be possible without much expense.

The Project Manager raised the possibility of an LCD screen but was unsure whether it would increase costs too much. The Industrial Designer said the team might have to choose between the screen and docking station. Marketing proposed a small, inexpensive, non-touchscreen display that could explain what a button does when pressed, because respondents found new remotes hard to learn and the older target group might have difficulty understanding new devices. The Project Manager supported adding basic feedback information but Marketing questioned whether the small screen would fit the costs. The Project Manager listed the emerging design considerations: attractive design, ease of learning, few buttons, a docking station, an LCD screen, and general functions. The Project Manager also supported standard materials, noting that older users would not care whether the cover was titanium or plastic. Marketing suggested older users might take better care of their remotes than younger users.

### Target-group and market considerations
The Project Manager asked whether the intended group was older people generally or people aged 40–80, and suggested the design might be for people over 60. The Project Manager compared this with a product specifically aimed at older users and asked what the team wanted to target. Marketing said that a product aimed at the genuinely elderly could benefit the company’s image and might have a good market if it were genuinely innovative, but further research was needed to assess the 60–80 group. The Industrial Designer questioned whether television sets differed across countries. The group also discussed the small display as a way to explain controls in different languages and adapt the product to different cultures; the Project Manager said a separate language button could be unnecessary if versions were offered for different markets. The Project Manager noted that only five minutes remained.

### Follow-up work and close
The Project Manager said the minutes would be placed in the project document folder. The Project Manager will place the minutes in the project document folder; for the next meeting, the Industrial Designer will prepare the components concept, the User Interface Designer the interface concept, and the team will address trend-watching, using the target group and requirements as guidance, with specific instructions to follow from the personal coach.","mom":"### Opening and agenda
The Project Manager opened the second meeting and said the team was moving into the functional-design phase. The goal was to agree on the user requirements, technical functional design, and working design so the project could proceed to the second phase. The Project Manager announced that air-conditioning work in wings C and E could cause temporary discomfort for a couple of days; it was expected to be cold, so the system would not be needed. The Project Manager would take the minutes. Each participant would present, with 40 minutes available for all presentations, discussion of the new project requirements that had been sent to the Project Manager, and decisions about which control functions to include. The Project Manager suggested about 7 minutes per presentation; Marketing volunteered to present first.

### Marketing research and recommendations
Freek Van Ponnen, the Market Expert, reported on usability-lab research in which users operated remote controls and completed a questionnaire; there were 100 test subjects. The team had also researched the market and age distribution. He said 75% of respondents considered their remote controls ugly, while a further 80% said they would pay more for a more attractive remote. Half said they used only about 10% of the buttons, and half said their remote tended to get lost in the room. Channel selection and volume selection each scored 10 out of 10 for relevance, the power button scored 9, and teletext scored 6.5. Audio, video, and channel-setting buttons were less frequently used but still considered somewhat important. Channel selection was reportedly used 168 times per hour.

Freek said 60% of the market consisted of users aged 16–45, while users aged 46–65 made up 40%. He described the younger group as interested in new features but critical and reluctant to spend money; the older group was less interested in features but spent more readily. He recommended a future-oriented, attractive remote aimed at ages 16–45, which he identified as the largest market segment and the main source of potential profit. He also said about one quarter of respondents thought remote controls caused RSI, and 34% found it difficult to learn to operate a new remote; he recommended accounting for both concerns in the design.

He suggested using few buttons and emphasizing the most frequently used controls, especially channel and audio selection, so they would be robust and less likely to break. Because many respondents lost their remotes, he proposed considering a docking station that could send a signal to make the remote beep and recharge its batteries. He cautioned that this could substantially increase production costs. He also said many respondents, particularly those aged 16–25, preferred an LCD screen; it remained feasible up to age 45, but would also increase production costs. The Project Manager invited questions about the functional requirements; the User Interface Designer and Industrial Designer had none.

### User-interface concept
The User Interface Designer presented an idea for a remote that could control multiple devices, such as a DVD player, television, and stereo, while remaining user-friendly. They proposed retaining familiar general controls, including a red on/off button, and using a touchscreen display for device-specific functions. Physical buttons would select the device, with a separate display area and buttons for each device rather than showing every function at once. The Designer recommended keeping the physical buttons simple and large enough for both older and younger users.

The Industrial Designer questioned whether a touchscreen would exceed the 12.5-euro price point. The User Interface Designer replied that a basic, single-colour touchscreen could be inexpensive, citing an internet example priced at 20 euros or less. The Marketing representative noted that a touchscreen could make the design attractive; the Industrial Designer cautioned that it would be fragile and could be scratched. The Project Manager suggested continuing with the remaining presentation before discussing requirements and design.

### Working-design presentation
The Industrial Designer explained that pressing a remote button causes the remote to identify the button and send an infrared signal to the television, which then changes channel or performs the indicated function. The circuit plate has conductive disks for each button; pressing one sends a signal to a chip, which controls the infrared LED. The Designer described the device as technically simple and recommended standard materials, such as simple plastics, and straightforward internal components to ensure robustness. They argued that the team should invest in aesthetics, design, and user interface rather than high-tech materials, which would sharply increase the price and add cost to every product, whereas the remote would only need to be designed once.

### Revised product requirements and target market
The Project Manager introduced new requirements: the remote would be suitable only for televisions, because supporting more functions would make it too complex and lengthen time to market. It should therefore be simple. The Project Manager proposed omitting teletext, reasoning that it would become obsolete as internet access became available on televisions, and mentioned internet as a possible function. The stated target was customers aged 40 and above, because the company was developing a new product specifically for younger customers; the Project Manager acknowledged that this differed from Marketing’s proposed younger target. The product should clearly express the corporate image through its design and operation.

Marketing objected to omitting teletext, arguing that television internet access was unlikely to be common among people aged 40 and above for perhaps the next 20 years, and that respondents had identified teletext as an important remote-control feature. Marketing also questioned whether the 40-plus market was large enough. The Project Manager responded that people aged 40 and above, including those over 50, represented the largest share of the population in Holland, and suggested a design using only two or three buttons could serve that segment. Marketing countered that this was not necessarily the largest market, and described older users as less critical and likely to accept any remote that worked and looked acceptable. Marketing said a distinctive, attractive remote would be more compelling to people aged 16–45, who were more critical and wanted a fancy product, while people over 40 mainly wanted it to work. The Industrial Designer suggested that suitable marketing could make a product for older customers successful, comparing the opportunity to an elderly-oriented mobile phone reported as a big success; the Designer said a change in project focus could still lead to sales, while emphasizing functionality as well as design.

The Project Manager proposed examining requirements for an older target group and restated that channel selection, volume selection, and power were important functions. Although Marketing noted that the board seemed to disagree about teletext, the Project Manager clarified that no vote had yet occurred and said teletext could be retained if it did not raise costs substantially. The User Interface Designer noted that deaf users needed teletext for subtitles, and Marketing agreed. No participant objected to retaining teletext. The Project Manager suggested a dedicated button for large subtitles, which could be useful to older users, and the Industrial Designer supported the idea.

### Control functions, docking station, and display
The Project Manager agreed that the remote should have few buttons and remain simple. Marketing said that, since the remote would operate only a television, it would not require many controls: number buttons from 0 to 9, next- and previous-channel controls, volume up and down, and some teletext buttons. Marketing argued that many television remotes already had a minimal set of buttons, so reducing the count alone would provide little competitive advantage. The Project Manager maintained that button placement and design mattered and could be improved with fewer buttons. Marketing replied that differentiating a television-only remote would be difficult and might require a substantial marketing campaign, one reason for limiting the product to television given the short time to market. The Project Manager suggested prioritizing a docking station or other additional functions rather than spending much time reducing button count; Marketing agreed that button placement mattered but did not warrant much time.

The Project Manager asked whether a docking station could fit the budget. The Industrial Designer said it should be possible if it was not too elaborate and the remote remained small. The Project Manager considered a distinctive docking station a potential advantage, and the group agreed to focus on extras. Marketing proposed researching what older users would want in a new remote. The Project Manager returned to the finding that 50% of respondents said their remotes tended to get lost. The group discussed an audio signal activated from the docking station, like a phone that rings when a button is pressed, as a way to locate the remote; the Project Manager thought this should be possible without much expense.

The Project Manager raised the possibility of an LCD screen but was unsure whether it would increase costs too much. The Industrial Designer said the team might have to choose between the screen and docking station. Marketing proposed a small, inexpensive, non-touchscreen display that could explain what a button does when pressed, because respondents found new remotes hard to learn and the older target group might have difficulty understanding new devices. The Project Manager supported adding basic feedback information but Marketing questioned whether the small screen would fit the costs. The Project Manager listed the emerging design considerations: attractive design, ease of learning, few buttons, a docking station, an LCD screen, and general functions. The Project Manager also supported standard materials, noting that older users would not care whether the cover was titanium or plastic. Marketing suggested older users might take better care of their remotes than younger users.

### Target-group and market considerations
The Project Manager asked whether the intended group was older people generally or people aged 40–80, and suggested the design might be for people over 60. The Project Manager compared this with a product specifically aimed at older users and asked what the team wanted to target. Marketing said that a product aimed at the genuinely elderly could benefit the company’s image and might have a good market if it were genuinely innovative, but further research was needed to assess the 60–80 group. The Industrial Designer questioned whether television sets differed across countries. The group also discussed the small display as a way to explain controls in different languages and adapt the product to different cultures; the Project Manager said a separate language button could be unnecessary if versions were offered for different markets. The Project Manager noted that only five minutes remained.

### Follow-up work and close
The Project Manager said the minutes would be placed in the project document folder. For the next meeting, the Industrial Designer would prepare the components concept, the User Interface Designer would prepare the user-interface concept, and the team would do trend-watching. The Project Manager asked everyone to keep the target group, requirements, and current trends in mind; specific instructions would be sent by the personal coach. The circuit plate has conductive disks for each button; pressing one sends a signal to a chip, which controls the infrared LED. The Designer described the device as technically simple and recommended standard materials, such as simple plastics, and straightforward internal components to ensure robustness. They argued that the team should invest in aesthetics, design, and user interface rather than high-tech materials, which would sharply increase the price and add cost to every product, whereas the remote would only need to be designed once.

### Revised product requirements and target market
The Project Manager introduced new requirements: the remote would be suitable only for televisions, because supporting more functions would make it too complex and lengthen time to market. It should therefore be simple. The Project Manager proposed omitting teletext, reasoning that it would become obsolete as internet access became available on televisions, and mentioned internet as a possible function. The stated target was customers aged 40 and above, because the company was developing a new product specifically for younger customers; the Project Manager acknowledged that this differed from Marketing’s proposed younger target. The product should clearly express the corporate image through its design and operation.

Marketing objected to omitting teletext, arguing that television internet access was unlikely to be common among people aged 40 and above for perhaps the next 20 years, and that respondents had identified teletext as an important remote-control feature. Marketing also questioned whether the 40-plus market was large enough. The Project Manager responded that people aged 40 and above, including those over 50, represented the largest share of the population in Holland, and suggested a design using only two or three buttons could serve that segment. Marketing countered that this was not necessarily the largest market, and described older users as less critical and likely to accept any remote that worked and looked acceptable. Marketing said a distinctive, attractive remote would be more compelling to people aged 16–45, who were more critical and wanted a fancy product, while people over 40 mainly wanted it to work. The Industrial Designer suggested that suitable marketing could make a product for older customers successful, comparing the opportunity to an elderly-oriented mobile phone reported as a big success; the Designer said a change in project focus could still lead to sales, while emphasizing functionality as well as design.

The Project Manager proposed examining requirements for an older target group and restated that channel selection, volume selection, and power were important functions. Although Marketing noted that the board seemed to disagree about teletext, the Project Manager clarified that no vote had yet occurred and said teletext could be retained if it did not raise costs substantially. The User Interface Designer noted that deaf users needed teletext for subtitles, and Marketing agreed. No participant objected to retaining teletext. The Project Manager suggested a dedicated button for large subtitles, which could be useful to older users, and the Industrial Designer supported the idea.

### Control functions, docking station, and display
The Project Manager agreed that the remote should have few buttons and remain simple. Marketing said that, since the remote would operate only a television, it would not require many controls: number buttons from 0 to 9, next- and previous-channel controls, volume up and down, and some teletext buttons. Marketing argued that many television remotes already had a minimal set of buttons, so reducing the count alone would provide little competitive advantage. The Project Manager maintained that button placement and design mattered and could be improved with fewer buttons. Marketing replied that differentiating a television-only remote would be difficult and might require a substantial marketing campaign, one reason for limiting the product to television given the short time to market. The Project Manager suggested prioritizing a docking station or other additional functions rather than spending much time reducing button count; Marketing agreed that button placement mattered but did not warrant much time.

The Project Manager asked whether a docking station could fit the budget. The Industrial Designer said it should be possible if it was not too elaborate and the remote remained small. The Project Manager considered a distinctive docking station a potential advantage, and the group agreed to focus on extras. Marketing proposed researching what older users would want in a new remote. The Project Manager returned to the finding that 50% of respondents said their remotes tended to get lost. The group discussed an audio signal activated from the docking station, like a phone that rings when a button is pressed, as a way to locate the remote; the Project Manager thought this should be possible without much expense.

The Project Manager raised the possibility of an LCD screen but was unsure whether it would increase costs too much. The Industrial Designer said the team might have to choose between the screen and docking station. Marketing proposed a small, inexpensive, non-touchscreen display that could explain what a button does when pressed, because respondents found new remotes hard to learn and the older target group might have difficulty understanding new devices. The Project Manager supported adding basic feedback information but Marketing questioned whether the small screen would fit the costs. The Project Manager listed the emerging design considerations: attractive design, ease of learning, few buttons, a docking station, an LCD screen, and general functions. The Project Manager also supported standard materials, noting that older users would not care whether the cover was titanium or plastic. Marketing suggested older users might take better care of their remotes than younger users.

### Target-group and market considerations
The Project Manager asked whether the intended group was older people generally or people aged 40–80, and suggested the design might be for people over 60. The Project Manager compared this with a product specifically aimed at older users and asked what the team wanted to target. Marketing said that a product aimed at the genuinely elderly could benefit the company’s image and might have a good market if it were genuinely innovative, but further research was needed to assess the 60–80 group. The Industrial Designer questioned whether television sets differed across countries. The group also discussed the small display as a way to explain controls in different languages and adapt the product to different cultures; the Project Manager said a separate language button could be unnecessary if versions were offered for different markets. The Project Manager noted that only five minutes remained.

### Follow-up work and close
The Project Manager said the minutes would be placed in the project document folder. For the next meeting, the Industrial Designer would prepare the components concept, the User Interface Designer would prepare the user-interface concept, and the team would do trend-watching. The Project Manager asked everyone to keep the target group, requirements, and current trends in mind; specific instructions would be sent by the personal coach. {"mom":"### Opening and agenda
The Project Manager opened the third meeting, describing it as the second phase and a conceptual-design meeting. The meeting would cover conceptual specifications for components and design, along with trend-watching. The agenda was an opening, three presentations, a decision on remote-control concepts, and a closing; about 40 minutes were available. The Project Manager asked whether anyone had encountered preparation problems, and the User Interface representative said no.

### Review of previous meeting’s requirements and target market
The Project Manager recapped the previous meeting’s agreed requirements: teletext, a docking station, an audio signal, a small screen, button information as an extra, and default materials. The intended customers were people aged 60 to 80. The Project Manager invited comments or additional ideas; none were raised.

### Marketing presentation: trend-watching and customer preferences
Marketing reported conducting market research, distributing additional questionnaires, and sending trend-watchers to Milan and Paris to gather current trends. Marketing also consulted additional trend-watchers after the original group returned. The findings ranked fancy design as the most important factor, innovativeness at about half as important, and ease of use at about half the importance of innovativeness. Innovativeness meant functions not found on other remote controls. Among people aged 60 to 80, these factors were more evenly weighted. Older customers preferred dark colours, recognisable shapes, and familiar materials; surveys particularly indicated a preference for wood.

Marketing recommended that the remote control and docking station blend into the room, avoiding eye-catching designs and keeping the appearance simple. The docking station and small screen were identified as key innovative features to include. Trend-watchers recommended a telephone-like form, with the remote lying flat in its docking station rather than standing upright, because the upright shape would be unfamiliar to older people. Marketing proposed two editions: one with a wood-like colour and possibly feel for more affluent customers, and one in grey-black for customers with less means. The Project Manager invited questions; the User Interface representative had none.

### User Interface presentation: controls and display
The User Interface representative presented research on interface design, following the previous meeting’s discussion of using few buttons. They proposed focusing on primary functions and an attractive way to control the remote. Suggested features included speech recognition, a small display, large buttons, and a dedicated subtitle button. A single press would show small subtitles; a double press would show larger subtitles for people unable to read small text. The basic controls would include power, sound on/off and volume, number buttons from zero to nine, and channel up/down. The display could show button functions and the current television channel. The power button could be placed in a familiar corner, the display at the top where people would look, and channel controls where the thumb could reach them easily. The representative said the form still needed discussion.

### Industrial design presentation: component options
The Industrial Designer described a basic battery as the energy source, with kinetic energy as an optional alternative generated by shaking the remote, like a watch. Choosing kinetic energy would make the docking station obsolete, so the designer questioned whether it was a practical option. The manufacturing department could provide a flat, single-curved, or double-curved casing, with no technical restrictions; the designer also suggested a rubber anti-slip belt. Buttons could be plastic or rubber. The chipset should be advanced to support an LCD screen. Although trend research showed that customers liked wood, it would raise the price and might not fit the product image unless the team created two product lines. The designer said form should follow function and that choices of casing, supplement, and buttons depended on the design.

### Energy source and speech recognition
The Project Manager opened the concept discussion by prioritising the energy source because it affected production price and product image. The Industrial Designer outlined four options: a normal battery, a hand dynamo, solar cells, and kinetic energy. The designer dismissed the hand dynamo as impractical because users would have to wind it before watching television, and considered solar cells unsuitable because not every room was sufficiently light. Marketing asked how kinetic energy worked; the Industrial Designer explained that shaking the remote powers it. Marketing objected that older customers would not want to shake the remote before use and noted that kinetic power would eliminate the docking station, which could be an important marketing feature. The User Interface representative noted that the docking station could recharge batteries and potentially include a lost-remote function.

The User Interface representative estimated that the small display would use little energy and that one battery could last six months or more. The Project Manager said older people liked to keep things in place and might not want remotes left around the room, so a docking station could give the remote a designated place. The Project Manager also suggested placing a button on the docking station to make the remote beep when lost, which they considered more efficient and cheaper than using voice recognition for that purpose; voice recognition could still be used for channels. Marketing asked about the effect of voice recognition on production price. The Industrial Designer had no pricing information and said they would ask the manufacturing department.

Marketing reported that the target group’s market research showed they would not pay more for speech recognition in a remote control. Marketing advised against including it if it raised the selling price, suggesting it would be better suited to another product aimed at younger people. Marketing clarified that the research question had asked whether people preferred the feature, not whether they would pay extra, and argued that an LCD screen could make the remote easier to use. The User Interface representative asked whether the research concerned a large or small display; Marketing said it concerned an LCD screen like those on advanced mobile phones, so it was fairly large. The Project Manager said the team could retain the LCD screen and extra information because users could ignore it, but proposed discarding voice recognition because it would significantly increase cost and would not make the remote much easier to use. With voice recognition excluded, the Project Manager said energy use would be low and chose a simple rechargeable battery used with a docking station as a cheaper, equally good option than kinetic energy. The Industrial Designer agreed it was the best choice, and the Project Manager confirmed the battery decision.

### Chipset decision
The Project Manager moved to the chipset. The Industrial Designer said there was no real choice because the display required an advanced chipset. The Project Manager confirmed that the team would use an advanced chip.

### Casing materials and changeable covers
The Project Manager raised the choice between wood, black and grey, or both. The Project Manager noted that wood was more expensive to produce but could attract older customers seeking an exclusive item to show their grandchildren. Marketing suggested the key preference might be the wood colour rather than actual wood, so a wood-coloured finish could be sufficient. The Industrial Designer was unsure whether a wood-coloured finish would cost more and said they would research it; the Project Manager noted that real wood could be more difficult to handle and shape.

The User Interface representative proposed a changeable casing, similar to mobile-phone covers, so the team could make one standard remote and sell separate cases. The Project Manager supported the idea as an unusual feature that could provide a marketing advantage, including the possibility of advertising a new case as a gift for a grandfather. Marketing agreed but said the team would need to examine design costs and make the remote suitable for both a wooden-looking cover and a plastic cover. Marketing proposed one remote design with different covers rather than two different remote designs. The Project Manager checked whether everyone agreed to changeable covers; the Industrial Designer and User Interface representative agreed.

### Casing shape and docking arrangement
Marketing asked the Industrial Designer to explain the flat, single-curved, and double-curved casing options. The Industrial Designer described a flat case as straight, as found on many older remotes, and said the manufacturing department could also supply single- or double-curved cases. These choices affected form only, not price or functionality, and were up to the design department. The Project Manager asked whether the remote needed to stand upright; Marketing said it only needed to lie flat. The Project Manager discussed placing the docking station on or beside the television and fitting the remote into it.

The Industrial Designer recommended choosing the casing first as the basis for the rest of the design, and sketched the three options. The flat case was described as conventional. The Industrial Designer said a curved case might help prevent repetitive strain injury. The Project Manager preferred the single-curved option because its angle could make the screen easier for older people to see while using the remote. The group discussed placing the display on the upper surface.

### Interface layout and ergonomics
The Project Manager invited ideas about the interface and layout. The User Interface representative said a regular form could be used, though it might not look especially distinctive. Marketing referred to the proposed channel buttons being on the right so the thumb could reach them, noting that many remotes cause repetitive strain injury. Marketing suggested placing corresponding controls on both the left and right for left-handed users and said this could also allow a symmetrical design. The User Interface representative asked whether channel controls could be on one side and volume controls on the other. Marketing and the Project Manager cautioned that extra or duplicated buttons could make the remote harder to use and confuse people, particularly if the buttons had the same labels. The Project Manager considered a reversible remote, but the group found that arranging plus and minus controls for opposite orientations would not work well. The Project Manager concluded that the functions were basic enough for left-handed users to operate without a special shape, and suggested keeping a conventional form while making it more attractive.

The group developed the layout around the single-curved case. The User Interface representative proposed shaping the back to fit the hand and placing channel buttons within thumb reach. The Project Manager preferred the display at the top, noting that the user’s hand might block it if it were elsewhere; the Industrial Designer agreed that placing it at the top was logical, as on a mobile phone. The Project Manager sketched a layout with the display above the buttons and space for left- and right-handed users. The User Interface representative asked that the on/off button remain at the top. Marketing preferred rounded corners, which the Project Manager supported as a friendlier appearance. The group noted the rubber anti-slip supplement.

### Next steps and close
The Project Manager said the group now had a general concept and materials direction. For the next meeting, the team would examine the look-and-feel design and ensure the remote reflected the corporate design image, with the corporate website suggested as a reference. The user-interface design and product evaluation were also next steps; the Industrial Designer and User Interface Designer would work together, with instructions expected from the coach. The Project Manager said the minutes would be placed in the folder. The team would continue the project and develop a design for older customers; the Project Manager thought they would first complete questionnaires and then receive a message. The Project Manager saved the work in the group folder and said it was available in the projects folder. The group would start again in 30 minutes."}

The Project Manager said the team would resume in 30 minutes.","mom":"### Opening and agenda
The Project Manager opened the third meeting, describing it as the second phase and a conceptual-design meeting. The meeting would cover conceptual specifications for components and design, along with trend-watching. The agenda was an opening, three presentations, a decision on remote-control concepts, and a closing; about 40 minutes were available. The Project Manager asked whether anyone had encountered preparation problems, and the User Interface representative said no. The Project Manager suggested getting started.

### Review of previous meeting’s requirements and target market
The Project Manager recapped the previous meeting’s agreed requirements: teletext, a docking station, an audio signal, a small screen, button information as an extra, and default materials. The intended customers were people aged 60 to 80. The Project Manager invited comments or additional ideas; none were raised.

### Marketing presentation: trend-watching and customer preferences
Marketing reported conducting market research, distributing additional questionnaires, and sending trend-watchers to Milan and Paris to gather current trends. Marketing also consulted additional trend-watchers after the original group returned. The findings ranked fancy design as the most important factor, innovativeness at about half as important, and ease of use at about half the importance of innovativeness. Innovativeness meant functions not found on other remote controls. Among people aged 60 to 80, these factors were more evenly weighted. Older customers preferred dark colours, recognisable shapes, and familiar materials; surveys particularly indicated a preference for wood.

Marketing recommended that the remote control and docking station blend into the room, avoiding eye-catching designs and keeping the appearance simple. The docking station and small screen were identified as key innovative features to include. Trend-watchers recommended a telephone-like form, with the remote lying flat in its docking station rather than standing upright, because the upright shape would be unfamiliar to older people. Marketing proposed two editions: one with a wood-like colour and possibly feel for more affluent customers, and one in grey-black for customers with less means. The Project Manager invited questions; the User Interface representative had none.

### User Interface presentation: controls and display
The User Interface representative presented research on interface design, following the previous meeting’s discussion of using few buttons. They proposed focusing on primary functions and an attractive way to control the remote. Suggested features included speech recognition, a small display, large buttons, and a dedicated subtitle button. A single press would show small subtitles; a double press would show larger subtitles for people unable to read small text. The basic controls would include power, sound on/off and volume, number buttons from zero to nine, and channel up/down. The display could show button functions and the current television channel. The power button could be placed in a familiar corner, the display at the top where people would look, and channel controls where the thumb could reach them easily. The representative said the form still needed discussion.

### Industrial design presentation: component options
The Industrial Designer described a basic battery as the energy source, with kinetic energy as an optional alternative generated by shaking the remote, like a watch. Choosing kinetic energy would make the docking station obsolete, so the designer questioned whether it was a practical option. The manufacturing department could provide a flat, single-curved, or double-curved casing, with no technical restrictions; the designer also suggested a rubber anti-slip belt. Buttons could be plastic or rubber. The chipset should be advanced to support an LCD screen. Although trend research showed that customers liked wood, it would raise the price and might not fit the product image unless the team created two product lines. The designer said form should follow function and that choices of casing, supplement, and buttons depended on the design.

### Energy source and speech recognition
The Project Manager opened the concept discussion by prioritising the energy source because it affected production price and product image. The Industrial Designer outlined four options: a normal battery, a hand dynamo, solar cells, and kinetic energy. The designer dismissed the hand dynamo as impractical because users would have to wind it before watching television, and considered solar cells unsuitable because not every room was sufficiently light. Marketing asked how kinetic energy worked; the Industrial Designer explained that shaking the remote powers it. Marketing objected that older customers would not want to shake the remote before use and noted that kinetic power would eliminate the docking station, which could be an important marketing feature. The User Interface representative noted that the docking station could recharge batteries and potentially include a lost-remote function.

The User Interface representative estimated that the small display would use little energy and that one battery could last six months or more. The Project Manager said older people liked to keep things in place and might not want remotes left around the room, so a docking station could give the remote a designated place. The Project Manager also suggested placing a button on the docking station to make the remote beep when lost, which they considered more efficient and cheaper than using voice recognition for that purpose; voice recognition could still be used for channels. Marketing asked about the effect of voice recognition on production price. The Industrial Designer did not have pricing information and committed to asking the manufacturing department. Marketing reported that the target group’s market research showed they would not pay more for speech recognition in a remote control. Marketing advised against including it if it raised the selling price, suggesting it would be better suited to another product aimed at younger people. Marketing clarified that the research question had asked whether people preferred the feature, not whether they would pay extra, and argued that an LCD screen could make the remote easier to use. The User Interface representative asked whether the research concerned a large or small display; Marketing said it concerned an LCD screen like those on advanced mobile phones, so it was fairly large. The Project Manager said the team could retain the LCD screen and extra information because users could ignore it, but proposed discarding voice recognition because it would significantly increase cost and would not make the remote much easier to use. With voice recognition excluded, the Project Manager said energy use would be low and chose a simple rechargeable battery used with a docking station as a cheaper, equally good option than kinetic energy. The Industrial Designer agreed it was the best choice, and the Project Manager confirmed the battery decision.

### Chipset decision
The Project Manager moved to the chipset. The Industrial Designer said there was no real choice because the display required an advanced chipset. The Project Manager confirmed that the team would use an advanced chip.

### Casing materials and changeable covers
The Project Manager raised the choice between wood, black and grey, or both. The Project Manager noted that wood was more expensive to produce but could attract older customers seeking an exclusive item to show their grandchildren. Marketing suggested the key preference might be the wood colour rather than actual wood, so a wood-coloured finish could be sufficient. The Industrial Designer was unsure whether a wood-coloured finish would cost more and committed to researching it; the Project Manager noted that real wood could be more difficult to handle and shape.

The User Interface representative proposed a changeable casing, similar to mobile-phone covers, so the team could make one standard remote and sell separate cases. The Project Manager supported the idea as an unusual feature that could provide a marketing advantage, including the possibility of advertising a new case as a gift for a grandfather. Marketing agreed but said the team would need to examine design costs and make the remote suitable for both a wooden-looking cover and a plastic cover. Marketing proposed one remote design with different covers rather than two different remote designs. The Project Manager checked whether everyone agreed to changeable covers; the Industrial Designer and User Interface representative agreed.

### Casing shape and docking arrangement
Marketing asked the Industrial Designer to explain the flat, single-curved, and double-curved casing options. The Industrial Designer described a flat case as straight, as found on many older remotes, and said the manufacturing department could also supply single- or double-curved cases. These choices affected form only, not price or functionality, and were up to the design department. The Project Manager asked whether the remote needed to stand upright; Marketing said it only needed to lie flat. The Project Manager discussed placing the docking station on or beside the television and fitting the remote into it.

The Industrial Designer recommended choosing the casing first as the basis for the rest of the design, and sketched the three options. The flat case was described as conventional. The Industrial Designer said a curved case might help prevent repetitive strain injury. The Project Manager preferred the single-curved option because its angle could make the screen easier for older people to see while using the remote. The group discussed placing the display on the upper surface.

### Interface layout and ergonomics
The Project Manager invited ideas about the interface and layout. The User Interface representative said a regular form could be used, though it might not look especially distinctive. Marketing referred to the proposed channel buttons being on the right so the thumb could reach them, noting that many remotes cause repetitive strain injury. Marketing suggested placing corresponding controls on both the left and right for left-handed users and said this could also allow a symmetrical design. The User Interface representative asked whether channel controls could be on one side and volume controls on the other. Marketing and the Project Manager cautioned that extra or duplicated buttons could make the remote harder to use and confuse people, particularly if the buttons had the same labels. The Project Manager considered a reversible remote, but the group found that arranging plus and minus controls for opposite orientations would not work well. The Project Manager concluded that the functions were basic enough for left-handed users to operate without a special shape, and suggested keeping a conventional form while making it more attractive. The Project Manager also said the remote might need to be made somewhat fancier.

The group developed the layout around the single-curved case. The User Interface representative proposed shaping the back to fit the hand and placing channel buttons within thumb reach. The Project Manager preferred the display at the top, noting that the user’s hand might block it if it were elsewhere; the Industrial Designer agreed that placing it at the top was logical, as on a mobile phone. The Project Manager sketched a layout with the display above the buttons and space for left- and right-handed users. The User Interface representative asked that the on/off button remain at the top. Marketing preferred rounded corners, which the Project Manager supported as a friendlier appearance. The group noted the rubber anti-slip supplement.

### Next steps and close
The Project Manager said the group now had a general concept and materials direction. For the next meeting, the team would examine the look-and-feel design and ensure the remote reflected the corporate design image, with the corporate website suggested as a reference. The user-interface design and product evaluation were also next steps; the Industrial Designer and User Interface Designer would work together, with instructions expected from the coach. The Project Manager said the minutes would be placed in the folder. The team would continue the project and develop a design for older customers; the Project Manager thought they would first complete questionnaires and then receive a message. The Project Manager saved the work in the group folder and said it was available in the projects folder. {"mom":"### Opening and agenda
The Project Manager opened the fourth and final meeting at 3:00 p.m. and said the team had 40 minutes, expecting to finish at 3:30 p.m. The meeting would cover the final design, evaluation of both the product and the project, and project closure. The agenda was a prototype presentation, setting evaluation criteria, reviewing finances against the €12.50-per-remote budget, project evaluation, and closing. Marketing apologized for arriving late because of traffic.

### Prototype presentation and initial design review
The Industrial Designer presented the concept developed with Richard. The layout included an on-off button, mute button, volume and channel selectors, plus/minus controls, a help button, number buttons from zero to nine, teletext and subtitle buttons, and the company logo. Holding the help button while pressing another button would show guidance on the LCD screen. The designer described it as a simple prototype whose reception would need to be tested with users.

Marketing asked whether this was the time to discuss functionality. On teletext navigation, Marketing noted that remotes commonly have buttons to advance to another page. The User Interface representative explained that users could enter a page number with the number buttons or use the channel-shifting control to move up and down through teletext pages.

The Project Manager recalled that earlier meetings had aimed for a simple remote with a few large buttons and questioned whether the design had too many. The Industrial Designer said most remotes have more buttons; the on-off control, volume and channel controls, number buttons, teletext, and subtitles were considered necessary. The designer suggested removing the dedicated mute button because pressing volume-down twice could mute the sound. The designer considered help necessary because users otherwise would not know what the buttons do. The User Interface representative cautioned that older users might not know about long-press shortcuts, so dedicated controls could be easier to understand. Marketing agreed that there was little benefit in designing a television-only remote with very few functions.

The Industrial Designer described the buttons as equal-sized, round, and marked with small logos for recognition; volume controls would use triangle symbols. The User Interface representative said the small display meant the design did not need LEDs. Rubber buttons in a contrasting colour to the case were selected so they would stand out.

### Finance review and cost-reduction options
The Project Manager moved to the finance review, noting that only 30 minutes remained and that producing the design for €12.50 would be difficult. The estimate included two batteries, although one might suffice; Marketing asked whether the battery was rechargeable, and the Project Manager confirmed that it was, reducing the cost by €2. The advanced chip was required, leaving little apparent scope to save there. A single-curved case cost €1 more than an uncurved one, but the Project Manager and Industrial Designer favored the curve for the design and to give the display prominence. The case material was plastic, already the cheapest option. The Project Manager identified the buttons as the largest cost and said the design had to come in at €12.50.

The team counted the buttons and discussed an estimated total of 16 or 17, including the help button; the Project Manager referred to a total cost of €18. The Project Manager proposed removing the help and mute buttons by using long presses, which was estimated to save €1 and bring the count to 15. Marketing questioned whether the volume and channel controls counted as two buttons each. The Project Manager thought each was one control, while the User Interface representative clarified that each large control physically comprised two buttons and cost more than smaller buttons. The Project Manager also suggested combining volume and channel functions, and Marketing proposed integrating three number buttons into one control to reduce costs. The Project Manager said combining controls might also improve the design.

The Project Manager warned that the LCD display itself appeared too expensive for the budget. The Industrial Designer said omitting it could also reduce chip costs, but the Project Manager questioned what would distinguish the remote without the display; Marketing identified the docking station as a possible differentiator, while the designer noted that the docking station was not included in the schematic or price. Marketing suggested changing suppliers, and the Project Manager mentioned a Polish supplier as an option.

The group considered using a scroll wheel instead of the ten number buttons. The Project Manager said this would save ten buttons; the wheel could show programme numbers on the LCD, and users could press it when the desired number appeared. Marketing questioned the usability and noted that older users might not know what a scroll wheel was. The Industrial Designer also questioned whether consolidating controls would make the remote harder for elderly people to use, citing the designer’s mother’s difficulty sending an SMS. Marketing said older users expected number buttons from one to zero. The Project Manager argued that simple television advertising and instructions in the guide could explain the wheel, and that the LCD could show how to use it and other controls. The designer suggested that pausing for half a second after scrolling could select the displayed channel, but Marketing felt this would undermine usability.

The Industrial Designer confirmed that an LCD screen required the advanced chip. The Project Manager noted that a flat case could save €1, while the Industrial Designer suggested removing one more button. The group considered dropping the subtitle button, but the Project Manager emphasized that teletext and subtitles were important functions and asked whether they could share one button. Marketing explained that subtitles could be accessed through teletext page 888: teletext would disappear while the subtitles remained. The group discussed whether repeated presses or navigating to page 888 could support a combined control, while recognizing that scrolling to the page could be difficult for older users.

The Project Manager sketched a reduced-button design with a scroll wheel and five buttons. The Industrial Designer proposed making the volume and channel controls work through the wheel: pressing the volume button would let users adjust volume with the wheel, and the same approach could be used for channels. This would save two buttons and make the wheel’s purpose clearer. The Project Manager endorsed the idea. The team said teletext could remain, and the designer suggested that reducing controls might allow a flatter case and a smaller overall remote. The designer described arranging the volume and channel controls level with the on-off button, with the screen behind and the scroll control below. The Project Manager said the button count could then be reduced to four, while Marketing observed that the current proposal still had five.

The group weighed the single-curved case against a flat design. The Project Manager explained that the single-curved casing required different manufacturing equipment from a flat one, while a different case shape could affect the cost. Marketing continued to prefer the single curve, but acknowledged that costs had to be cut and proposed seeking more money from the board or checking market research for options. The Project Manager agreed to retain the single curve to emphasize the LCD and help functions, and said a prominent display would support the guidance features. Marketing warned that the design looked unfamiliar to older users and would require substantial marketing to sell. The User Interface representative noted that older people might recognize scroll controls from radios and channel-changing devices; the Project Manager suggested making the control stick out more, like familiar old-style buttons. The Project Manager said a five-button design might look less intimidating, while Marketing warned that five buttons could also seem confusing or insufficient.

### Product evaluation
The Project Manager moved to project evaluation, noting that 15 minutes remained and that the meeting was on schedule. Marketing said the evaluation criteria came from a literature study and analysis of previously established requirements. The criteria included whether the remote was attractive in shape and feel, innovative, easy to use and learn, functional without excessive or useless functions, affordable, suitable for the target group, and recognizable as the company’s product. Marketing noted that evaluating the design had been difficult because the previous meeting minutes were unavailable; the Project Manager explained that the digital pen had failed to upload its data and its software download was producing errors.

For design attractiveness, the group rated the design 6 out of 7. For innovation, the Project Manager proposed 7, citing the LCD screen, docking station, scroll controls, and other features; the discussion included a joking reference to having only €0.20 for the docking station. On ease of use, the group settled between 4 and 5, with Marketing choosing 4, particularly in relation to older users. The team agreed the design included the wanted functions, was not overloaded, and was relatively slim; the Project Manager suggested a score of 7 for the number and usefulness of functions.

Marketing asked whether the design addressed common remote-control frustrations, including losing the remote and RSI. The Industrial Designer said they had not considered those issues. The Project Manager identified remotes as ugly, not very functional, and easy to lose. On whether production costs met the preset limits, Marketing said they did at that point. For fit with the target group, the Industrial Designer proposed 3. The Project Manager and Marketing questioned whether the new radio-style control was suitable for older users: the designer considered it too fancy and flashy, and Marketing said older people would not necessarily expect a radio button on a remote. The Project Manager proposed 4, while Marketing preferred 2 and the User Interface representative 3; the group recorded 3. The team considered the company recognizable through the logo, the company’s fashion-oriented slogan, and removable front covers.

Marketing and the Project Manager calculated the evaluation result as 41 out of 49, described as approximately 80 percent; the Project Manager then stated 84 percent and called it a good score. Marketing concluded the evaluation.

### Project-process evaluation and meeting tools
The Project Manager asked whether the team had followed the right project phases. Marketing said the finance review should have happened much earlier, during the design phase, because the team lacked price information. The Project Manager agreed. Asked whether there had been room for creativity, Marketing said not much, attributing the limitation to the finance sheet; the Industrial Designer said there had been room, but finance constrained it. Marketing also said they would have liked to consider younger users and internet access so users could access content of their own.

The team agreed that roles and responsibilities had been clear and that collaboration had worked, including during the final phase. The Industrial Designer said the tasks were structured step by step and easy to follow. On the tools, the designer described drawing on the smart board as frustrating but the digital pen as useful. The Project Manager noted that the pen had failed to download its data, and the smart board was described as irritating. The Project Manager asked whether the team would have preferred a flip chart; participants suggested a flip chart or a more precise, faster digital tool. The User Interface representative said digital presentation material was easier to share, save, and place online or in a shared folder, but Marketing had been unable to open the file on a laptop. The Project Manager thought a smart-board application might be needed and said the material should be exportable as an image. The group agreed that sharing information was possible, though the pen and network created difficulties.

Asked for ideas for improving meetings, the User Interface representative suggested entering individual ratings on a computer, as at a university, so scores could be combined automatically. The Project Manager agreed that this would be better for evaluation criteria. The Project Manager also said the price list should have been reviewed before the team developed the full design.

### Budget, target market, and project close
The Project Manager asked whether costs were within budget. Marketing said they were, and the Industrial Designer qualified this by noting that the team was not going to make a docking station. The Project Manager agreed that this was important and said the docking station might justify a slightly higher remote price, though it was cheap to make. The team discussed whether the product could attract the projected market of 15 million; Marketing recalled a figure of 50,000, and the Project Manager said 15 million might be attainable through exports, especially to America, describing the product as innovative.

Marketing suggested that the scroll control might appeal more to younger users than older ones and proposed refocusing the product. The Project Manager suggested marketing it to everyone or targeting different markets with interchangeable front covers. The Project Manager proposed testing fashionable covers to see whether they attracted younger buyers. Marketing agreed that this could make the product more popular with younger people, even if the covers were interchangeable. The Project Manager then proposed a small celebration, but noted that one more questionnaire remained. The Project Manager said outstanding questions could be raised or placed in the project folder and said the final presentation would be prepared.
