{"summary":"The team held its fourth and final meeting, beginning at 3:00 p.m. with 40 minutes allocated and an expected finish at 3:30 p.m. The Project Manager said the project would close today. They reviewed the final remote design against a target production cost of €12.50 per remote. The prototype included an on/off button, mute, volume and channel controls, plus/minus, help, number keys from zero to nine, teletext, subtitles, an LCD screen and the company logo. Help guidance would appear on the LCD when a user held the help button while pressing another. The designer said user testing would be needed. The group discussed keeping controls understandable for older users, selected contrasting rubber buttons, and preferred the single-curved case because it emphasizes the display.

The cost estimate was about €17–€18, above the €12.50 target. One rechargeable battery rather than two could save €2; the advanced chip was needed for the LCD, plastic was already the least expensive case material, and the single-curved case cost €1 more than a flat one. The team considered reducing or combining buttons, removing the LCD, using a flat case, changing suppliers (including a Polish supplier), and seeking more funding. Marketing noted that older people may expect number buttons and find a scroll wheel unfamiliar; the Project Manager suggested explaining the wheel in advertising and instructions and using the LCD to provide guidance. The group developed a simpler concept with a scroll wheel and five buttons, retaining the LCD and potentially teletext. The Industrial Designer proposed using the wheel for volume and channel after selecting the corresponding control, saving two buttons and clarifying the wheel’s purpose. The Project Manager supported retaining the single-curved case to emphasize the LCD and help functions. The budget target remained €12.50; the group did not settle on a final cost figure in the transcript.

The product evaluation rated fanciness 6/7, innovation 7/7, ease of use about 4/7, functionality 7/7, and target-group fit 3/7. The logo and removable front covers were cited as supporting company recognition. The result was 41/49; the Project Manager called this 84%, while the earlier calculation was described as approximately 80%. The group noted that the remote did not address common frustrations such as losing a remote or RSI. For project-process evaluation, participants said pricing and finance information should have been available earlier in the design phase and that budget constraints limited creativity. They praised clear roles, collaboration and structured tasks. Drawing on the Smart Board was difficult, although the digital pen was useful; pen data upload and file-sharing access caused problems. A flip chart, a faster and more precise digital tool, and computer-based individual scoring with automatic aggregation were discussed as possible improvements.

The team discussed broadening the market beyond older users, including younger customers attracted by fashionable interchangeable front covers; the Project Manager proposed testing such covers. The Project Manager said participants would complete one more questionnaire in their rooms and would return in about 10 minutes with the final project presentation and summary.","mom":"### Opening and agenda
The Project Manager opened the fourth and final meeting at 3:00 p.m., said the team had 40 minutes and expected to finish at 3:30 p.m., and stated that the project would close today. The meeting would cover the final design, product and project evaluation, and project closure. The agenda was a prototype presentation, setting evaluation criteria, reviewing finances against the €12.50-per-remote budget, project evaluation, and closing. Marketing apologized for arriving late because of traffic.

### Prototype presentation and initial design review
The Industrial Designer presented the concept developed with Richard. The layout included an on-off button, mute button, volume and channel selectors, plus/minus controls, a help button, number buttons from zero to nine, teletext and subtitle buttons, and the company logo. Holding the help button while pressing another button would show guidance on the LCD screen. The designer described it as a simple prototype whose reception would need to be tested with users.

Marketing asked whether this was the time to discuss functionality. On teletext navigation, Marketing noted that remotes commonly have buttons to advance to another page. The User Interface representative explained that users could enter a page number with the number buttons or use the channel-shifting control to move up and down through teletext pages.

The Project Manager recalled that earlier meetings had aimed for a simple remote with a few large buttons and questioned whether the design had too many. The Industrial Designer said most remotes have more buttons; the on-off control, volume and channel controls, number buttons, teletext, and subtitles were considered necessary. The designer suggested removing the dedicated mute button because pressing volume-down twice could mute the sound. The designer considered help necessary because users otherwise would not know what the buttons do. The User Interface representative cautioned that older users might not know about long-press shortcuts, so dedicated controls could be easier to understand. Marketing agreed that there was little benefit in designing a television-only remote with very few functions.

The Industrial Designer described the buttons as equal-sized, round, and marked with small logos for recognition; volume controls would use triangle symbols. The User Interface representative said the small display meant the design did not need LEDs. Rubber buttons in a contrasting colour to the case were selected so they would stand out.

### Finance review and cost-reduction options
The Project Manager moved to the finance review, noting that only 30 minutes remained and that producing the design for €12.50 would be difficult. The estimate included two batteries, although one might suffice; Marketing asked whether the battery was rechargeable, and the Project Manager confirmed that it was, reducing the cost by €2. The advanced chip was required, leaving little apparent scope to save there. A single-curved case cost €1 more than an uncurved one, but the Project Manager and Industrial Designer favored the curve for the design and to give the display prominence. The case material was plastic, already the cheapest option. The Project Manager identified the buttons as the largest cost and said the design had to come in at €12.50.

The team counted the buttons and discussed an estimated total of 16 or 17, including the help button; the Project Manager referred to a total cost of €18. The Project Manager proposed removing the help and mute buttons by using long presses, which was estimated to save €1 and bring the count to 15. Marketing questioned whether the volume and channel controls counted as two buttons each. The Project Manager thought each was one control, while the User Interface representative clarified that each large control physically comprised two buttons and cost more than smaller buttons. The Project Manager also suggested combining volume and channel functions, and Marketing proposed integrating three number buttons into one control to reduce costs. The Project Manager said combining controls might also improve the design.

The Project Manager warned that the LCD display itself appeared too expensive for the budget. The Industrial Designer said omitting it could also reduce chip costs, but the Project Manager questioned what would distinguish the remote without the display; Marketing identified the docking station as a possible differentiator, while the designer noted that the docking station was not included in the schematic or price. Marketing suggested changing suppliers, and the Project Manager mentioned a Polish supplier as an option.

The group considered using a scroll wheel instead of the ten number buttons. The Project Manager said this would save ten buttons; the wheel could show programme numbers on the LCD, and users could press it when the desired number appeared. Marketing questioned the usability and noted that older users might not know what a scroll wheel was. The Industrial Designer also questioned whether consolidating controls would make the remote harder for elderly people to use, citing the designer’s mother’s difficulty sending an SMS. Marketing said older users expected number buttons from one to zero. The Project Manager argued that simple television advertising and instructions in the guide could explain the wheel, and that the LCD could show how to use it and other controls. The designer suggested that pausing for half a second after scrolling could select the displayed channel, but Marketing felt this would undermine usability.

The Industrial Designer confirmed that an LCD screen required the advanced chip. The Project Manager noted that a flat case could save €1, while the Industrial Designer suggested removing one more button. The group considered dropping the subtitle button, but the Project Manager emphasized that teletext and subtitles were important functions and asked whether they could share one button. Marketing explained that subtitles could be accessed through teletext page 888: teletext would disappear while the subtitles remained. The group discussed whether repeated presses or navigating to page 888 could support a combined control, while recognizing that scrolling to the page could be difficult for older users.

The Project Manager sketched a reduced-button design with a scroll wheel and five buttons. The Industrial Designer proposed making the volume and channel controls work through the wheel: pressing the volume button would let users adjust volume with the wheel, and the same approach could be used for channels. This would save two buttons and make the wheel’s purpose clearer. The Project Manager endorsed the idea. The team said teletext could remain, and the designer suggested that reducing controls might allow a flatter case and a smaller overall remote. The designer described arranging the volume and channel controls level with the on-off button, with the screen behind and the scroll control below. The Project Manager said the button count could then be reduced to four, while Marketing observed that the current proposal still had five.

The group weighed the single-curved case against a flat design. The Project Manager explained that the single-curved casing required different manufacturing equipment from a flat one, while a different case shape could affect the cost. Marketing continued to prefer the single curve, but acknowledged that costs had to be cut and proposed seeking more money from the board or checking market research for options. The Project Manager agreed to retain the single curve to emphasize the LCD and help functions, and said a prominent display would support the guidance features. Marketing warned that the design looked unfamiliar to older users and would require substantial marketing to sell. The User Interface representative noted that older people might recognize scroll controls from radios and channel-changing devices; the Project Manager suggested making the control stick out more, like familiar old-style buttons. The Project Manager said a five-button design might look less intimidating, while Marketing warned that five buttons could also seem confusing or insufficient.

### Product evaluation
The Project Manager moved to project evaluation, noting that 15 minutes remained and that the meeting was on schedule. Marketing said the evaluation criteria came from a literature study and analysis of previously established requirements. The criteria included whether the remote was attractive in shape and feel, innovative, easy to use and learn, functional without excessive or useless functions, affordable, suitable for the target group, and recognizable as the company’s product. Marketing noted that evaluating the design had been difficult because the previous meeting minutes were unavailable; the Project Manager explained that the digital pen had failed to upload its data and its software download was producing errors.

For design attractiveness, the group rated the design 6 out of 7. For innovation, the Project Manager proposed 7, citing the LCD screen, docking station, scroll controls, and other features; the discussion included a joking reference to having only €0.20 for the docking station. On ease of use, the group settled between 4 and 5, with Marketing choosing 4, particularly in relation to older users. The team agreed the design included the wanted functions, was not overloaded, and was relatively slim; the Project Manager suggested a score of 7 for the number and usefulness of functions.

Marketing asked whether the design addressed common remote-control frustrations, including losing the remote and RSI. The Industrial Designer said they had not considered those issues. The Project Manager identified remotes as ugly, not very functional, and easy to lose. On whether production costs met the preset limits, Marketing said they did at that point. For fit with the target group, the Industrial Designer proposed 3. The Project Manager and Marketing questioned whether the new radio-style control was suitable for older users: the designer considered it too fancy and flashy, and Marketing said older people would not necessarily expect a radio button on a remote. The Project Manager proposed 4, while Marketing preferred 2 and the User Interface representative 3; the group recorded 3. The team considered the company recognizable through the logo, the company’s fashion-oriented slogan, and removable front covers.

Marketing and the Project Manager calculated the evaluation result as 41 out of 49, described as approximately 80 percent; the Project Manager then stated 84 percent and called it a good score. Marketing concluded the evaluation.

### Project-process evaluation and meeting tools
The Project Manager asked whether the team had followed the right project phases. Marketing said the finance review should have happened much earlier, during the design phase, because the team lacked price information. The Project Manager agreed. Asked whether there had been room for creativity, Marketing said not much, attributing the limitation to the finance sheet; the Industrial Designer said there had been room, but finance constrained it. Marketing also said they would have liked to consider younger users and internet access so users could access content of their own.

The team agreed that roles and responsibilities had been clear and that collaboration had worked, including during the final phase. The Industrial Designer said the tasks were structured step by step and easy to follow. On the tools, the designer described drawing on the smart board as frustrating but the digital pen as useful. The Project Manager noted that the pen had failed to download its data, and the smart board was described as irritating. The Project Manager asked whether the team would have preferred a flip chart; participants suggested a flip chart or a more precise, faster digital tool. The User Interface representative said digital presentation material was easier to share, save, and place online or in a shared folder, but Marketing had been unable to open the file on a laptop. The Project Manager thought a smart-board application might be needed and said the material should be exportable as an image. The group agreed that sharing information was possible, though the pen and network created difficulties.

Asked for ideas for improving meetings, the User Interface representative suggested entering individual ratings on a computer, as at a university, so scores could be combined automatically. The Project Manager agreed that this would be better for evaluation criteria. The Project Manager also said the price list should have been reviewed before the team developed the full design.

### Budget, target market, and project close
The Project Manager asked whether costs were within budget. Marketing said they were, and the Industrial Designer qualified this by noting that the team was not going to make a docking station. The Project Manager agreed that this was important and said the docking station might justify a slightly higher remote price, though it was cheap to make. The team discussed whether the product could attract the projected market of 15 million; Marketing recalled a figure of 50,000, and the Project Manager said 15 million might be attainable through exports, especially to America, describing the product as innovative.

Marketing suggested that the scroll control might appeal more to younger users than older ones and proposed refocusing the product. The Project Manager suggested marketing it to everyone or targeting different markets with interchangeable front covers. The Project Manager proposed testing fashionable covers to see whether they attracted younger buyers. Marketing agreed that this could make the product more popular with younger people, even if the covers were interchangeable. The Project Manager then proposed a small celebration, but noted that one more questionnaire remained. The Project Manager said outstanding questions could be raised or placed in the project folder and said the final presentation would be prepared. The Project Manager planned to return in about 10 minutes to present the project summary; participants were told they would receive a questionnaire in their rooms and meet again in about 10 minutes. The Project Manager said participants would complete one more questionnaire in their rooms and would return in about 10 minutes with the final project presentation and summary.","mom":"### Opening and agenda
The Project Manager opened the fourth and final meeting at 3:00 p.m., said the team had 40 minutes and expected to finish at 3:30 p.m., and stated that the project would close today. The meeting would cover the final design, product and project evaluation, and project closure. The agenda was a prototype presentation, setting evaluation criteria, reviewing finances against the €12.50-per-remote budget, project evaluation, and closing. Marketing apologized for arriving late because of traffic.

### Prototype presentation and initial design review
The Industrial Designer presented the concept developed with Richard. The layout included an on-off button, mute button, volume and channel selectors, plus/minus controls, a help button, number buttons from zero to nine, teletext and subtitle buttons, and the company logo. Holding the help button while pressing another button would show guidance on the LCD screen. The designer described it as a simple prototype whose reception would need to be tested with users.

Marketing asked whether this was the time to discuss functionality. On teletext navigation, Marketing noted that remotes commonly have buttons to advance to another page. The User Interface representative explained that users could enter a page number with the number buttons or use the channel-shifting control to move up and down through teletext pages.

The Project Manager recalled that earlier meetings had aimed for a simple remote with a few large buttons and questioned whether the design had too many. The Industrial Designer said most remotes have more buttons; the on-off control, volume and channel controls, number buttons, teletext, and subtitles were considered necessary. The designer suggested removing the dedicated mute button because pressing volume-down twice could mute the sound. The designer considered help necessary because users otherwise would not know what the buttons do. The User Interface representative cautioned that older users might not know about long-press shortcuts, so dedicated controls could be easier to understand. Marketing agreed that there was little benefit in designing a television-only remote with very few functions.

The Industrial Designer described the buttons as equal-sized, round, and marked with small logos for recognition; volume controls would use triangle symbols. The User Interface representative said the small display meant the design did not need LEDs. Rubber buttons in a contrasting colour to the case were selected so they would stand out.

### Finance review and cost-reduction options
The Project Manager moved to the finance review, noting that only 30 minutes remained and that producing the design for €12.50 would be difficult. The estimate included two batteries, although one might suffice; Marketing asked whether the battery was rechargeable, and the Project Manager confirmed that it was, reducing the cost by €2. The advanced chip was required, leaving little apparent scope to save there. A single-curved case cost €1 more than an uncurved one, but the Project Manager and Industrial Designer favored the curve for the design and to give the display prominence. The case material was plastic, already the cheapest option. The Project Manager identified the buttons as the largest cost and said the design had to come in at €12.50.

The team counted the buttons and discussed an estimated total of 16 or 17, including the help button; the Project Manager referred to a total cost of €18. The Project Manager proposed removing the help and mute buttons by using long presses, which was estimated to save €1 and bring the count to 15. Marketing questioned whether the volume and channel controls counted as two buttons each. The Project Manager thought each was one control, while the User Interface representative clarified that each large control physically comprised two buttons and cost more than smaller buttons. The Project Manager also suggested combining volume and channel functions, and Marketing proposed integrating three number buttons into one control to reduce costs. The Project Manager said combining controls might also improve the design.

The Project Manager warned that the LCD display itself appeared too expensive for the budget. The Industrial Designer said omitting it could also reduce chip costs, but the Project Manager questioned what would distinguish the remote without the display; Marketing identified the docking station as a possible differentiator, while the designer noted that the docking station was not included in the schematic or price. Marketing suggested changing suppliers, and the Project Manager mentioned a Polish supplier as an option.

The group considered using a scroll wheel instead of the ten number buttons. The Project Manager said this would save ten buttons; the wheel could show programme numbers on the LCD, and users could press it when the desired number appeared. Marketing questioned the usability and noted that older users might not know what a scroll wheel was. The Industrial Designer also questioned whether consolidating controls would make the remote harder for elderly people to use, citing the designer’s mother’s difficulty sending an SMS. Marketing said older users expected number buttons from one to zero. The Project Manager argued that simple television advertising and instructions in the guide could explain the wheel, and that the LCD could show how to use it and other controls. The designer suggested that pausing for half a second after scrolling could select the displayed channel, but Marketing felt this would undermine usability.

The Industrial Designer confirmed that an LCD screen required the advanced chip. The Project Manager noted that a flat case could save €1, while the Industrial Designer suggested removing one more button. The group considered dropping the subtitle button, but the Project Manager emphasized that teletext and subtitles were important functions and asked whether they could share one button. Marketing explained that subtitles could be accessed through teletext page 888: teletext would disappear while the subtitles remained. The group discussed whether repeated presses or navigating to page 888 could support a combined control, while recognizing that scrolling to the page could be difficult for older users.

The Project Manager sketched a reduced-button design with a scroll wheel and five buttons. The Industrial Designer proposed making the volume and channel controls work through the wheel: pressing the volume button would let users adjust volume with the wheel, and the same approach could be used for channels. This would save two buttons and make the wheel’s purpose clearer. The Project Manager endorsed the idea. The team said teletext could remain, and the designer suggested that reducing controls might allow a flatter case and a smaller overall remote. The designer described arranging the volume and channel controls level with the on-off button, with the screen behind and the scroll control below. The Project Manager said the button count could then be reduced to four, while Marketing observed that the current proposal still had five.

The group weighed the single-curved case against a flat design. The Project Manager explained that the single-curved casing required different manufacturing equipment from a flat one, while a different case shape could affect the cost. Marketing continued to prefer the single curve, but acknowledged that costs had to be cut and proposed seeking more money from the board or checking market research for options. The Project Manager agreed to retain the single curve to emphasize the LCD and help functions, and said a prominent display would support the guidance features. Marketing warned that the design looked unfamiliar to older users and would require substantial marketing to sell. The User Interface representative noted that older people might recognize scroll controls from radios and channel-changing devices; the Project Manager suggested making the control stick out more, like familiar old-style buttons. The Project Manager said a five-button design might look less intimidating, while Marketing warned that five buttons could also seem confusing or insufficient.

### Product evaluation
The Project Manager moved to project evaluation, noting that 15 minutes remained and that the meeting was on schedule. Marketing said the evaluation criteria came from a literature study and analysis of previously established requirements. The criteria included whether the remote was attractive in shape and feel, innovative, easy to use and learn, functional without excessive or useless functions, affordable, suitable for the target group, and recognizable as the company’s product. Marketing noted that evaluating the design had been difficult because the previous meeting minutes were unavailable; the Project Manager explained that the digital pen had failed to upload its data and its software download was producing errors.

For design attractiveness, the group rated the design 6 out of 7. For innovation, the Project Manager proposed 7, citing the LCD screen, docking station, scroll controls, and other features; the discussion included a joking reference to having only €0.20 for the docking station. On ease of use, the group settled between 4 and 5, with Marketing choosing 4, particularly in relation to older users. The team agreed the design included the wanted functions, was not overloaded, and was relatively slim; the Project Manager suggested a score of 7 for the number and usefulness of functions.

Marketing asked whether the design addressed common remote-control frustrations, including losing the remote and RSI. The Industrial Designer said they had not considered those issues. The Project Manager identified remotes as ugly, not very functional, and easy to lose. On whether production costs met the preset limits, Marketing said they did at that point. For fit with the target group, the Industrial Designer proposed 3. The Project Manager and Marketing questioned whether the new radio-style control was suitable for older users: the designer considered it too fancy and flashy, and Marketing said older people would not necessarily expect a radio button on a remote. The Project Manager proposed 4, while Marketing preferred 2 and the User Interface representative 3; the group recorded 3. The team considered the company recognizable through the logo, the company’s fashion-oriented slogan, and removable front covers.

Marketing and the Project Manager calculated the evaluation result as 41 out of 49, described as approximately 80 percent; the Project Manager then stated 84 percent and called it a good score. Marketing concluded the evaluation.

### Project-process evaluation and meeting tools
The Project Manager asked whether the team had followed the right project phases. Marketing said the finance review should have happened much earlier, during the design phase, because the team lacked price information. The Project Manager agreed. Asked whether there had been room for creativity, Marketing said not much, attributing the limitation to the finance sheet; the Industrial Designer said there had been room, but finance constrained it. Marketing also said they would have liked to consider younger users and internet access so users could access content of their own.

The team agreed that roles and responsibilities had been clear and that collaboration had worked, including during the final phase. The Industrial Designer said the tasks were structured step by step and easy to follow. On the tools, the designer described drawing on the smart board as frustrating but the digital pen as useful. The Project Manager noted that the pen had failed to download its data, and the smart board was described as irritating. The Project Manager asked whether the team would have preferred a flip chart; participants suggested a flip chart or a more precise, faster digital tool. The User Interface representative said digital presentation material was easier to share, save, and place online or in a shared folder, but Marketing had been unable to open the file on a laptop. The Project Manager thought a smart-board application might be needed and said the material should be exportable as an image. The group agreed that sharing information was possible, though the pen and network created difficulties.

Asked for ideas for improving meetings, the User Interface representative suggested entering individual ratings on a computer, as at a university, so scores could be combined automatically. The Project Manager agreed that this would be better for evaluation criteria. The Project Manager also said the price list should have been reviewed before the team developed the full design.

### Budget, target market, and project close
The Project Manager asked whether costs were within budget. Marketing said they were, and the Industrial Designer qualified this by noting that the team was not going to make a docking station. The Project Manager agreed that this was important and said the docking station might justify a slightly higher remote price, though it was cheap to make. The team discussed whether the product could attract the projected market of 15 million; Marketing recalled a figure of 50,000, and the Project Manager said 15 million might be attainable through exports, especially to America, describing the product as innovative.

Marketing suggested that the scroll control might appeal more to younger users than older ones and proposed refocusing the product. The Project Manager suggested marketing it to everyone or targeting different markets with interchangeable front covers. The Project Manager proposed testing fashionable covers to see whether they attracted younger buyers. Marketing agreed that this could make the product more popular with younger people, even if the covers were interchangeable. The Project Manager then proposed a small celebration, but noted that one more questionnaire remained. The Project Manager said outstanding questions could be raised or placed in the project folder and said the final presentation would be prepared. The Project Manager planned to return in about 10 minutes to present the project summary; participants were told they would receive a questionnaire in their rooms and meet again in about 10 minutes. The Project Manager hoped the digital pen would download its software or data.

Marketing said they would type the evaluation score into the bottom of the form (line 1088). The Project Manager expected the team could reach the 15-million market figure if the product were exported, especially to America (lines 1319–1324)."}

{"mom":"### Opening and meeting agenda
Project Manager Danny Wolfs welcomed the team to the kick-off meeting. Before starting, he explained that cameras were recording them and that the pie-shaped devices were microphones. He asked participants to keep laptops positioned so their faces remained visible to the cameras. Danny outlined the agenda: introductions, an acquaintance exercise and smart-board training, the project plan and discussion, and a short closing.

### Introductions and project aim
Danny introduced himself as Project Manager. Juergen Toffs introduced himself as User Interface Designer, another participant identified himself as Industrial Designer, and Tim introduced himself as Marketing Expert. Danny said the project aim was to create a new remote control that would be original, trendy, and user-friendly. He described three stages: functional design, covering what functions the remote should have and why; conceptual design, considering at a broad level how to make it; and detailed design, examining technical feasibility. Each stage would include individual work and a meeting.

### Smart-board training and introductions exercise
Danny explained that one of the two smart boards was for presentations, including PowerPoint or Word files, and the other was for drawing. Documents to be displayed should be saved in the shared folder rather than My Documents. Drawings made on the board must be saved and must not be deleted. The team then practiced by drawing favorite animals on the whiteboard on the left, using different colors and pen widths, and explaining why they chose each animal. Danny said the exercise was intended to help the team get to know one another and have some fun before tackling the harder work. He demonstrated using the pen, advised not to rest a hand on the board’s sensor area, and noted that drawing was not fully real-time and could take a few seconds to appear. Danny drew a cat named Simba, explaining that he and his household had a cat by that name because it resembled the lion in The Lion King; he also said his cat was red and he had red hair. Tim drew a turtle because he liked Teenage Mutant Hero Turtles. Juergen drew a dog, explaining that his household had a dog a few years earlier and had not got another after it died. The Industrial Designer drew a rabbit, identified as the white rabbit from The Matrix. The group joked about the drawings and the available time; Danny said they had twenty-five minutes and later said he had been keeping an eye on the time. He described the drawing program as easy to use.

### Project constraints and initial design discussion
Danny said the remote’s selling price would be 25 euros and production cost must not exceed 20.5 euros. He considered a highly advanced, high-definition, ultra-modern remote unlikely at a price of 12.5 euros. The required profit was 50 million euros; the group discussed that this would require about two million remotes at a selling price of 25 euros. Danny said the market was international, covering essentially the whole world, at least countries with televisions. He invited the team to consider their experience using remote controls at home and suggest useful features that could distinguish the new product.

Juergen said the most important function was switching channels and recommended keeping the remote as basic as possible, rather than combining controls for television, DVD, radio, and other devices. Tim presented marketing considerations: the remote should be intuitive, small, fairly cheap, priced at 25 euros, and brand-independent so its use would not depend on the brand of a television or other equipment. Tim also favored a multipurpose remote because most existing remotes served only one purpose and a multipurpose product could add a feature and stand out in the market. He suggested considering a technology other than infrared, such as radio waves or Bluetooth, because infrared could fail when someone stood in front of the television; he acknowledged that this might increase cost. He also proposed an LCD screen that could show upcoming programs for the channel being watched. Danny agreed that the team should focus on features that add something to the market, while cautioning that innovation should not come at the expense of user-friendliness and price. Tim clarified that these were marketing perspectives and that he was not an expert in user-interface design.

### Individual work and next meeting
Danny said the next meeting would start in thirty minutes and that participants would receive individual assignments, with feedback presumably by email. The Industrial Designer was to examine the working design, and Juergen was to examine technical functions. Juergen said the team first needed to agree what they were making, including whether the remote would be for multiple systems; he said technical functions depended on knowing which machines it would work with and whether it would use a text screen or Bluetooth. Tim and the Industrial Designer suggested that the team could first prepare lists of requirements and general mock-ups or ideas, then decide and develop them further at the next meeting. The Industrial Designer said they could take it from there; Tim suggested removing obsolete details later. Danny proposed that each person consider what was most important from their own perspective, then bring the pieces together at the next meeting. He added that they needed some agreement on the basic plan so user requirements would fit the technical functions, while distinguishing this from decisions about individual components, which he considered a later step. Danny closed the meeting, saying participants would receive specific instructions from their personal coaches and that he would see them in thirty minutes."}

{"summary":"Project Manager Danny Wolfs introduced the kickoff agenda: introductions, getting acquainted through smart-board training, agreeing a project plan, discussion, and closing. The project is to create a new remote control that is original, trendy, and user-friendly, progressing through functional design, conceptual design, and detailed design, each divided into individual work and a meeting. The team learned to use the two smart boards, including saving drawings and not deleting them, then did a favorite-animal drawing exercise; the drawings were a cat named Simba, a turtle inspired by Teenage Mutant Hero Turtles, a dog, and a rabbit identified as the white rabbit from The Matrix. The stated selling price is €25, production cost must not exceed €20.50, and the target profit is €50 million; Danny estimated this would require selling two million remotes, with an international market in countries that have television. Ideas raised included keeping basic channel switching and ease of use, while Marketing proposed a compact, inexpensive, brand-independent, multipurpose remote, alternative transmission such as radio waves or Bluetooth, and an LCD screen showing upcoming programs; the team stressed balancing innovation with usability and price. The team agreed that members should prepare individual user requirements, technical functions, and general design ideas or mock-ups, then align them so the requirements fit technical feasibility; specific instructions would come from personal coaches, and the next meeting was due to start in 30 minutes.","mom":"### Opening and meeting agenda
Project Manager Danny Wolfs welcomed the team to the kick-off meeting. Before starting, he explained that cameras were recording them and that the pie-shaped devices were microphones. He asked participants to keep laptops positioned so their faces remained visible to the cameras. Danny outlined the agenda for today: introductions, an acquaintance exercise and smart-board training, the project plan and discussion, and a short closing. He said he would introduce himself and that it was good for participants to introduce themselves.

### Introductions and project aim
Danny introduced himself as Project Manager. Juergen Toffs introduced himself as User Interface Designer, another participant identified himself as Industrial Designer, and Tim introduced himself as Marketing Expert. Danny said the project aim was to create a new remote control that would be original, trendy, and user-friendly. He described three stages: functional design, covering what functions the remote should have and why; conceptual design, considering at a broad level how to make it; and detailed design, examining technical feasibility. Each stage would include individual work and a meeting.

### Smart-board training and introductions exercise
Danny explained that one of the two smart boards was for presentations, including PowerPoint or Word files, and the other was for drawing. Documents to be displayed should be saved in the shared folder rather than My Documents. Drawings made on the board must be saved and must not be deleted. The team then practiced by drawing favorite animals on the whiteboard on the left, using different colors and pen widths, and explaining why they chose each animal. Danny said the exercise was intended to help the team get to know one another and have some fun before tackling the harder work. He demonstrated using the pen, advised not to rest a hand on the board’s sensor area, and noted that drawing was not fully real-time and could take a few seconds to appear. The exercise was compared to Pictionary, with a joke that the first person to guess correctly would get a raise. Danny drew a cat named Simba, explaining that he and his household had a cat by that name because it resembled the lion in The Lion King; he also said his cat was red and he had red hair. Tim drew a turtle because he liked Teenage Mutant Hero Turtles. Juergen drew a dog, explaining that his household had a dog a few years earlier and had not got another after it died. The Industrial Designer drew a rabbit, identified as the white rabbit from The Matrix. The group joked about the drawings and the available time; Danny said they had twenty-five minutes and later said he had been keeping an eye on the time. He described the drawing program as easy to use.

### Project constraints and initial design discussion
Danny said the remote’s selling price would be 25 euros and production cost must not exceed 20.5 euros. He considered a highly advanced, high-definition, ultra-modern remote unlikely at a price of 12.5 euros. The required profit was 50 million euros; the group discussed that this would require about two million remotes at a selling price of 25 euros. Danny said the market was international, covering essentially the whole world, at least countries with televisions. He invited the team to consider their experience using remote controls at home and suggest useful features that could distinguish the new product.

Juergen said the most important function was switching channels and recommended keeping the remote as basic as possible, rather than combining controls for television, DVD, radio, and other devices. Tim presented marketing considerations: the remote should be intuitive, small, fairly cheap, priced at 25 euros, and brand-independent so its use would not depend on the brand of a television or other equipment. Tim also favored a multipurpose remote because most existing remotes served only one purpose and a multipurpose product could add a feature and stand out in the market. He suggested considering a technology other than infrared, such as radio waves or Bluetooth, because infrared could fail when someone stood in front of the television; he acknowledged that this might increase cost. He also proposed an LCD screen that could show upcoming programs for the channel being watched. Danny agreed that the team should focus on features that add something to the market, while cautioning that innovation should not come at the expense of user-friendliness and price. Tim clarified that these were marketing perspectives and that he was not an expert in user-interface design.

### Individual work and next meeting
Danny said the next meeting would start in thirty minutes and that participants would receive individual assignments, with feedback presumably by email. The Industrial Designer was to examine the working design, and Juergen was to examine technical functions. Juergen said the team first needed to agree what they were making, including whether the remote would be for multiple systems; he said technical functions depended on knowing which machines it would work with and whether it would use a text screen or Bluetooth. The Industrial Designer and Tim suggested that the team could first prepare individual lists of requirements and general mock-ups or ideas, then decide and develop them further at the next meeting. The Industrial Designer said they could take it from there; Tim suggested removing obsolete details later. Danny proposed that each person consider what was most important from their own perspective, then bring the pieces together at the next meeting. He added that they needed some agreement on the basic plan so user requirements would fit the technical functions, while distinguishing this from decisions about individual components, which he considered a later step. Danny closed the meeting, saying participants would receive specific instructions from their personal coaches and that he would see them in thirty TS3007b: {"title":"Functional design review of a simple, accessible TV remote","summary":"The Project Manager opened the functional design review by asking each team member to present work from the previous 30-minute work period, limiting presentations to about 10 minutes each; meeting minutes and those from the prior session were available in the shared folder. The management board’s four points were that teletext may be outdated as internet becomes the main focus, the remote should control only the television rather than be multipurpose, the new product should attract customers younger than 40 (current customers are 40 and older), and the slogan and logo should be more recognizable on the remote. Marketing reported findings from a questionnaire of 100 respondents: the two age groups were 16–45 and 46–65, with market shares stated as about 65% and 35%; younger users favored advanced features such as an LCD screen and speech recognition, while 75% found most remotes ugly and 80% said they would pay more for a stylish one. The most important frequently used controls were channel switching, teletext, and volume; Marketing recommended focusing on those controls, making them larger, reducing or combining less-used buttons, and considering a TV-side holder because users often lose remotes. The Industrial Designer’s teardown found that current remotes use infrared and simple, low-cost components; Bluetooth would require compatible television hardware and add cost, while receiving signals would also require extra components, so the recommendation was to keep the remote simple and infrared-only, use an ordinary replaceable battery, and provide visible feedback when a button is pressed. The User Interface presentation likewise emphasized clear, large, accessible primary controls, fewer visible functions, and keeping key actions direct; the group discussed touchscreens, menus, and hidden or secondary controls, while noting that television menus vary and many sets lack menu structures. The team favored a touch-based design that keeps primary controls consistently accessible and uses a separate screen area for extra functions, with Marketing and the Industrial Designer supporting the proposal; they also discussed a flip-open alternative, older users’ familiarity with conventional controls, and parental channel restrictions, which the Project Manager deferred as a later-stage issue. They considered storing television profiles or codes in remote memory to match different models, but acknowledged compatibility and setup challenges; firmware updates via USB or FireWire, internet-connected holders, or a service center were explored, with service-center or shop updates considered a low-cost option. The group voted for the right-hand design, and the User Interface participant supported it because familiar-looking displayed buttons could help elderly users. The Project Manager confirmed the meeting minutes were updated in the shared folder, announced a lunch break followed by 30 minutes of individual work, and said instructions for the next meeting would arrive by email; the return time was clarified as 30 minutes after lunch, with a possible 12:45 or 1:00 time raised for confirmation. The team also discussed saving the session material as a JPEG image in the project documents and agreed to complete the questionnaire after lunch."}

{"mom":"### Meeting plan and management-board guidance
The Project Manager said each participant, but not the Project Manager, would present the work completed during the previous half hour at the functional design meeting. The Project Manager would take minutes and place them in the shared folder at the end of the session; minutes from the previous session were already there. The Project Manager reported four important points from an email from the management board: teletext was becoming outdated and the internet would be the main focus; the remote control should be for television only, not multi-purpose; existing customers were aged 40 and over, while the new remote should reach people under 40; and, as a longer-term consideration, the company wanted its slogan and logo to be more recognizable on the remote. The group had 40 minutes for presentations, with no more than 10 minutes per presentation, and could use the smartboards, Word files, or other facilities. The Project Manager invited Tim to begin.

### Marketing research and recommendations
Marketing presented findings from a questionnaire conducted by the usability lab with 100 respondents; the marketing department had prepared a report. Marketing described two audience groups: ages 16–45 and ages 46–65. The first group accounted for about 65 percent of the market share, and the second for 35 percent. Younger users were more interested in new technology such as an LCD screen on the remote and speech recognition; interest in these technologies declined with age. Marketing said 75 percent of users considered most remote controls very ugly, and 80 percent would pay more for a remote that looked stylish.

Marketing reported that a frequency-of-use and importance assessment identified channel switching, teletext, and volume controls as the three most important functions. Respondents were asked which buttons they used most and how often, and separately how important those buttons were; the results were multiplied to produce the ranking. The Project Manager noted the management board’s view that teletext would be displaced by the internet. Marketing responded that teletext was currently the best way to access information on a television and that people used teletext rather than the internet through a remote control, since internet capability was not yet incorporated.

Marketing recommended targeting the 16–45 age group because it was the largest audience, at 65 percent, and was expected to generate the most revenue; people in that range watched more television than older people. Marketing also recommended improving the most-used functions—channel switching, teletext, and volume controls—and addressing the tendency for users to lose their remote by designing a holder on the side of the television. In discussion, Marketing clarified that improving the functions meant emphasizing the buttons people actually used, since many buttons on remotes went unused. The most-used buttons should be larger, and less-used functions might be combined under a single button or otherwise reduced to leave fewer buttons and make the remote quicker and easier to learn. The Industrial Designer suggested that a long press could access a different function; Marketing agreed this could suit minor functions.

### Industrial design and technical constraints
The Industrial Designer said they had examined current remote controls by taking them apart, studying their appearance, operation, components, and connections, and preparing a scheme of how the elements were organized. Current remotes were generally infrared, as were televisions and stereos. A Bluetooth remote would require a television with Bluetooth as well, adding cost for the user and making a low-cost product harder to achieve. The simple structure of existing remotes could help keep the new remote relatively inexpensive. Bluetooth might be possible, but the Industrial Designer doubted it would fit the budget and suggested Marketing investigate it; personally, the Industrial Designer preferred not to use Bluetooth or radio waves.

Marketing asked whether Bluetooth or a radio receiver could instead be put in a television-side holder connected to the television. The Industrial Designer said that could be attractive but would still leave the infrared function in place and would shift, rather than remove, the problem. The Industrial Designer also proposed exploring a speech-activated remote-finding feature: when someone asked where the remote was, it could beep. The cost of that feature was unknown.

The Industrial Designer recommended a readily available replaceable battery, so users could buy a new one when the old battery stopped working. A button press would close a switch, send current through the circuit, and light a bulb to reassure users that the press registered. The signal would pass through a chip, be processed into electronic signals, and be sent to the infrared bulb for receipt and interpretation by the television. The Industrial Designer favored a simple design without excessive gadgets or functions, infrared transmission without reception, and no television input. In their view, supporting teletext through infrared would require adding a receiver to the remote, increasing components, design work, size, time, and cost. They therefore advised against a receiver and recommended basic functions, possibly using one button for multiple functions or concealing less-used buttons.

### User-interface principles and touch-screen discussion
The User Interface representative said the design should balance appearance, technical feasibility, and ease of use. A remote should look good without compromising usability. Because many functions make a device harder to use, the representative recommended limiting functions or avoiding showing them all at once; a hierarchical structure could help when there were many functions. A touch screen was raised as a possibility, though its feasibility with an infrared-only remote that could not receive signals was uncertain. The representative emphasized clear, simple buttons and pointed out that a crowded remote could make it difficult to find teletext or press the intended button. Play, back, and stop were cited as important controls.

The User Interface representative said the remote should be for television only, with few options and direct-action buttons rather than requiring an initial selection. The Project Manager asked how that recommendation fit with combining multiple functions in one button. The representative said this involved weighing a small number of options against a less original or less multi-purpose design, versus using many buttons. Marketing suggested a touch screen or LCD that kept general functions such as play and channel switching in the center, with menus such as settings at the top or bottom. The User Interface representative asked whether menus should appear on the television or be contained on the remote, and recommended displaying menu choices on the television rather than relying on complicated button combinations or long presses. Marketing cautioned that television menus differ and a remote’s menu might not match the television’s actual menus. The Industrial Designer added that some televisions lack menus or have only simple ones, limiting compatibility.

The User Interface representative recommended large, clear buttons, accepting that some options might be lost in favor of making channel, volume, and teletext controls immediately accessible. Advanced options could be placed elsewhere on the remote, perhaps behind a small cover or on a touch screen. Essential actions such as standby and channel changing should always be available without navigating menus, and users should receive feedback when a button is pressed so they know the remote or television has responded. The representative summarized the principle as keeping the design simple and reducing functionality where necessary so important controls remain accessible.

Marketing supported the touch-screen idea, referring to a television news item about telephones for older people with large touch-screen images for calling and hanging up. Enlarging the displayed images could make the remote more suitable for older users and visually oriented. The User Interface representative suggested keeping primary buttons visible, designing the remote to fit comfortably in the hand, and adding a logo and an attractive form. If a touch screen proved too difficult, a flip-open design could reveal additional options.

The group discussed keeping primary controls permanently accessible while using part of a touch screen for extra functions. The User Interface representative proposed a large touch screen with the same primary controls always available and the lower portion reserved for other functions, comparing the concept to an iPod. The Industrial Designer supported a touch-screen area with a limited set of menus and sub-items, noting it could allow later improvement. The Project Manager asked whether the proposal was for a fully touch-screen remote. Marketing and the Industrial Designer supported that direction, while the User Interface representative stressed that the same essential buttons must always remain accessible and only special options should use the remaining touch-screen area. The Project Manager raised the concern that older users might not be accustomed to touch screens and recommended retaining traditional controls such as teletext and volume, while placing more difficult functions on the screen. Marketing replied that large numbers on an LCD could help; the User Interface representative said touch-screen controls could be displayed to look like actual buttons. The Industrial Designer observed that touching a screen differs from pressing a physical button and said the target audience should guide the choice. The group noted that the intended audience was under 40 and that younger users liked new, fashionable technology; Marketing mentioned that Microsoft had developed a touch-screen concept for multimedia applications.

### Parental controls and television compatibility
Marketing proposed parental control using a PIN code so parents could access all channels while children without the code could not switch to violent channels. The Industrial Designer said feasibility would depend on the television. The Industrial Designer explained that channel assignments differ between televisions: for example, channel 15 may correspond to different content on different sets, so a remote cannot assume a universal channel order. The User Interface representative interpreted the proposal as first matching the remote to the television, then allowing parents to set a password so children could not change television settings such as color or volume. Marketing suggested that a parent could log in, identify a channel as unsuitable, and restrict it to parents. The User Interface representative proposed keeping parental control as a separate menu option. The Project Manager said the idea was useful but should be revisited at a later stage rather than broaden the current discussion.

The Project Manager summarized the discussion as a need to keep the remote simple while allowing additional options to be hidden rather than crowding it with buttons. The group had also considered a single controller for each television, with menus and parental controls handled by the remote rather than by the television. Marketing noted that television menus are not identical, making television-specific menu displays problematic. The User Interface representative suggested synchronizing the remote with the television and exploring whether the remote could identify the television brand and present compatible options. The Project Manager cautioned that the product was intended for an international market. The User Interface representative argued that universal remotes already support many televisions, while the Industrial Designer noted that such remotes must be programmed to match a television and can be troublesome. The Industrial Designer also said that receiving television information would require a receiver in the remote, adding complexity.

The User Interface representative and Marketing discussed existing universal remotes, which can be configured by entering a code found in a manual. The User Interface representative gave an example of finding a Philips model code, pressing a sequence such as 455, and then seeing the available menu options. Marketing suggested storing television types and corresponding options as profiles in the remote’s memory: entering a television identifier, such as 1410, would bring up its profile. The group considered the storage requirement modest; the User Interface representative said universal-remote manuals could list three or four hundred televisions at most, including old and new models. Marketing warned that a newly purchased television might not be included in the remote’s profiles, requiring a new remote or an update.

### Firmware updates and service options
The group considered ways to update remote-control firmware when a new television was not already supported. Marketing proposed a USB or FireWire connection so the remote could connect to a PC and download new firmware from the internet. The Industrial Designer noted that not everyone had a PC at home. The User Interface representative and Marketing suggested taking the remote to a shop or service center for an update. The Industrial Designer also proposed using the television-side holder as a possible connection point to a telephone line or internet connection, but recognized that this would return to the issue of adding a receiver and cost. Marketing considered updates at a service center or shop the cheapest approach and suggested a docking station where the remote could be placed and updated by pressing start. The Industrial Designer agreed this seemed best; Marketing noted that people do not buy a television every week.

### Presentation close, break, and follow-up
The Project Manager said the minutes from the second meeting had been completed, with four management-board points added as reminders, along with summaries of what participants had said and their individual views. The Project Manager identified the meeting’s central design issue as keeping the remote simple while allowing further options to be hidden, and noted the discussion about making remote-controlled functions, including menus and parental controls, work across televisions. The Project Manager said there were five minutes remaining during the later discussion.

The Project Manager then said the session was nearly over and announced a lunch break, followed by 30 minutes of individual work. The Project Manager would update the minutes in the shared folder and said instructions for the next meeting would arrive by email; participants should wait for the email and complete the work during the 30 minutes. When asked when to return, the Project Manager initially stated a 30-minute break. The User Interface representative suggested a quarter to one; Marketing thought the break might be 45 minutes. The Project Manager said that would mean returning at one o’clock and suggested checking with the personal coach. The group agreed on the timing. The Project Manager thanked everyone and called it a good session. Participants briefly discussed saving the material to shared documents; the Project Manager said the files were stored in SmartBoard XDK, and others suggested saving or exporting an image, including as JPEG. The Project Manager said the questionnaire would be completed after lunch, explaining that they were hungry."}
