{"summary":"The Project Manager opened the functional design review by asking each team member to present work from the previous 30-minute work period, limiting presentations to about 10 minutes each; meeting minutes and those from the prior session were available in the shared folder. The management board’s four points were that teletext may be outdated as internet becomes the main focus, the remote should control only the television rather than be multipurpose, the new product should attract customers younger than 40 (current customers are 40 and older), and the slogan and logo should be more recognizable on the remote. Marketing reported findings from a questionnaire of 100 respondents: the two age groups were 16–45 and 46–65, with market shares stated as about 65% and 35%; younger users favored advanced features such as an LCD screen and speech recognition, while 75% found most remotes ugly and 80% said they would pay more for a stylish one. The most important frequently used controls were channel switching, teletext, and volume; Marketing recommended focusing on those controls, making them larger, reducing or combining less-used buttons, and considering a TV-side holder because users often lose remotes. The Industrial Designer’s teardown found that current remotes use infrared and simple, low-cost components; Bluetooth would require compatible television hardware and add cost, while receiving signals would also require extra components, so the recommendation was to keep the remote simple and infrared-only, use an ordinary replaceable battery, and provide visible feedback when a button is pressed. The User Interface presentation likewise emphasized clear, large, accessible primary controls, fewer visible functions, and keeping key actions direct; the group discussed touchscreens, menus, and hidden or secondary controls, while noting that television menus vary and many sets lack menu structures. The team favored a touch-based design that keeps primary controls consistently accessible and uses a separate screen area for extra functions, with Marketing and the Industrial Designer supporting the proposal; they also discussed a flip-open alternative, older users’ familiarity with conventional controls, and parental channel restrictions, which the Project Manager deferred as a later-stage issue. They considered storing television profiles or codes in remote memory to match different models, but acknowledged compatibility and setup challenges; firmware updates via USB or FireWire, internet-connected holders, or a service center were explored, with service-center or shop updates considered a low-cost option. The group voted for the right-hand design, and the User Interface participant supported it because familiar-looking displayed buttons could help elderly users. The Project Manager confirmed the meeting minutes were updated in the shared folder, announced a lunch break followed by 30 minutes of individual work, and said instructions for the next meeting would arrive by email; the return time was clarified as 30 minutes after lunch, with a possible 12:45 or 1:00 time raised for confirmation. The team also discussed saving the session material as a JPEG image in the project documents and agreed to complete the questionnaire after lunch.","mom":"### Meeting plan and management-board guidance
The Project Manager said each participant, but not the Project Manager, would present the work completed during the previous half hour at the functional design meeting. The Project Manager would take minutes and place them in the shared folder at the end of the session; minutes from the previous session were already there. The Project Manager reported four important points from an email from the management board: teletext was becoming outdated and the internet would be the main focus; the remote control should be for television only, not multi-purpose; existing customers were aged 40 and over, while the new remote should reach people under 40; and, as a longer-term consideration, the company wanted its slogan and logo to be more recognizable on the remote. The group had 40 minutes for presentations, with no more than 10 minutes per presentation, and could use the smartboards, Word files, or other facilities. The Project Manager invited Tim to begin.

### Marketing research and recommendations
Marketing presented findings from a questionnaire conducted by the usability lab with 100 respondents; the marketing department had prepared a report. Marketing described two audience groups: ages 16–45 and ages 46–65. The first group accounted for about 65 percent of the market share, and the second for 35 percent. Younger users were more interested in new technology such as an LCD screen on the remote and speech recognition; interest in these technologies declined with age. Marketing said 75 percent of users considered most remote controls very ugly, and 80 percent would pay more for a remote that looked stylish.

Marketing reported that a frequency-of-use and importance assessment identified channel switching, teletext, and volume controls as the three most important functions. Respondents were asked which buttons they used most and how often, and separately how important those buttons were; the results were multiplied to produce the ranking. The Project Manager noted the management board’s view that teletext would be displaced by the internet. Marketing responded that teletext was currently the best way to access information on a television and that people used teletext rather than the internet through a remote control, since internet capability was not yet incorporated.

Marketing recommended targeting the 16–45 age group because it was the largest audience, at 65 percent, and was expected to generate the most revenue; people in that range watched more television than older people. Marketing also recommended improving the most-used functions—channel switching, teletext, and volume controls—and addressing the tendency for users to lose their remote by designing a holder on the side of the television. In discussion, Marketing clarified that improving the functions meant emphasizing the buttons people actually used, since many buttons on remotes went unused. The most-used buttons should be larger, and less-used functions might be combined under a single button or otherwise reduced to leave fewer buttons and make the remote quicker and easier to learn. The Industrial Designer suggested that a long press could access a different function; Marketing agreed this could suit minor functions.

### Industrial design and technical constraints
The Industrial Designer said they had examined current remote controls by taking them apart, studying their appearance, operation, components, and connections, and preparing a scheme of how the elements were organized. Current remotes were generally infrared, as were televisions and stereos. A Bluetooth remote would require a television with Bluetooth as well, adding cost for the user and making a low-cost product harder to achieve. The simple structure of existing remotes could help keep the new remote relatively inexpensive. Bluetooth might be possible, but the Industrial Designer doubted it would fit the budget and suggested Marketing investigate it; personally, the Industrial Designer preferred not to use Bluetooth or radio waves.

Marketing asked whether Bluetooth or a radio receiver could instead be put in a television-side holder connected to the television. The Industrial Designer said that could be attractive but would still leave the infrared function in place and would shift, rather than remove, the problem. The Industrial Designer also proposed exploring a speech-activated remote-finding feature: when someone asked where the remote was, it could beep. The cost of that feature was unknown.

The Industrial Designer recommended a readily available replaceable battery, so users could buy a new one when the old battery stopped working. A button press would close a switch, send current through the circuit, and light a bulb to reassure users that the press registered. The signal would pass through a chip, be processed into electronic signals, and be sent to the infrared bulb for receipt and interpretation by the television. The Industrial Designer favored a simple design without excessive gadgets or functions, infrared transmission without reception, and no television input. In their view, supporting teletext through infrared would require adding a receiver to the remote, increasing components, design work, size, time, and cost. They therefore advised against a receiver and recommended basic functions, possibly using one button for multiple functions or concealing less-used buttons.

### User-interface principles and touch-screen discussion
The User Interface representative said the design should balance appearance, technical feasibility, and ease of use. A remote should look good without compromising usability. Because many functions make a device harder to use, the representative recommended limiting functions or avoiding showing them all at once; a hierarchical structure could help when there were many functions. A touch screen was raised as a possibility, though its feasibility with an infrared-only remote that could not receive signals was uncertain. The representative emphasized clear, simple buttons and pointed out that a crowded remote could make it difficult to find teletext or press the intended button. Play, back, and stop were cited as important controls.

The User Interface representative said the remote should be for television only, with few options and direct-action buttons rather than requiring an initial selection. The Project Manager asked how that recommendation fit with combining multiple functions in one button. The representative said this involved weighing a small number of options against a less original or less multi-purpose design, versus using many buttons. Marketing suggested a touch screen or LCD that kept general functions such as play and channel switching in the center, with menus such as settings at the top or bottom. The User Interface representative asked whether menus should appear on the television or be contained on the remote, and recommended displaying menu choices on the television rather than relying on complicated button combinations or long presses. Marketing cautioned that television menus differ and a remote’s menu might not match the television’s actual menus. The Industrial Designer added that some televisions lack menus or have only simple ones, limiting compatibility.

The User Interface representative recommended large, clear buttons, accepting that some options might be lost in favor of making channel, volume, and teletext controls immediately accessible. Advanced options could be placed elsewhere on the remote, perhaps behind a small cover or on a touch screen. Essential actions such as standby and channel changing should always be available without navigating menus, and users should receive feedback when a button is pressed so they know the remote or television has responded. The representative summarized the principle as keeping the design simple and reducing functionality where necessary so important controls remain accessible.

Marketing supported the touch-screen idea, referring to a television news item about telephones for older people with large touch-screen images for calling and hanging up. Enlarging the displayed images could make the remote more suitable for older users and visually oriented. The User Interface representative suggested keeping primary buttons visible, designing the remote to fit comfortably in the hand, and adding a logo and an attractive form. If a touch screen proved too difficult, a flip-open design could reveal additional options.

The group discussed keeping primary controls permanently accessible while using part of a touch screen for extra functions. The User Interface representative proposed a large touch screen with the same primary controls always available and the lower portion reserved for other functions, comparing the concept to an iPod. The Industrial Designer supported a touch-screen area with a limited set of menus and sub-items, noting it could allow later improvement. The Project Manager asked whether the proposal was for a fully touch-screen remote. Marketing and the Industrial Designer supported that direction, while the User Interface representative stressed that the same essential buttons must always remain accessible and only special options should use the remaining touch-screen area. The Project Manager raised the concern that older users might not be accustomed to touch screens and recommended retaining traditional controls such as teletext and volume, while placing more difficult functions on the screen. Marketing replied that large numbers on an LCD could help; the User Interface representative said touch-screen controls could be displayed to look like actual buttons. The Industrial Designer observed that touching a screen differs from pressing a physical button and said the target audience should guide the choice. The group noted that the intended audience was under 40 and that younger users liked new, fashionable technology; Marketing mentioned that Microsoft had developed a touch-screen concept for multimedia applications.

### Parental controls and television compatibility
Marketing proposed parental control using a PIN code so parents could access all channels while children without the code could not switch to violent channels. The Industrial Designer said feasibility would depend on the television. The Industrial Designer explained that channel assignments differ between televisions: for example, channel 15 may correspond to different content on different sets, so a remote cannot assume a universal channel order. The User Interface representative interpreted the proposal as first matching the remote to the television, then allowing parents to set a password so children could not change television settings such as color or volume. Marketing suggested that a parent could log in, identify a channel as unsuitable, and restrict it to parents. The User Interface representative proposed keeping parental control as a separate menu option. The Project Manager said the idea was useful but should be revisited at a later stage rather than broaden the current discussion.

The Project Manager summarized the discussion as a need to keep the remote simple while allowing additional options to be hidden rather than crowding it with buttons. The group had also considered a single controller for each television, with menus and parental controls handled by the remote rather than by the television. Marketing noted that television menus are not identical, making television-specific menu displays problematic. The User Interface representative suggested synchronizing the remote with the television and exploring whether the remote could identify the television brand and present compatible options. The Project Manager cautioned that the product was intended for an international market. The User Interface representative argued that universal remotes already support many televisions, while the Industrial Designer noted that such remotes must be programmed to match a television and can be troublesome. The Industrial Designer also said that receiving television information would require a receiver in the remote, adding complexity.

The User Interface representative and Marketing discussed existing universal remotes, which can be configured by entering a code found in a manual. The User Interface representative gave an example of finding a Philips model code, pressing a sequence such as 455, and then seeing the available menu options. Marketing suggested storing television types and corresponding options as profiles in the remote’s memory: entering a television identifier, such as 1410, would bring up its profile. The group considered the storage requirement modest; the User Interface representative said universal-remote manuals could list three or four hundred televisions at most, including old and new models. Marketing warned that a newly purchased television might not be included in the remote’s profiles, requiring a new remote or an update.

### Firmware updates and service options
The group considered ways to update remote-control firmware when a new television was not already supported. Marketing proposed a USB or FireWire connection so the remote could connect to a PC and download new firmware from the internet. The Industrial Designer noted that not everyone had a PC at home. The User Interface representative and Marketing suggested taking the remote to a shop or service center for an update. The Industrial Designer also proposed using the television-side holder as a possible connection point to a telephone line or internet connection, but recognized that this would return to the issue of adding a receiver and cost. Marketing considered updates at a service center or shop the cheapest approach and suggested a docking station where the remote could be placed and updated by pressing start. The Industrial Designer agreed this seemed best; Marketing noted that people do not buy a television every week.

### Presentation close, break, and follow-up
The Project Manager said the minutes from the second meeting had been completed, with four management-board points added as reminders, along with summaries of what participants had said and their individual views. The Project Manager identified the meeting’s central design issue as keeping the remote simple while allowing further options to be hidden, and noted the discussion about making remote-controlled functions, including menus and parental controls, work across televisions. The Project Manager said there were five minutes remaining during the later discussion.

The Project Manager then said the session was nearly over and announced a lunch break, followed by 30 minutes of individual work. The Project Manager would update the minutes in the shared folder and said instructions for the next meeting would arrive by email; participants should wait for the email and complete the work during the 30 minutes. When asked when to return, the Project Manager initially stated a 30-minute break. The User Interface representative suggested a quarter to one; Marketing thought the break might be 45 minutes. The Project Manager said that would mean returning at one o’clock and suggested checking with the personal coach. The group agreed on the timing. The Project Manager thanked everyone and called it a good session. Participants briefly discussed saving the material to shared documents; the Project Manager said the files were stored in SmartBoard XDK, and others suggested saving or exporting an image, including as JPEG. {"mom":"### Meeting purpose and agenda
The Project Manager opened the conceptual design meeting for Real Reaction, saying it followed the same format as the previous meeting. The group would hear three presentations and reach decisions on remote-control component and user-interface concepts. The Project Manager would take notes and place the minutes in the shared folder. At the end, the Project Manager also planned to share information from a master class attended during lunch.

### Component research and user groups
The Industrial Designer, Janus, presented a review of products used by two age groups: people below 45 and those above 45. He said older users preferred traditional materials such as wood and chrome, straightforward shapes, and luxurious styles. Younger, more dynamic users preferred soft materials, bright colours, rounded and curved shapes, and products associated with sports and gaming. He used the Teletubbies as an example of a soft, colourful aesthetic.

### Power source
Janus compared battery power with kinetic power, explaining that kinetic energy is generated by movement and could recharge the remote when picked up. He considered solar power too, but said solar panels would need light, preferably sunlight, and would occupy space otherwise available for the interface; ordinary light would provide less energy than a battery. He preferred kinetic power as a higher-tech option whose costs were not much greater than a normal battery. The Project Manager questioned whether ordinary remote-control movement would provide enough energy. Janus said picking up and using the remote should generate enough, and it could be shaken if needed. The group discussed combining a battery with kinetic charging. The User Interface representative and Marketing supported a combination, and the Project Manager also preferred both. Janus noted that this would add some cost; the discussion included a fifty-cent amount, though the exact point being priced was unclear.

### Case shape and material
Janus said a standard square case seemed boring and proposed either a single curve or a double curve. He described the double-curved design as adding dimensions and giving the remote a younger, more dynamic, high-tech appearance. Marketing asked for a drawing, and Janus sketched examples, explaining that a less standard shape could leave more room for creativity. On materials, Janus preferred rubber over plastic because rubber felt soft, while he associated plastic with a cheap feel. Marketing and the Project Manager agreed with rubber. The User Interface representative supported rubber provided the case remained firm rather than bendable; Janus said the chip set and LCD screen would hold it firm. The group also discussed whether a touch screen had to be square. Marketing observed that screens are generally square and that the surrounding case could shape the appearance, but could not cover part of the LCD. Janus agreed that a case designed around it could resolve that issue.

### Buttons, screen, and chip set
Janus said the team had previously discussed traditional buttons versus a touch screen and proposed retaining the LCD screen. Traditional buttons could use a simple chip set, whereas an LCD screen would require an advanced chip set and bring additional costs. He said the team should keep budget feasibility in mind and revert to simple buttons if the advanced option proved unaffordable. Marketing expected sales of ten million units and suggested that a large company in Korea or Taiwan, such as Samsung, might offer a substantial chip discount; Marketing added that chips were usually no more than one dollar. Janus agreed that cost might not be a major issue. In the later discussion, the group indicated agreement with the LCD/touch-screen direction and the advanced chip set if using the LCD.

### Marketing research and target audience
Marketing reported that the team’s research and development department had travelled to Paris and Milan the previous week for trend-watching. They asked people of different ages and income levels about design, materials, and how much they would spend. Marketing said the primary audience was people below 40, who preferred fresh, basic fruit-inspired colours, including green, strawberry red, and banana yellow, and spongy or soft materials. The secondary audience, people above 40, preferred dark, traditional colours and materials such as wood. The Project Manager questioned whether wood was suitable for constructing a remote; the discussion clarified the suggestion as a wood-like case or finish rather than necessarily solid wood. Marketing said the group had decided to target people below 40, so the older audience’s preferences would not apply. Marketing’s overall design recommendations were a fancy, technological, innovative, easy-to-use remote, with fresh colours for the main audience.

### Customisation and additional features
Marketing proposed removable covers, like those in the mobile-phone market, so customers could customise the remote’s colour—for example, replacing a red cover with a green one. Marketing also endorsed rubber as a material aligned with current trends and said it could improve safety if the remote were dropped. Based on the Paris and Milan research, Marketing recommended relatively hard rubber, like that used on ordinary mobile phones. The team also discussed speech recognition and games. Marketing said speech recognition was innovative and that the market was interested in new technologies, but warned that it could be very expensive. The Project Manager and User Interface representative raised concerns that voice commands could be triggered by loud television sounds. Marketing proposed games such as Snake or Tetris for younger users and connected the idea to mobile phones; the group noted that games could be useful during a boring programme or while at college. The Project Manager concluded that games should be included but voice recognition should not.

### User-interface proposal
The User Interface representative presented a simple PowerPoint mock-up, intended to be developed into a more dynamic drawing. The proposal used one large touch screen, with primary buttons kept clearly visible. The menu structure would be changeable: pressing a system option could display multiple choices, potentially five or ten, and other options could appear when needed. The representative described a one-hand grip, with the middle narrow enough to sit in the hand but the remote somewhat broader because thumb-only use would be difficult. The proposed layout placed the main buttons within thumb reach and the menu structure for the other hand, with program buttons, volume and program controls, and a large LCD menu area. The User Interface representative stressed avoiding too many functions at once, keeping menus simple, limiting levels, and making settings such as television brightness or colour accessible without navigating through multiple screens or repeated presses. Less-used functions such as teletext could be placed in the menu. Marketing suggested a back-and-forth button like the one in Internet Explorer for switching between two channels; the User Interface representative agreed it could be useful but preferred placing it in the menu structure.

### Parental control
The Project Manager said parental control was a worthwhile feature, given concerns that children might watch sex or violence on television. Marketing described a parent-and-child login concept, while the User Interface representative cautioned that the process needed to be fast and simple rather than making users wait 20 seconds or remember complicated settings. The discussion considered profiles and simple parent/child selection, as well as restricting certain channels or programmes and applying time limits, including blocking channels after 10 o’clock. The Industrial Designer warned that profile functionality could require considerable programming resources and time. The Project Manager argued that there was a large market for parental controls and that many people under 40 had young children. The User Interface representative suggested making profiles an optional menu feature so the basic remote remained simple; Marketing agreed it should be plain when sold, with users able to install the feature themselves. The group debated whether the control could be implemented through the remote alone, since children could still use the television’s own controls. They considered channel restrictions, a clock in the remote to stop transmissions after a set time, and programme-rating or guide data, but noted that maintaining programme information could be difficult. The Industrial Designer suggested a separate receiver device or separate basic and deluxe remote models, but the Project Manager opposed an optional separate device and favoured incorporating the feature as profiles in the remote. The User Interface representative recommended making parental control a menu option that could be selected at purchase, with a password or similar setup. The Project Manager’s closing summary was that parental control would be incorporated but must not be too complex.

### Decisions and consensus
The Project Manager summarised the decisions: the remote would combine a battery with kinetic charging; have a double-curved rubber case in a bright, fruity colour with a removable cover; and use a touch screen. The remote should not have too many buttons, and its menu should be easy to use with few levels. Parental control would be included without excessive complexity, and games would be included; voice recognition would not. The participants indicated consensus.

### View modes and user customisation
After the summary, Marketing suggested offering an expert view and a simple view. The User Interface representative described a simple menu by default, with a full list of programmable options appearing when users entered system properties. The Industrial Designer suggested allowing advanced users to configure the remote themselves, choosing which buttons to include, such as a back-and-forward button or controls for only two channels. The group agreed to carry the idea forward for a later meeting.

### Master-class input and branding
The Project Manager shared two points from a master class: knowledge management and knowledge sharing, including learning from other companies, were currently important; and a survey indicated that customers preferred buying from one large provider rather than from organisations partnering with it. The Project Manager said Real Reaction should therefore present itself as a large, trustworthy company. Marketing proposed the product name “R to the third power” or “R3,” expanded as “Real Reaction Remote.” The Project Manager suggested a unified Real Reaction brand and a short startup animation or logo, with the motto “We put fashion in electronics.” The User Interface representative said a logo could be remembered even if shown for 0.5 seconds, while the Industrial Designer suggested a small logo on the LCD. The group preferred a small, unobtrusive icon rather than a continually spinning animation, which the User Interface representative called annoying.

### Next steps and close
The Project Manager said the next meeting would begin in 30 minutes. A subsequent session would have the Industrial Designer and User Interface representative work together on a prototype drawn on the SMARTboard; the Marketing representative would work on product evaluation. Specific instructions would be sent by email. The Project Manager thanked the group and said the meeting had been productive. The participants exchanged thanks and farewells."}

{"summary":"The team met to develop Real Reaction remote-control concepts through three presentations and decide on component and user-interface directions. The Project Manager said the minutes would go in the shared folder. The Industrial Designer, Janus (also addressed as Jans), compared age-group preferences: people below 45 favored soft, colourful, rounded designs, while older users favored traditional materials such as wood and chrome, straightforward shapes, and luxurious styles. Marketing reported that its research team visited Paris and Milan the previous week and found that the main audience, people below 40, preferred fresh fruit-like colours and soft materials; the team chose to target that audience. The hardware concept combines a battery with kinetic charging, a double-curved rubber case with a removable, flashy fruit-coloured cover, and a touchscreen. The Industrial Designer said an LCD would require an advanced chipset, while conventional buttons could use a simpler chipset; Marketing estimated sales of ten million units and suggested a possible chip discount from a large manufacturer such as Samsung. The interface should keep primary controls visible, limit the number of functions shown at once, and use clear, shallow menus; a back-and-forth channel button could be placed in the menu. An expert view or user-programmable controls for advanced users were also discussed for consideration at a later meeting. The team agreed to include games, omit voice recognition, and include parental control without making the remote too complex. Discussion considered simple parent/child profiles, passwords, restrictions by channel or time (including after 10 o’clock), and the difficulty of preventing children from using the television’s own controls. Marketing proposed removable covers for personalisation and branding the product as R3 (“Real Reaction Remote”). The Project Manager shared master-class points on knowledge sharing, learning from other companies, benchmarking, and presenting Real Reaction as a single, large, trustworthy provider. The Project Manager said the next meeting would start in 30 minutes. For the next session, Industrial Design and User Interface will work together on a prototype drawn on the SMARTboard; Marketing will handle product evaluation. The Project Manager said specific instructions would be sent by email.","mom":"### Meeting purpose and agenda
The Project Manager opened the conceptual design meeting for Real Reaction, saying it followed the same format as the previous meeting. The group would hear three presentations and reach decisions on remote-control component and user-interface concepts. The Project Manager would take notes and place the minutes in the shared folder. At the end, the Project Manager also planned to share information from a master class attended during lunch.

### Component research and user groups
The Industrial Designer, Janus (addressed as Jans), presented a review of products used by two age groups: people below 45 and those above 45. He said older users preferred traditional materials such as wood and chrome, straightforward shapes, and luxurious styles. Younger, more dynamic users preferred soft materials, bright colours, rounded and curved shapes, and products associated with sports and gaming. He used the Teletubbies as an example of a soft, colourful aesthetic.

### Power source
Janus compared battery power with kinetic power, explaining that kinetic energy is generated by movement and could recharge the remote when picked up. He considered solar power too, but said solar panels would need light, preferably sunlight, and would occupy space otherwise available for the interface; ordinary light would provide less energy than a battery. He preferred kinetic power as a higher-tech option whose costs were not much greater than a normal battery. The Project Manager questioned whether ordinary remote-control movement would provide enough energy. Janus said picking up and using the remote should generate enough, and it could be shaken if needed. The group discussed combining a battery with kinetic charging. The User Interface representative and Marketing supported a combination, and the Project Manager also preferred both. Janus noted that this would add some cost; the discussion included a fifty-cent amount, though the exact point being priced was unclear.

### Case shape and material
Janus said a standard square case seemed boring and proposed either a single curve or a double curve. He described the double-curved design as adding dimensions and giving the remote a younger, more dynamic, high-tech appearance. Marketing asked for a drawing, and Janus sketched examples, explaining that a less standard shape could leave more room for creativity. On materials, Janus preferred rubber over plastic because rubber felt soft, while he associated plastic with a cheap feel. Marketing and the Project Manager agreed with rubber. The User Interface representative supported rubber provided the case remained firm rather than bendable; Janus said the chipset and LCD screen would hold it firm. The group also discussed whether a touchscreen had to be square. Marketing observed that screens are generally square and that the surrounding case could shape the appearance, but could not cover part of the LCD. Janus agreed that a case designed around it could resolve that issue.

### Buttons, screen, and chipset
Janus said the team had previously discussed traditional buttons versus a touchscreen and proposed retaining the LCD screen. Traditional buttons could use a simple chipset, whereas an LCD screen would require an advanced chipset and bring additional costs. He said the team should keep budget feasibility in mind and revert to simple buttons if the advanced option proved unaffordable. Marketing expected sales of ten million units and suggested that a large company in Korea or Taiwan, such as Samsung, might offer a substantial chip discount; Marketing added that chips were usually no more than one dollar. Janus agreed that cost might not be a major issue. In the later discussion, the group indicated agreement with the LCD/touchscreen direction and the advanced chipset if using the LCD.

### Marketing research and target audience
Marketing reported that the team’s research and development department had travelled to Paris and Milan the previous week for trend-watching. They asked people of different ages and income levels about design, materials, and how much they would spend. Marketing said the primary audience was people below 40, who preferred fresh, basic fruit-inspired colours, including green, strawberry red, and banana yellow, and spongy or soft materials. The secondary audience, people above 40, preferred dark, traditional colours and materials such as wood. The Project Manager questioned whether wood was suitable for constructing a remote; the discussion clarified the suggestion as a wood-like case or finish rather than necessarily solid wood. Marketing said the group had decided to target people below 40, so the older audience’s preferences would not apply. Marketing’s overall design recommendations were a fancy, technological, innovative, easy-to-use remote, with fresh colours for the main audience.

### Customisation and additional features
Marketing proposed removable covers, like those in the mobile-phone market, so customers could customise the remote’s colour—for example, replacing a red cover with a green one. Marketing also endorsed rubber as a material aligned with current trends and said it could improve safety if the remote were dropped. Based on the Paris and Milan research, Marketing recommended relatively hard rubber, like that used on ordinary mobile phones. The team also discussed speech recognition and games. Marketing said speech recognition was innovative and that the market was interested in new technologies, but warned that it could be very expensive. The Project Manager and User Interface representative raised concerns that voice commands could be triggered by loud television sounds. Marketing proposed games such as Snake or Tetris for younger users and connected the idea to mobile phones; the group noted that games could be useful during a boring programme or while at college. The Project Manager concluded that games should be included but voice recognition should not.

### User-interface proposal
The User Interface representative presented a simple PowerPoint mock-up, intended to be developed into a more dynamic drawing. The proposal used one large touchscreen, with primary buttons kept clearly visible. The menu structure would be changeable: pressing a system option could display multiple choices, potentially five or ten, and other options could appear when needed. The representative described a one-hand grip, with the middle narrow enough to sit in the hand but the remote somewhat broader because thumb-only use would be difficult. The proposed layout placed the main buttons within thumb reach and the menu structure for the other hand, with program buttons, volume and program controls, and a large LCD menu area. The User Interface representative stressed avoiding too many functions at once, keeping menus simple, limiting levels, and making settings such as television brightness or colour accessible without navigating through multiple screens or repeated presses. Less-used functions such as teletext could be placed in the menu. Marketing suggested a back-and-forth button like the one in Internet Explorer for switching between two channels; the User Interface representative agreed it could be useful but preferred placing it in the menu structure.

### Parental control
The Project Manager said parental control was a worthwhile feature, given concerns that children might watch sex or violence on television. Marketing described a parent-and-child login concept, while the User Interface representative cautioned that the process needed to be fast and simple rather than making users wait 20 seconds or remember complicated settings. The discussion considered profiles and simple parent/child selection, as well as restricting certain channels or programmes and applying time limits, including blocking channels after 10 o’clock. The Industrial Designer warned that profile functionality could require considerable programming resources and time. The Project Manager argued that there was a large market for parental controls and that many people under 40 had young children. The User Interface representative suggested making profiles an optional menu feature so the basic remote remained simple; Marketing agreed it should be plain when sold, with users able to install the feature themselves. The group debated whether the control could be implemented through the remote alone, since children could still use the television’s own controls. They considered channel restrictions, a clock in the remote to stop transmissions after a set time, and programme-rating or guide data, but noted that maintaining programme information could be difficult. The Industrial Designer suggested a separate receiver device or separate basic and deluxe remote models, but the Project Manager opposed an optional separate device and favoured incorporating the feature as profiles in the remote. The User Interface representative recommended making parental control a menu option that could be selected at purchase, with a password or similar setup. The Project Manager’s closing summary was that parental control would be incorporated but must not be too complex.

### Decisions and consensus
The Project Manager summarised the decisions: the remote would combine a battery with kinetic charging; have a double-curved rubber case in a bright, fruity colour with a removable cover; and use a touchscreen. The remote should not have too many buttons, and its menu should be easy to use with few levels. Parental control would be included without excessive complexity, and games would be included; voice recognition would not. The participants indicated consensus.

### View modes and user customisation
After the summary, Marketing suggested offering an expert view and a simple view. The User Interface representative described a simple menu by default, with a full list of programmable options appearing when users entered system properties. The Industrial Designer suggested allowing advanced users to configure the remote themselves, choosing which buttons to include, such as a back-and-forward button or controls for only two channels. The Project Manager said the group would take the idea to another meeting.

### Master-class input and branding
The Project Manager shared two points from a master class: knowledge management and knowledge sharing, including learning from other companies and benchmarking, were currently important; and a survey indicated that customers preferred buying from one large provider rather than from organisations partnering with it. The Project Manager said Real Reaction should therefore present itself as a large, trustworthy company. Marketing proposed the product name “R to the third power” or “R3,” expanded as “Real Reaction Remote.” The Project Manager suggested a unified Real Reaction brand and a short startup animation or logo, with the motto “We put fashion in electronics.” The User Interface representative said a logo could be remembered even if shown for 0.5 seconds, while the Industrial Designer suggested a small logo on the LCD. The group preferred a small, unobtrusive icon rather than a continually spinning animation, which the User Interface representative called annoying. Marketing asked who had given the master class; the Project Manager identified Franz Mehler.

### Next steps and close
The Project Manager said the next meeting would begin in 30 minutes. A subsequent session would have the Industrial Designer and User Interface representative work together on a prototype drawn on the SMARTboard; the Marketing representative would work on product evaluation. Specific instructions would be sent by email. The Project Manager thanked the group and said the meeting had been productive. {"mom":"### Meeting agenda and prototype presentation
The Project Manager said they would take the minutes and had no presentation of their own. The agenda was a prototype presentation by G_ and G_, followed by evaluation criteria, work on a finance Excel file that had to be completed later, a check that costs stayed below €12.50, an evaluation of the process using the SMARTboard and laptops, and a closing. The Project Manager said they had 40 minutes and handed the presentation to G_ and G_; the group clarified that the presenters were J_ and J_.

### Prototype concept and form
The User Interface presenter described the first concept as a single-touchscreen remote. The team had worked out how to hold it and where to place buttons, aiming for a shape that could be comfortably held in one hand by left- or right-handed users. They had made it thinner and said the form also had an artistic meaning. Buttons on top would be reachable with the thumb, while the menu structure could be accessed with the other hand; the remote should also be accessible using that hand. The Industrial Designer described a basic remote with an LCD screen, main buttons that could later be changed in a personal profile, a standard delivered button setup, and a more advanced menu with submenus. The team showed front and back views and explained that two raised areas were intended to give the design a youthful, dynamic and artistic effect, balance it so it would lie flat on a table without rolling, and make it sit in the hand like an old telephone. Rubber layers would cover the straight screen panel so the exterior looked more fluid and rounded. The raised areas could house electronics and help make the design thinner. The User Interface presenter said the maximum thickness for holding it was 1.5 centimetres, leaving room for a battery and other electronic chips; the touchscreen layer and wires could be kept thin in the middle to improve grip.

### Appearance, colours and removable covers
The Industrial Designer said the raised form was intended to look youthful and dynamic, while the team wanted an adult version rather than a children’s remote like the Weemote. The team initially considered white or metallic grey as technological colours. The User Interface presenter proposed exchangeable covers so younger buyers could choose orange, red, blue or purple, while older buyers could select a more appealing white remote. Marketing suggested offering the remote without a cover so customers could choose one in the shop; the User Interface presenter replied that a cheap standard cover, perhaps white, was necessary to cover the LCD screen, with additional covers available for extra revenue. The Project Manager emphasized that the target was younger people and referred to survey results from Milan and Paris indicating that older people were more willing to spend on extra features. The Project Manager therefore suggested making flashy, fruity colours standard and more sophisticated, traditional or luxury options extras; the Industrial Designer agreed that this sounded logical. Marketing proposed a wood-style cover for older users. The group discussed a wood-style colour, white and a couple of hip fruity colours, with a restrained fruity colour as the standard rather than very bright orange, purple or yellow. The Project Manager said standard colours should be attractive and flashy but not too much.

### Group evaluation of the prototype
Marketing explained that the prototype would be evaluated against the previously established user requirements and trend analysis using a seven-point scale, with decisions made by group consensus. The group evaluated multiple statements, including whether the remote was designed for people under 40, whether it was beautiful or looked fancy, whether its channel-switching buttons were big and clear, whether it was easy to find, whether it had fresh fruity colours and soft material, whether it was easy to use, whether it was innovative, whether it had speech recognition or built-in games, and whether it had parental advisory functionality. For the under-40 statement, the Industrial Designer argued the product was also intended for people over 40; the group settled on 3, describing it as primarily aimed at younger users but also suitable for older people. The group treated the remote as beautiful and fancy, and agreed that the channel buttons were big and clear. They marked the claim that teletext buttons were present as false because teletext was in the menu, while volume buttons were present. The team discussed whether the distinctive shape and colours would make the remote easier to find if misplaced at home. The Industrial Designer suggested 4, between the judgments on the scale, and the group discussed that the unusual shape could help it stand out among other remotes. For fresh colours, the User Interface presenter argued for 2 because they had decided not to use overly flashy colours. They described the material as rubber and somewhat soft, and settled on 3. On ease of use, the group agreed the design could be easier: visible primary buttons helped, but reducing buttons would compromise functionality and the intended look. The Industrial Designer and Project Manager voted 2. The group judged the remote innovative, but marked speech recognition false. They counted the built-in games as a feature because games were included in a submenu, though the User Interface presenter suggested a lower rating because they were not a full game. The group also discussed the parental advisory function and whether added functions were included in the cost.

### Production-cost calculation and redesign
The Project Manager said the production cost had to be calculated and remain under €12.50; if the cost met that limit, the team could proceed to project evaluation, otherwise they would need a redesign. They entered component estimates, including a battery at 1, kinetic power at 1, solar cells at 0, and an advanced chip at €3. They discussed the sample sensor and speech-recognition component, and whether the casing was flat, single-curved or double-curved. The Project Manager said the total had reached €11 before all entries were complete. The Industrial Designer later said the estimate was €4 over budget. The group considered making the casing single-curved or uncurved, cutting the kinetic feature, and removing other cost items. The Project Manager said kinetic power would bring the total to €13.50 and require a flat design, which would be a compromise. The Industrial Designer said changing from double-curved to single-curved would solve the budget problem. The group also noted that wood was cheaper than rubber and discussed the possibility of using a special wood-style colour as an add-on. They ultimately revised the design and said the costs were within the budget at €12.50. They clarified that the final casing was single-curved, not double-curved, and that the planned energy source was batteries rather than the previously discussed alternatives. The group noted that added functions such as Tetris and Snake were under parental control, and discussed whether parental control had been included in the cost; Marketing said it would be developed in-house, though it would still incur some cost.

### Project-process evaluation and SMARTboard feedback
The Project Manager asked whether there had been room for creativity in group or individual meetings. Marketing said there had not been much room, mainly because the team received fixed information and was expected to work from it, without being able to search the internet independently. The Industrial Designer said Marketing and the User Interface role, including Daniel, had less creative freedom, while the designers had more room for creativity. The group discussed leadership and the first meeting. Marketing said leadership had been poor and that the first meeting was somewhat unstructured; they suggested it could have been structured more clearly, and said they had spoken for most of that meeting. The Project Manager agreed they had also been dissatisfied with the first meeting, but said the later meetings improved and led to good decisions and more consensus. The User Interface presenter said the group worked together but each person had a separate task; the Industrial Designer said the two designers worked well together and had no hard feelings. The group also discussed trouble with the digital pen. They said it was difficult to write and draw accurately, required pressure and took too long; the Project Manager attributed the main issue to needing a SMARTboard masterclass. The User Interface presenter said the idea was good but the pen did not work properly and added little value compared with using a normal pen and scanner. Marketing said they had brought the pen to the first two meetings but did not use it after the first meeting. The group described the SMARTboard as useful overall but the pen as not user-friendly; drawing and writing took a long time and lacked precision, and the eraser was too large for erasing a line neatly.

### Suggestions for improving the collaboration software
The group said the software’s functionality was available but was not ideal and took too much time to use, particularly in short presentations or meetings with many participants. The User Interface presenter said that in a management meeting each person might have only two minutes to make a case, and it would be preferable to prepare material in PowerPoint and use a flip-board for the few things that needed drawing. Marketing proposed a decision or voting application in which participants could select a rating from 1 to 7. The Project Manager suggested combining this with a screen for writing, as a voting mechanism. The Industrial Designer cautioned that voting could reduce discussion and lead people to follow an earlier vote, but agreed that entering scores through an application would make the results easier to process. The group also suggested adding text-entry functions, tools for circles and squares, and the ability to insert pictures or clip art from a scanner. They discussed hyperlinks as another possible way to add material.

### End report, final decisions and close
The Project Manager said an end report was required to record the meetings and decisions, and that they were working on it. Marketing said there were 10 minutes left to finish the report. The Project Manager proposed working on it together and said it was a draft of about 75 pages; the report was not fully finished and was in a read-only version, but Marketing noted it could be saved under another name. The Project Manager summarized that the remote should have the most-used functions immediately visible, be simple and clear to use, and appeal to younger users. Marketing specified channel switching at the top as the most-used function and teletext and volume among the important functions. The group said the buttons would be on top and the menu at the bottom, and that the design would use an LCD touchscreen. They agreed that the conclusion should explain why the design decisions were made, including the flat LCD design and the cost-related changes. The Project Manager said the costs were within budget and the project had been evaluated, but the end report still needed completion. The meeting ended after the Project Manager declared it finished."}

{"summary":"The meeting began with a 40-minute agenda: a prototype presentation by J_ and J_, evaluation criteria, finance work in an Excel file to be completed later, a process evaluation using the SMARTboard and laptops, and closing. The Project Manager set a production-cost limit of €12.50. The prototype team presented a single-touchscreen remote designed to be held in either hand, with thumb-accessible top buttons and a menu intended for the other hand. The LCD screen would have a curved overlay and rubber layers; the remote’s maximum thickness was 1.5 centimetres. Raised bumps were intended to create a youthful, dynamic, artistic appearance, keep the remote from rolling on a table, and allow it to sit in the hand like an old telephone. The designers wanted an adult version rather than a children’s Weemote. They considered white or metallic grey, wood-style covers, and restrained fruity colours, with optional covers as add-ons. The Project Manager favored an attractive, somewhat flashy standard colour and suggested that premium traditional or luxury options could be extras. The group also discussed whether the distinctive shape and colours would make the remote easier to find if lost.

Marketing led a group-consensus evaluation using a seven-point scale against earlier user requirements and trend analysis. The group considered suitability for people below and above 40, appearance, channel and volume buttons, teletext access, visibility and findability, colours, soft material, ease of use, innovation, speech recognition, built-in games, and parental advisory. They agreed on a rating of 3 for the claim that the remote was designed for people under 40, as it primarily targeted younger people while also appealing to older users. They treated the remote as beautiful and fancy, agreed the channel buttons were big and clear, marked teletext buttons as absent because teletext was in the menu, and confirmed volume buttons were present. They discussed a rating of 4 for findability, 2 for fresh fruity colours, and 3 for soft rubber material. The group said ease of use could be improved but settled on 2, noting that reducing buttons would sacrifice functionality and appearance. They judged it innovative, marked speech recognition false, and counted built-in games because games were in a submenu, despite debate about their limited scope. Marketing later reported a mean evaluation score of 1.86, interpreting the requirements as between one and two, or very true.

The group calculated component costs against the €12.50 ceiling. The estimates included zero for a hand dynamo, solar cells, and several unnecessary components; €1 for a battery and kinetic power; and €3 for an advanced chip. The running total reached €11 before the remaining entries, and the Industrial Designer said the estimate was €4 over budget. They discussed dropping kinetic power, changing the double-curved casing to single-curved or flat, and treating wood-style finishes or other features as optional. The Project Manager said kinetic power would bring the total to €13.50 and require a flat design. The group chose a single-curved redesign, which brought the listed cost to €12.50; they proceeded on the assumption that this was the fixed price. The final energy source was batteries. They also discussed parental-control costs: Marketing said it could be developed in-house, though it would still incur some cost.

During the project-process review, Marketing said the first meeting was somewhat unstructured and could have been structured more clearly; the Project Manager agreed they had been dissatisfied with it. The Project Manager said the later two meetings produced good decisions and greater consensus. Participants said Marketing and the User Interface role, including Daniel, had less creative freedom because they relied on supplied information, while the designers had more. They described teamwork as people working together while each had a separate task; the two designers said they worked well together and had no hard feelings. Participants also discussed leadership and trouble using the SMARTboard pen. They found the digital pen slow, imprecise, and not user-friendly; the Project Manager thought a SMARTboard masterclass might address the main issue. Suggestions included normal-pen input, faster software, text entry, shape tools, image insertion, and a voting application. The group noted that voting could reduce discussion but might make scores easier to process.

The Project Manager said an end report covering the meetings and decisions was still being completed. Marketing said there were 10 minutes left to finish it; the Project Manager suggested working on it together and described a draft of about 75 pages. The report was read-only and unfinished, but Marketing said it could be saved under another name. The final review reiterated that the most-used functions should be visible, channel switching should be at the top, and teletext and volume were important; the group said the menu would be at the bottom and the remote would use an LCD touchscreen. They said the conclusion should explain the design decisions, including the flat LCD design and cost-related changes. The Project Manager said the costs were within budget and the project had been evaluated, but the end report still needed completion. The meeting concluded after a final reminder to save before making changes.","mom":"### Meeting agenda and prototype presentation
The Project Manager said they would take the minutes and had no presentation of their own. The agenda was a prototype presentation by G_ and G_, followed by evaluation criteria, work on a finance Excel file that had to be completed later, a check that costs stayed below €12.50, an evaluation of the process using the SMARTboard and laptops, and a closing. The Project Manager said they had 40 minutes and handed the presentation to G_ and G_; the group clarified that the presenters were J_ and J_. The Project Manager said the cost limit was twelve and a half euros and that the group needed to leave time for the calculations.

### Prototype concept and form
The User Interface presenter described the first concept as a single-touchscreen remote. The team had worked out how to hold it and where to place buttons, aiming for a shape that could be comfortably held in one hand by left- or right-handed users. They had made it thinner and said the form also had an artistic meaning. Buttons on top would be reachable with the thumb, while the menu structure could be accessed with the other hand; the remote should also be accessible using that hand. The Industrial Designer described a basic remote with an LCD screen, main buttons that could later be changed in a personal profile, a standard delivered button setup, and a more advanced menu with submenus. The team showed front and back views and explained that two raised areas were intended to give the design a youthful, dynamic and artistic effect, balance it so it would lie flat on a table without rolling, and make it sit in the hand like an old telephone. Rubber layers would cover the straight screen panel so the exterior looked more fluid and rounded. The raised areas could house electronics and help make the design thinner. The User Interface presenter said the maximum thickness for holding it was 1.5 centimetres, leaving room for a battery and other electronic chips; the touchscreen layer and wires could be kept thin in the middle to improve grip.

### Appearance, colours and removable covers
The Industrial Designer said the raised form was intended to look youthful and dynamic, while the team wanted an adult version rather than a children’s remote like the Weemote. The team initially considered white or metallic grey as technological colours. The User Interface presenter proposed exchangeable covers so younger buyers could choose orange, red, blue or purple, while older buyers could select a more appealing white remote. Marketing suggested offering the remote without a cover so customers could choose one in the shop; the User Interface presenter replied that a cheap standard cover, perhaps white, was necessary to cover the LCD screen, with additional covers available for extra revenue. The Project Manager emphasized that the target was younger people and referred to survey results from Milan and Paris indicating that older people were more willing to spend on extra features. The Project Manager therefore suggested making flashy, fruity colours standard and more sophisticated, traditional or luxury options extras; the Industrial Designer agreed that this sounded logical. Marketing proposed a wood-style cover for older users. The group discussed a wood-style colour, white and a couple of hip fruity colours, with a restrained fruity colour as the standard rather than very bright orange, purple or yellow. The Project Manager said standard colours should be attractive and flashy but not too much.

### Group evaluation of the prototype
Marketing explained that the prototype would be evaluated against the previously established user requirements and trend analysis using a seven-point scale, with decisions made by group consensus. The group evaluated multiple statements, including whether the remote was designed for people under 40, whether it was beautiful or looked fancy, whether its channel-switching buttons were big and clear, whether it was easy to find, whether it had fresh fruity colours and soft material, whether it was easy to use, whether it was innovative, whether it had speech recognition or built-in games, and whether it had parental advisory functionality. For the under-40 statement, the Industrial Designer argued the product was also intended for people over 40; the group settled on 3, describing it as primarily aimed at younger users but also suitable for older people. The group treated the remote as beautiful and fancy, and agreed that the channel buttons were big and clear. They marked the claim that teletext buttons were present as false because teletext was in the menu, while volume buttons were present. The team discussed whether the distinctive shape and colours would make the remote easier to find if misplaced at home. The Industrial Designer suggested 4, between the judgments on the scale, and the group discussed that the unusual shape could help it stand out among other remotes. For fresh colours, the User Interface presenter argued for 2 because they had decided not to use overly flashy colours. They described the material as rubber and somewhat soft, and settled on 3. On ease of use, the group agreed the design could be easier: visible primary buttons helped, but reducing buttons would compromise functionality and the intended look. The Industrial Designer and Project Manager voted 2. The group judged the remote innovative, but marked speech recognition false. They counted the built-in games as a feature because games were included in a submenu, though the User Interface presenter suggested a lower rating because they were not a full game. The group also discussed the parental advisory function and whether added functions were included in the cost. Marketing later gave the mean evaluation as 1.86 and explained that the requirements fell between 1 and 2, or were very true.

### Production-cost calculation and redesign
The Project Manager said the production cost had to be calculated and remain under €12.50; if the cost met that limit, the team could proceed to project evaluation, otherwise they would need a redesign. They entered component estimates, including a battery at 1, kinetic power at 1, solar cells at 0, and an advanced chip at €3. They discussed the sample sensor and speech-recognition component, and whether the casing was flat, single-curved or double-curved. The Project Manager said the total had reached €11 before all entries were complete. The Industrial Designer later said the estimate was €4 over budget. The group considered making the casing single-curved or uncurved, cutting the kinetic feature, and removing other cost items. The Project Manager said kinetic power would bring the total to €13.50 and require a flat design, which would be a compromise. The Industrial Designer said changing from double-curved to single-curved would solve the budget problem. The group also noted that wood was cheaper than rubber and discussed the possibility of using a special wood-style colour as an add-on. They ultimately revised the design and said the costs were within the budget at €12.50. They clarified that the final casing was single-curved, not double-curved, and that the planned energy source was batteries rather than the previously discussed alternatives. The group noted that added functions such as Tetris and Snake were under parental control, and discussed whether parental control had been included in the cost; Marketing said it would be developed in-house, though it would still incur some cost.

### Project-process evaluation and SMARTboard feedback
The Project Manager asked whether there had been room for creativity in group or individual meetings. Marketing said there had not been much room, mainly because the team received fixed information and was expected to work from it, without being able to search the internet independently. The Industrial Designer said Marketing and the User Interface role, including Daniel, had less creative freedom, while the designers had more room for creativity. The group discussed leadership and the first meeting. Marketing said leadership had been poor and that the first meeting was somewhat unstructured; they suggested it could have been structured more clearly, and said they had spoken for most of that meeting. The Project Manager agreed they had also been dissatisfied with the first meeting, but said the later meetings improved and led to good decisions and more consensus. The User Interface presenter said the group worked together but each person had a separate task; the Industrial Designer said the two designers worked well together and had no hard feelings. The group also discussed trouble with the digital pen. They said it was difficult to write and draw accurately, required pressure and took too long; the Project Manager attributed the main issue to needing a SMARTboard masterclass. The User Interface presenter said the idea was good but the pen did not work properly and added little value compared with using a normal pen and scanner. Marketing said they had brought the pen to the first two meetings but did not use it after the first meeting. The group described the SMARTboard as useful overall but the pen as not user-friendly; drawing and writing took a long time and lacked precision, and the eraser was too large for erasing a line neatly.

### Suggestions for improving the collaboration software
The group said the software’s functionality was available but was not ideal and took too much time to use, particularly in short presentations or meetings with many participants. The User Interface presenter said that in a management meeting each person might have only two minutes to make a case, and it would be preferable to prepare material in PowerPoint and use a flip-board for the few things that needed drawing. Marketing proposed a decision or voting application in which participants could select a rating from 1 to 7. The Project Manager suggested combining this with a screen for writing, as a voting mechanism. The Industrial Designer cautioned that voting could reduce discussion and lead people to follow an earlier vote, but agreed that entering scores through an application would make the results easier to process. The group also suggested adding text-entry functions, tools for circles and squares, and the ability to insert pictures or clip art from a scanner. They discussed hyperlinks as another possible way to add material.

### End report, final decisions and close
The Project Manager said an end report was required to record the meetings and decisions, and that they were working on it. Marketing said there were 10 minutes left to finish the report. The Project Manager proposed working on it together and said it was a draft of about 75 pages; the report was not fully finished and was in a read-only version, but Marketing noted it could be saved under another name. The Project Manager summarized that the remote should have the most-used functions immediately visible, be simple and clear to use, and appeal to younger users. Marketing specified channel switching at the top as the most-used function and teletext and volume among the important functions. The group said the buttons would be on top and the menu at the bottom, and that the design would use an LCD touchscreen. They agreed that the conclusion should explain why the design decisions were made, including the flat LCD design and the cost-related changes. The Project Manager said the costs were within budget and the project had been evaluated, but the end report still needed completion.
